\delta(s)
=
s-(1-\overline s).
For
s=\sigma+it,
\delta(s)
=
2\sigma-1.
Hence
|\delta(s)|^2
=
(2\sigma-1)^2.
This vanishes exactly on the critical line.
But this observation is purely geometric.

 It says nothing about whether zeros of \xi must satisfy \delta(\rho)=0.

7.13 Weighted Zero Localization Functional
One can define
J(s)
=
|\xi(s)|^2
+
\lambda
\left(
\operatorname{Re}s-\frac12
\right)^2,
\qquad
\lambda>0.
This has a penalty favoring the critical line.
However, such a functional does not prove that off-line zeros cannot exist.
At an off-line zero \rho,
J(\rho)
=
\lambda
\left(
\beta-\frac12
\right)^2
>0,
while a nonzero critical-line point may have larger or smaller value depending on |\xi|.
The penalty was inserted by definition; it was not derived from a theorem forcing the
zero set.

7.14 Nonnegative Energy Functionals

 A common strategy is to construct
\mathcal J[\xi]
\ge0
and attempt to show its minimum occurs precisely when all zeros lie on the critical line.
For this to prove the hypothesis, at least three properties are needed.
Required properties
Exact zero-set equivalence
\mathcal J=0
\iff
\text{all nontrivial zeros lie on }\operatorname{Re}s=\frac12.
Independent nonnegativity proof
\mathcal J\ge0
without assuming the hypothesis.
Well-defined convergence
All sums, products, and integrals used to define \mathcal J must converge or be
rigorously regularized.
A functional lacking any one of these is not yet an equivalent criterion.

7.15 Trivial Nonnegative Functionals
For example,
\mathcal J_0
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
with positive weights w(\rho), would satisfy
\mathcal J_0=0

 if and only if all zeros lie on the critical line—assuming the sum converges and includes
all zeros.
But evaluating or proving vanishing of this functional is exactly as hard as proving the
hypothesis. It merely restates the claim.
Proposition 7.9 — Equivalent reformulation is not automatically progress
Writing the Riemann Hypothesis as the vanishing of a nonnegative sum does not prove
it unless the vanishing is established independently.
Proof
The equivalence changes notation but not logical difficulty. ∎

7.16 Hadamard Product
The completed function is an entire function of order one and admits a canonical
product representation. In an appropriate normalization,
\xi(s)
=
\xi(0)
\prod_\rho
\left(
1-\frac{s}{\rho}
\right)
when zeros are paired or the product is interpreted in its canonical form.
More carefully, a genus-one product may be written with exponential factors,
\xi(s)
=
e^{A+Bs}
\prod_\rho
\left(
1-\frac{s}{\rho}

 \right)
e^{s/\rho}.
The exact presentation depends on how symmetric pairing is handled.

7.17 Logarithmic Derivative
Away from zeros,
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}
can be expressed as a sum over zeros.
Formally,
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}
=
B
+
\sum_\rho
\left(
\frac{1}{s-\rho}
+
\frac{1}{\rho}
\right).
With symmetric regularization, simplified versions are available.
This identity connects the analytic behavior of \xi to the geometry of its zero set.

7.18 Logarithmic Potential
Define
U(s)
=
-\log|\xi(s)|
away from zeros.

 Near a simple zero \rho,
\xi(s)
=
\xi'(\rho)(s-\rho)
+
O((s-\rho)^2),
so
U(s)
=
-\log|s-\rho|
-\log|\xi'(\rho)|
+
o(1).
Thus zeros behave like logarithmic singularities of the potential.

7.19 Laplacian of the Logarithmic Potential
In two real dimensions, the distributional identity
\Delta\log|s-\rho|
=
2\pi\delta_\rho
holds.
Therefore, formally,
\Delta\log|\xi(s)|
=
2\pi
\sum_\rho
m_\rho\delta_\rho
away from contributions of nonzero analytic prefactors.

 Here m_\rho is the zero multiplicity.
This identifies the zeros as point sources in logarithmic-potential language.
It does not constrain those sources to the critical line.

7.20 Functional Symmetry of the Potential
Because
|\xi(s)|
=
|\xi(1-\overline s)|,
the potential satisfies
U(s)
=
U(1-\overline s).
Therefore U is mirror symmetric about the critical line.
Again, mirror symmetry permits paired off-line singularities.

7.21 Transverse Coordinate
Write
s
=
\frac12+x+it,
where x measures horizontal displacement from the critical line.
The functional symmetry gives
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
=
\overline{

 \xi\!\left(\frac12-x+it\right)
}.
Therefore
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
\right|
=
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12-x+it\right)
\right|.
Thus
U(x,t)=U(-x,t).

7.22 First Transverse Derivative
If U is differentiable at x=0, then evenness implies
\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}(0,t)=0.
Proposition 7.10 — Critical line is a stationary symmetry line
At points where \xi(1/2+it)\neq0, the transverse derivative of
\log|\xi|
vanishes on the critical line.
Proof
An even differentiable function has zero first derivative at the origin. ∎
This stationarity is automatic from symmetry and does not indicate that the line is a
minimum.

7.23 Transverse Second Derivative

 For a nonvanishing analytic function f, \log|f| is harmonic:
\Delta\log|f|=0.
With coordinates x,t,
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\log|\xi|
+
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}\log|\xi|
=
0
away from zeros.
Therefore on the critical line,
\partial_x^2\log|\xi|
=
-\partial_t^2\log|\xi|.
The sign of the transverse curvature is not fixed globally.

Proposition 7.11 — Symmetry does not imply transverse minimality
An even function can have a minimum, maximum, or higher-order saddle at the origin.
Proof by examples
f(x)=x^2
has a minimum,
f(x)=-x^2
has a maximum,
and
f(x)=x^4
has a flat minimum.

 All are even. ∎
Thus a zero transverse first derivative on the critical line proves no confinement.

7.24 Transverse Hessian of |\xi|^2
Define
F(x,t)
=
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
\right|^2.
Then
F(x,t)=F(-x,t).
At x=0,
F_x=0.
The second derivative is
F_{xx}
=
2|\xi_x|^2
+
2\operatorname{Re}
\left(
\overline\xi\,\xi_{xx}
\right).
At a critical-line zero \rho=1/2+i\gamma, where \xi(\rho)=0,
F_{xx}(0,\gamma)
=
2|\xi'(\rho)|^2

 for a simple zero, after identifying \partial_x with complex differentiation along the real
direction.
Hence a simple critical-line zero is locally quadratic in the transverse direction.

7.25 Local Shape Near a Simple Zero
Let \rho be a simple zero.
Then
\xi(s)
=
\xi'(\rho)(s-\rho)
+
O(|s-\rho|^2).
Therefore
|\xi(s)|^2
=
|\xi'(\rho)|^2|s-\rho|^2
+
O(|s-\rho|^3).
Theorem 7.12 — Local isotropic leading order
To leading order, the squared modulus near a simple zero is radially symmetric in the
complex plane.
Proof
The leading term depends only on
|s-\rho|^2.
∎
Therefore local Hessian positivity of |\xi|^2 at a zero does not distinguish whether the
zero is on or off the critical line. Every simple zero is locally a strict minimum of |\xi|^2.

 7.26 Failure of Local-Minimum Arguments
Corollary 7.13
The fact that
|\xi(s)|^2\ge0
and vanishes at a zero does not favor critical-line zeros over off-line zeros.
Proof
Every zero, wherever located, is a global minimum of the nonnegative function |\xi|^2,
with minimum value zero. ∎
A local or global minimization of |\xi|^2 finds zeros, not their required real part.

7.27 Symmetric Off-Line Pair Potential
Suppose an off-line pair at fixed height is
\rho_\pm
=
\frac12\pm a+i\gamma,
\qquad
a>0.
Consider the factor
P(s)
=
(s-\rho_+)(s-\rho_-).
On the horizontal line t=\gamma, write
s=\frac12+x+i\gamma.
Then

 P(s)
=
(x-a)(x+a)
=
x^2-a^2.
Therefore
|P(s)|^2
=
(x^2-a^2)^2.
At the symmetry axis x=0,
|P|^2=a^4,
while the zeros occur at x=\pm a.

Proposition 7.14 — A symmetric off-line pair can make the critical line a local
maximum
For
f(x)=(x^2-a^2)^2,
f''(0)=-4a^2<0.
Proof
f'(x)=4x(x^2-a^2),
f''(x)=12x^2-4a^2.
At x=0, the result follows. ∎
Thus symmetric off-line zeros naturally produce a ridge, not a valley, on the critical line
at the same height.
This illustrates why transverse curvature information could be relevant—but proving a
global sign condition strong enough to exclude every off-line pair is the hard part.

 7.28 Quartet Factor
For an off-line quartet,
\rho=\frac12+a+i\gamma,
1-\overline\rho=\frac12-a+i\gamma,
and their conjugates, define
Q(s)
=
\prod_{\omega\in\{\rho,1-\overline\rho,\overline\rho,1-\rho\}}
(s-\omega).
On the critical line,
s=\frac12+it.
Then the quartet contribution is real and nonnegative after suitable pairing:
Q\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\left[
a^2+(t-\gamma)^2
\right]
\left[
a^2+(t+\gamma)^2
\right].
This factor does not vanish for real t when a\neq0.
An off-line quartet therefore modifies the magnitude of \xi on the critical line without
creating a critical-line zero at the same height.

7.29 Can Off-Line Quartets Cancel?
Products do not “cancel” zeros in the ordinary sense.

 If \rho is a zero of an entire function, multiplying by other nonzero factors does not
remove it.
Only a pole at the same point could cancel a zero, but \xi is entire and its canonical
product has no such poles.
Theorem 7.15 — Distinct zeros cannot cancel in an entire product
A zero at \rho remains a zero regardless of the presence of other zeros at symmetric
locations.
Proof
Factor locally:
\xi(s)
=
(s-\rho)^m g(s),
where g(\rho)\neq0.
Other distinct zeros contribute factors nonzero at \rho. Therefore the multiplicity m
remains. ∎
The phrase “phase cancellation between symmetric zero pairs” must not be used as
though zeros could annihilate one another algebraically.

7.30 Cancellation of Contributions to Derived Quantities
Symmetric zeros can cancel in certain sums.
For example, terms odd under
\rho\mapsto1-\overline\rho
may cancel when summed over a symmetric quartet.
But cancellation in a derived statistic does not remove the zeros themselves.

 A valid proof must identify the exact statistic, prove convergence, and show why
vanishing of that statistic excludes—not merely hides—off-line zeros.

7.31 A Symmetric Sum That Always Vanishes
Consider
S
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)
w(\rho),
with weights symmetric under reflection:
w(\rho)=w(1-\overline\rho).
Each off-line pair contributes
a\,w+(-a)\,w=0.
Proposition 7.16 — Vanishing first moment does not imply the hypothesis
A symmetric zero set automatically has zero centered first moment, even if off-line zeros
exist.
Proof
Reflection pairs cancel term by term. ∎
A useful criterion must involve an even, nonnegative measure such as squared
displacement, not a signed first moment.

7.32 Second Moment
Define formally

 M_2
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
\qquad
w(\rho)>0.
Then every term is nonnegative.
If the sum converges and includes every nontrivial zero,
M_2=0
if and only if the Riemann Hypothesis holds.
Theorem 7.17 — Weighted-square equivalence
Under convergence and strictly positive weights,
M_2=0
\iff
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12
for every included zero.
Proof
A sum of nonnegative terms is zero if and only if every term is zero. ∎
This is a valid equivalent formulation, but proving M_2=0 remains the full problem.

7.33 Truncated Numerical Second Moment
Let
M_2(T)
=
\sum_{|\operatorname{Im}\rho|\le T}

 \left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2.
If all numerically verified zeros up to height T lie on the critical line, then
M_2(T)=0
within numerical precision.
This establishes only a finite-height verification.
It says nothing directly about zeros above T.

7.34 Finite Verification Boundary
Proposition 7.18 — No finite computation proves the universal claim
Verifying that the first N zeros lie on the critical line does not prove that every zero does.
Proof
A universal statement over an infinite set cannot be deduced solely from finitely many
checked instances without an additional theorem reducing the infinite case to those
instances. ∎
Numerical verification is valuable evidence and a consistency check, but not a complete
proof.

7.35 Argument Principle
For a meromorphic function f with no zeros or poles on a closed contour C,
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\oint_C
\frac{f'(s)}{f(s)}\,ds
=
N_Z-N_P,

 where zeros and poles are counted with multiplicity inside C.
For \xi, which is entire,
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\oint_C
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}\,ds
=
N_Z.
This allows rigorous zero counting in finite regions if the contour integral is controlled.

7.36 Zero Counting Does Not Localize Horizontally
The argument principle counts total zeros inside a region.
To prove the hypothesis, one must compare:
the number of zeros in the full critical strip up to height T;
the number of zeros found on the critical line up to height T.
If these counts agree for all T, the hypothesis follows.
Finite verification proves equality only up to a finite height.

7.37 Hardy’s Z-Function
Define
Z(t)
=
e^{i\vartheta(t)}
\zeta\!\left(\frac12+it\right),
with \vartheta(t) chosen so that Z(t) is real for real t.
Zeros of Z(t) correspond to zeros of \zeta on the critical line.
Sign changes of Z(t) locate odd-multiplicity critical-line zeros.

 This is a genuine line-restricted tool, unlike the identically vanishing symmetry defect.

7.38 Limitation of the Z-Function
Finding many zeros of Z(t) proves many critical-line zeros exist.
It does not exclude additional off-line zeros unless combined with a total zero count.
Therefore a complete finite-height verification requires both:
locating all critical-line zeros up to T;
proving the total number of strip zeros up to T is the same.
7.39 Riemann–von Mangoldt Counting Formula
The number N(T) of nontrivial zeros with imaginary part between 0 and T, counted with
multiplicity, satisfies
N(T)
=
\frac{T}{2\pi}
\log\left(\frac{T}{2\pi}\right)
\frac{T}{2\pi}
+
O(\log T).
More precise versions include an argument term involving \zeta.
This formula counts zeros but does not prove their real parts.

7.40 Equivalent Criteria
The Riemann Hypothesis has many genuine equivalent formulations.
Examples include statements involving:
bounds on summatory arithmetic functions;

 positivity conditions;
zero-free regions;
the Li coefficients;
spectral interpretations, if fully established;
growth bounds for \zeta or related functions.
An equivalent criterion is useful only when its truth can be established by methods not
already assuming the hypothesis.

7.41 Li’s Criterion
Define Li coefficients by
\lambda_n
=
\frac{1}{(n-1)!}
\left.
\frac{d^n}{ds^n}
\left[
s^{n-1}\log\xi(s)
\right]
\right|_{s=1}.
Li’s criterion states that the Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to
\lambda_n>0
for every positive integer n.
This is a true positivity reformulation.
Yet proving infinitely many inequalities remains difficult.

7.42 Why Li-Type Positivity Is Different
The symmetry defect
D(s)

 vanishes because of an identity valid everywhere.
Li coefficients instead encode the entire zero distribution through derivatives of \log\xi.
Their positivity is not already guaranteed by the functional equation.
Therefore they carry genuine additional content.

7.43 Hilbert–Pólya Direction
A spectral proof would seek a self-adjoint operator H whose eigenvalues correspond to
the imaginary parts of nontrivial zeros:
H\psi_n=\gamma_n\psi_n,
with zeros
\rho_n=\frac12+i\gamma_n.
Self-adjointness would force \gamma_n\in\mathbb R.
However, to prove the hypothesis one must construct the operator and establish exact
spectral correspondence.
A merely suggestive Hamiltonian or numerical similarity is insufficient.

7.44 Necessary Burden for a Spectral Proof
A valid Hilbert–Pólya-style proof requires:
a precisely defined Hilbert space;
a densely defined operator;
proof of self-adjointness or an appropriate equivalent;
proof of discrete or controlled spectrum;
exact identification of the spectral determinant or counting function with \xi;
multiplicity correspondence;
exclusion of extra eigenvalues and missing zeros.
Without these, the construction remains a conjectural analogy.

 7.45 A Transverse Coherence Hamiltonian
Suppose one defines an operator
H_\perp
=
-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
+
V(x,t)
in the transverse coordinate x=\sigma-1/2.
To infer the Riemann Hypothesis, one would need to prove that zero states of the
relevant spectral problem occur only at
x=0.
This requires a theorem linking eigenfunctions or eigenvalues of H_\perp exactly to
zeros of \xi.
A potential built from |\xi| may encode the zeros, but unless the spectral equivalence is
rigorous, the construction is only a repackaging.

7.46 Circular Potential Construction
For example, defining
V(s)
=
|\xi(s)|^2
and observing that minima occur at zeros is circular if the goal is to derive the zero
locations.
The potential was built using the very function whose zeros are being investigated.
This may be useful for visualization or numerical search, but not automatically for proof.

 7.47 Symmetric Off-Line Pair Contradiction: Required Form
A valid contradiction argument would need to assume an off-line zero
\rho=\frac12+a+i\gamma,
\qquad
a\neq0,
derive the full quartet, and then prove that the quartet violates an independently
established theorem.
Possible contradiction targets might include:
positivity of a rigorously derived quadratic form;
a zero-counting identity;
a spectral self-adjointness theorem;
a growth bound;
an arithmetic explicit formula.
Symmetry alone supplies the quartet but no contradiction.

7.48 Why “No Phase Cancellation” Is Insufficient
Suppose a proposed functional contains contributions
J(\rho)+J(1-\overline\rho).
To claim they cannot cancel, one must prove:
the contributions are well defined;
their signs are controlled;
the infinite sum converges;
no other zeros contribute compensating terms;
the resulting nonzero quantity contradicts a known identity.
Merely asserting that symmetric pairs cannot cancel does not establish any of these.

7.49 Positive Pair Contribution
A promising form is an even pair functional,

 Q(\rho)
=
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
\qquad
w(\rho)>0.
Then the mirror pair contributes
2a^2w(\rho)
when the weights are symmetric.
This cannot cancel within the pair.
But one still must prove the sum of all such positive contributions is zero from
independent mathematics.
That final step is equivalent to proving the hypothesis.

7.50 Explicit-Formula Route
The zeros enter explicit formulas connecting prime-counting quantities to sums over
\rho.
A proof might derive a bound on an arithmetic error term strong enough to imply
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12.
This route uses arithmetic information beyond the functional equation.
Any residual-coherence interpretation would need to reproduce such a rigorous bound,
not merely visualize symmetry.

7.51 Non-Circularity Checklist
For every proposed proof ingredient, ask:

 Does this identity already follow from the functional equation?
Does it vanish or hold everywhere, not only at zeros?
Was the critical-line penalty inserted by definition?
Does the argument assume all zeros can be paired in the desired way?
Does it exchange an infinite proof for finite numerical evidence?
Does it use \xi to construct a potential whose minima are then said to explain \xi’s
zeros?
Is the key positivity independent of the hypothesis?
Are convergence and regularization justified?
Is every zero included with multiplicity?
Does the conclusion exclude off-line quartets rather than merely respect their
symmetry?
A failure on any central item leaves the proof incomplete.

7.52 A Corrected Defect Concept
One may define a geometric displacement defect for a zero \rho,
\Delta_\rho
=
\rho-(1-\overline\rho)
=
2
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right).
Then
|\Delta_\rho|^2
=
4
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2.
A global defect could be

 \mathcal D
=
\sum_\rho
w(\rho)|\Delta_\rho|^2.
Under suitable positive weights and convergence,
\mathcal D=0
is equivalent to the hypothesis.
This is mathematically honest—but it is a reformulation, not yet a proof.

7.53 Central No-Go Theorem
Theorem 7.19 — Functional-equation defect no-go
Let F be any function satisfying
F(s)
=
\overline{F(1-\overline s)}
for all s.
Define
D_F(s)
=
F(s)
\overline{F(1-\overline s)}.
Then
D_F\equiv0.
Therefore no conclusion about the location of zeros of F can be obtained from the
condition

 D_F(s)=0.
Proof
The defining symmetry gives the identity immediately. Since the condition is satisfied at
every point, it cannot distinguish zeros or fixed points of the symmetry. ∎
This theorem applies directly to the completed zeta function.

7.54 Central Quartet Theorem
Theorem 7.20 — Exact content of the functional symmetry
For every nontrivial zero \rho of \xi:
\overline\rho,
\quad
1-\rho,
\quad
1-\overline\rho
are also zeros.
This symmetry implies the Riemann Hypothesis if and only if every zero is fixed by the
mirror map
\rho\mapsto1-\overline\rho.
Proof
The first statement follows from conjugation and the functional equation.
The mirror fixed-point condition is
\rho=1-\overline\rho,
equivalent to
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12.

 Thus the hypothesis is precisely the assertion that every zero is a fixed point rather than
a member of a distinct mirror pair. ∎
This isolates the unresolved step exactly.

7.55 Conditional Positive-Energy Theorem
Theorem 7.21 — What would be sufficient
Suppose one constructs a convergent functional
\mathcal E
=
\sum_\rho
w(\rho)
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2,
with
w(\rho)>0,
and proves independently—without assuming the Riemann Hypothesis—that
\mathcal E=0.
Then the Riemann Hypothesis follows.
Proof
Every term is nonnegative. A sum of nonnegative terms equals zero only if every term
vanishes. Therefore
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12
for every zero. ∎
The difficulty is the independent proof that \mathcal E=0, not the final implication.

 7.56 Proof Boundaries
This chapter establishes:
the completed zeta functional equation and conjugation symmetry;
the critical line as the fixed set of mirror reflection;
exact vanishing of the proposed symmetry-defect operator;
the impossibility of using that defect to localize zeros;
quartet symmetry of off-line zeros;
the logical distinction between symmetry and fixed-point confinement;
logarithmic-potential and Hadamard-product interpretations;
local behavior of |\xi|^2 near simple zeros;
why every simple zero is locally a minimum of |\xi|^2;
how off-line symmetric pairs affect transverse curvature;
why zeros cannot cancel one another in an entire product;
how signed statistics may cancel while positive squared displacement cannot;
the limitations of finite numerical verification;
the correct burden for spectral, positivity, or contradiction proofs;
a precise non-circularity checklist;
sufficient—but not yet established—positive-energy criteria equivalent to the hypothesis.
It does not prove the Riemann Hypothesis. It proves which symmetry-based
approaches are valid, which are identically empty, and what additional theorem would
actually be required.

The Fibonacci companion matrix has eigenvalues
\varphi
and

Direct solution of the quadratic equation. ∎

Let
P

A
=
P

Hence
A^n
=
P
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi^n&0\\
0&\psi^n
\end{bmatrix}
P^{-1}.
This gives a closed form for the Fibonacci sequence.

 8.6 Binet’s Formula
Theorem 8.3 — Exact closed form
F_n
=
\frac{
\varphi^n-\psi^n
}{
\sqrt5
}.
Proof
Because the recurrence has characteristic roots \varphi and \psi, every solution has the
form
F_n=c_1\varphi^n+c_2\psi^n.
The initial conditions give
0=c_1+c_2,
and
1=c_1\varphi+c_2\psi.
Thus
c_2=-c_1,
and
1=c_1(\varphi-\psi).
Since
\varphi-\psi=\sqrt5,

 c_1=\frac1{\sqrt5},
\qquad
c_2=-\frac1{\sqrt5}.
∎

8.7 Asymptotic Ratio
Theorem 8.4 — Fibonacci ratio convergence
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
=
\varphi.
Proof
Using Binet’s formula,
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
=
\frac{
\varphi^{n+1}-\psi^{n+1}
}{
\varphi^n-\psi^n
}.
Divide numerator and denominator by \varphi^n:
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
=
\frac{
\varphi-\psi(\psi/\varphi)^n
}{
1-(\psi/\varphi)^n
}.
Since

 \left|\frac\psi\varphi\right|
=
\varphi^{-2}<1,
the correction tends to zero. ∎

8.8 Exact Error Bound
From Binet’s formula,
F_n
=
\frac{\varphi^n}{\sqrt5}
\frac{\psi^n}{\sqrt5}.
Since
|\psi|<1,
\left|
F_n-\frac{\varphi^n}{\sqrt5}
\right|
=
\frac{|\psi|^n}{\sqrt5}
<
\frac12
for all n\ge1.
Corollary 8.5 — Nearest-integer formula
F_n
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{\varphi^n}{\sqrt5}
+
\frac12
\right\rfloor.

 8.9 Fibonacci Addition Formula
Theorem 8.6
For integers m\ge1 and n\ge0,
F_{m+n}
=
F_{m-1}F_n
+
F_mF_{n+1}.
Proof by induction on n
For n=0,
F_m
=
F_{m-1}F_0+F_mF_1
=
F_m.
Assume the identity holds for n and n-1. Then
\begin{aligned}
F_{m+n+1}
&=
F_{m+n}+F_{m+n-1}\\
&=
F_{m-1}(F_n+F_{n-1})
+
F_m(F_{n+1}+F_n)\\
&=
F_{m-1}F_{n+1}
+
F_mF_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}

 ∎

8.10 Doubling Identities
Set m=n in the addition formula:
F_{2n}
=
F_n(F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}).
Because
F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}
=
2F_{n+1}-F_n,
F_{2n}
=
F_n(2F_{n+1}-F_n).
Also,
F_{2n+1}
=
F_n^2+F_{n+1}^2.
These formulas support fast doubling algorithms.

8.11 Cassini’s Identity
Theorem 8.7 — Cassini
F_{n+1}F_{n-1}-F_n^2
=
(-1)^n.
Proof using determinants
Since

 \det A=-1,
\det A^n=(-1)^n.
A standard power formula is
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
Therefore
\det A^n
=
F_{n+1}F_{n-1}-F_n^2
=
(-1)^n.
∎
Cassini’s identity expresses an alternating residual of exact magnitude one.

8.12 Matrix-Power Formula
Theorem 8.8
For n\ge1,
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
Proof by induction

 For n=1,
A
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_2&F_1\\
F_1&F_0
\end{bmatrix}.
Assume true for n. Then
A^{n+1}
=
A^nA
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}+F_n&F_{n+1}\\

\end{bmatrix},
which equals
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+2}&F_{n+1}\\
F_{n+1}&F_n
\end{bmatrix}.
∎

8.13 General Second-Order Recurrence
Consider

 x_{n+1}
=
ax_n+bx_{n-1}.
The companion matrix is
A_{a,b}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a&b\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
Its characteristic equation is
\lambda^2-a\lambda-b=0.
The qualitative behavior depends on:
the spectral radius;
whether the roots are real or complex;
multiplicity;
initial conditions.
Fibonacci recursion is the special case
a=b=1.

8.14 Stability Classification
For
v_{n+1}=Av_n,
the origin is asymptotically stable if
\rho(A)<1.
The Fibonacci matrix has
\rho(A)=\varphi>1,

 so unnormalized Fibonacci recursion grows exponentially.
A normalized recurrence may be defined by
\widehat v_n
=
\varphi^{-n}v_n.
Then the dominant mode becomes stationary and the conjugate mode decays as
\left(
-\varphi^{-2}
\right)^n.

8.15 Projective Convergence
Let
r_n
=
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}.
Then
r_{n+1}
=
1+\frac1{r_n}.
Define
T(r)
=
1+\frac1r.
Its fixed points satisfy
r=1+\frac1r,
so

 r^2-r-1=0.
The positive fixed point is \varphi.

Proposition 8.9 — Local contraction at \varphi
T'(r)
=
-\frac1{r^2}.
Therefore
|T'(\varphi)|
=
\varphi^{-2}<1.
Hence \varphi is locally attracting on the positive real line.

8.16 Möbius-Map Interpretation
The ratio update
T(r)
=
\frac{r+1}{r}
is a Möbius transformation represented projectively by the Fibonacci matrix
A
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
Thus the golden-ratio fixed point is the projective eigenvector direction of the recurrence
matrix.

 8.17 Modular Fibonacci Sequences
Fix an integer modulus
m\ge2.
Consider the Fibonacci sequence modulo m:
F_n\bmod m.
The recurrence state is the ordered pair
(F_{n+1},F_n)\bmod m.
There are only
m^2
possible ordered pairs.

Theorem 8.10 — Eventual periodicity
The Fibonacci sequence modulo m is eventually periodic.
Proof
The pair-state evolves deterministically in a finite state space of size m^2. Therefore
some pair must repeat. From that repetition onward, deterministic evolution repeats
cyclically. ∎

8.18 Pure Periodicity
Because
A
is invertible modulo m whenever
\gcd(\det A,m)=1,

 and
\det A=-1,
the map is invertible modulo every m.
Theorem 8.11 — No transient
The Fibonacci sequence modulo m is purely periodic from the initial pair
(1,0).
Proof
The state transition is bijective on the finite pair space because -1 is invertible modulo
m.
A repeated state therefore lies on a cycle with no non-cyclic transient. Since the initial
state itself has a predecessor, it belongs to the cycle. ∎
The period is called the Pisano period.

8.19 Period Bound
Because the nonzero reachable pair states lie inside a set of at most
m^2
elements,
\pi(m)\le m^2
is an immediate crude bound.
Sharper bounds depend on number-theoretic structure.

8.20 Closure as State Return
For a deterministic recurrence

 z_{n+1}=T(z_n),
define closure after N steps by
z_N=z_0.
Definition 8.1 — Exact discrete closure
The orbit closes with period N if
T^N(z_0)=z_0
and N is the least positive integer with this property.
For Fibonacci recursion over the integers, the unnormalized orbit does not close except
at the zero state.
Modulo m, closure occurs because the state space is finite.

8.21 Residual Closure
In continuous or floating-point settings, exact return may be replaced by a residual
\varepsilon_N
=
\|T^N(z_0)-z_0\|.
Define normalized closure error
\eta_N
=
\frac{
\|T^N(z_0)-z_0\|
}{
1+\|z_0\|
}.
A small residual indicates approximate return under the chosen norm and
representation.

 It does not imply exact periodicity unless a theorem converts the numerical bound into
an exact statement.

8.22 Spectral Condition for Linear Closure
For
z_{n+1}=Az_n,
exact closure after N steps requires
A^Nz_0=z_0.
If closure is required for every initial state, then
A^N=I.
Theorem 8.12 — Eigenvalue condition
If A is diagonalizable and
A^N=I,
then every eigenvalue of A is an N-th root of unity.
Proof
For an eigenvector v,
Av=\lambda v.
Then
A^Nv=\lambda^Nv.
Because A^N=I,
\lambda^Nv=v,
so
\lambda^N=1.

 ∎
The Fibonacci eigenvalue \varphi is not a root of unity, so the real Fibonacci transfer
matrix cannot generate exact finite closure.

8.23 Normalized Fibonacci Closure
Define
B
=
\varphi^{-1}A.
Its eigenvalues are
1
and
-\varphi^{-2}.
Repeated application converges toward the dominant eigenline rather than cycling.
Theorem 8.13 — Rank-one asymptotic closure
B^n
\rightarrow
P_\varphi
as n\to\infty, where P_\varphi is the spectral projector onto the golden-ratio eigenvector.
Proof
Diagonalization gives
B^n
=
P
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\

 0&(-\varphi^{-2})^n
\end{bmatrix}
P^{-1}.
The second eigenvalue tends to zero. ∎
This is asymptotic directional stabilization, not periodic closure.

8.24 Fibonacci Words
Define words over an alphabet \{A,B\} by
W_0=B,
\qquad
W_1=A,
and
W_{n+1}=W_nW_{n-1}.
Then the word length satisfies
|W_{n+1}|
=
|W_n|+|W_{n-1}|.
With the chosen initial conditions,
|W_n|=F_{n+1}.

Theorem 8.14 — Fibonacci word length
|W_n|=F_{n+1}.
Proof
The lengths satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence with
|W_0|=1=F_1,

 and
|W_1|=1=F_2.
Uniqueness of recurrence solutions gives the result. ∎

8.25 Symbol Counts
Let
a_n
be the number of A symbols in W_n, and
b_n
the number of B symbols.
Then
a_{n+1}=a_n+a_{n-1},
and
b_{n+1}=b_n+b_{n-1}.
From the initial words,
a_n=F_n,
\qquad
b_n=F_{n-1}
for appropriate indexing.
Hence the frequency ratio approaches \varphi.

8.26 Substitution Rule
The infinite Fibonacci word can be generated by the substitution

 A\mapsto AB,
B\mapsto A.
The substitution matrix is
S
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix},
the same Fibonacci matrix.
The Perron–Frobenius eigenvector determines the asymptotic symbol frequencies.

8.27 Symbol Frequencies
The positive eigenvector is
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
Normalize by the sum
\varphi+1=\varphi^2.
Therefore the asymptotic frequencies are
f_A
=
\frac{\varphi}{\varphi^2}
=
\frac1{\varphi},
and

 f_B
=
\frac1{\varphi^2}.
They sum to one because
\varphi^{-1}+\varphi^{-2}=1.

8.28 Fibonacci Braid Recursion
Let B_N be a braid group.
Choose two braid elements
X,Y\in B_N.
Define recursively
\beta_0=Y,
\qquad
\beta_1=X,
and
\beta_{n+1}
=
\beta_n\beta_{n-1}.
This is a group-valued Fibonacci recursion.
Because braid multiplication is generally noncommutative, order matters.

8.29 Exponent Sum Recurrence
Apply the braid-group abelianization
e:B_N\rightarrow\mathbb Z.
Then

 e(\beta_{n+1})
=
e(\beta_n)+e(\beta_{n-1}).
Theorem 8.15 — Fibonacci exponent sum
If
e(\beta_0)=p,
\qquad
e(\beta_1)=q,
then
e(\beta_n)
=
F_nq+F_{n-1}p
for n\ge1.
Proof
The exponent sum converts braid multiplication into integer addition, so the sequence
satisfies the ordinary Fibonacci recurrence with the stated initial values. ∎
The full braid element contains more information than its exponent sum.

8.30 Noncommutative Word Growth
Let \ell(\beta) denote unreduced word length in a fixed generating representation.
Before simplification,
\ell(\beta_{n+1})
=
\ell(\beta_n)+\ell(\beta_{n-1}).
After applying braid relations and cancellation,

 \ell_{\min}(\beta_{n+1})
\le
\ell_{\min}(\beta_n)
+
\ell_{\min}(\beta_{n-1}).
Equality need not hold.

8.31 Matrix Representation of Braids
Let
\rho:B_N\rightarrow GL(k,\mathbb C)
be a representation.
Then
M_n
=
\rho(\beta_n)
satisfies
M_{n+1}
=
M_nM_{n-1}.
This is a nonlinear matrix recurrence because matrix multiplication replaces addition.
Its behavior depends on:
noncommutativity;
spectral radii;
common invariant subspaces;
representation parameters.
8.32 Commuting Case
If

 M_0M_1=M_1M_0,
then all matrices generated by the recursion commute.
In a simultaneous eigenbasis, each scalar eigenvalue sequence satisfies
\mu_{n+1}
=
\mu_n\mu_{n-1}.
Taking logarithms where defined,
y_n=\log\mu_n
gives
y_{n+1}=y_n+y_{n-1}.
Thus
y_n
=
F_ny_1+F_{n-1}y_0.
Therefore
\mu_n
=
\mu_1^{F_n}
\mu_0^{F_{n-1}}.

8.33 The Multiplicative Fibonacci Recurrence
Consider positive scalars satisfying
x_{n+1}=x_nx_{n-1}.
Theorem 8.16
x_n
=

 x_1^{F_n}
x_0^{F_{n-1}}
for n\ge1.
Proof
Take logarithms and apply the additive Fibonacci solution, or prove directly by induction.
∎
This recurrence typically grows far faster than ordinary Fibonacci numbers when
x_0,x_1>1.

8.34 Braid Closure
A braid \beta\in B_N can be closed by connecting corresponding top and bottom strand
endpoints.
Denote the closure by
\widehat\beta.
Different braid words may have isotopic closures.
Markov’s theorem characterizes when two braids have equivalent closures through:
conjugation;
stabilization and destabilization.
Thus equality of braid-group elements is stronger than equality of closed links.

8.35 Recursive Braid Closure
For recursively generated braids \beta_n, one may ask whether
\widehat{\beta_n}
eventually repeats up to isotopy.
This is not implied by Fibonacci recurrence.

 A proof would require:
a finite quotient representation;
periodicity in an invariant;
or a direct Markov-equivalence argument.
8.36 Finite Quotient Periodicity
Suppose a group homomorphism maps
\rho:B_N\rightarrow G
into a finite group G.
Then the pair state
(\rho(\beta_n),\rho(\beta_{n-1}))
lies in the finite set
G\times G.
Theorem 8.17 — Eventual periodicity in a finite quotient
The recursive braid sequence is eventually periodic after projection into any finite group
representation.
Proof
The pair update is deterministic on a finite state space. ∎
This establishes periodicity of the quotient image, not of the full braid sequence.

8.37 Transfer Matrices
A local strand rule may be encoded by transfer matrices
T_A,
\qquad
T_B.

 For a word
W=s_1s_2\cdots s_n,
define
T(W)
=
T_{s_n}\cdots T_{s_1},
with order chosen according to propagation convention.
For Fibonacci words,
W_{n+1}=W_nW_{n-1},
so
T_{n+1}
=
T_{n-1}T_n
or the reversed product, depending on convention.
Order must be fixed explicitly.

8.38 Trace Map
For certain unimodular 2\times2 transfer matrices, define
x_n
=
\frac12\operatorname{tr}T_n.
Under Fibonacci multiplication, traces may satisfy a nonlinear recurrence of the form
x_{n+1}
=
2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}.
This is the Fibonacci trace map.

 Its precise derivation requires:
determinant-one matrices;
the specific multiplication convention;
the Cayley–Hamilton identity.
8.39 Cayley–Hamilton Identity for SL(2)
Let
M\in SL(2,\mathbb C).
Then
M^2-(\operatorname{tr}M)M+I=0.
Therefore
M^{-1}
=
(\operatorname{tr}M)I-M.
This identity is central to deriving trace recurrences.

8.40 Fricke Identity
For
A,B\in SL(2,\mathbb C),
define
x=\frac12\operatorname{tr}A,
y=\frac12\operatorname{tr}B,
z=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(AB).
The commutator trace is related to
x^2+y^2+z^2-2xyz.

 Depending on normalization,
\operatorname{tr}
(ABA^{-1}B^{-1})
determines an invariant surface for the trace map.
This structure appears in quasiperiodic transfer problems.

8.41 Fibonacci Trace-Map Invariant
For the recurrence
x_{n+1}
=
2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2},
define
I_n
=
x_{n+1}^2+x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2
2x_{n+1}x_nx_{n-1}
1.
Theorem 8.18 — Trace-map invariant
I_n=I_{n-1}.
Proof
Substitute
x_{n+1}=2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}
into I_n, expand, and collect terms. The expression reduces exactly to

 x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2+x_{n-2}^2
2x_nx_{n-1}x_{n-2}
1
=
I_{n-1}.
∎
This is a genuine conserved residual for the trace recurrence.

8.42 Residual Closure Functional for Recurrences
Given a recurrence state
z_n,
define an invariant candidate
I(z_n).
The residual is
r_n
=
I(z_{n+1})-I(z_n).
Exact closure of the invariant means
r_n=0
for all n.
Numerically, report
|r_n|
and compare it with precision and conditioning.
A small invariant residual does not imply the full state has closed.

 8.43 State Closure Versus Invariant Closure
Proposition 8.19
It is possible that
I(z_{n+1})=I(z_n)
for every n, while
z_{n+1}\neq z_n.
Proof by example
A rotation on the unit circle preserves
I(x,y)=x^2+y^2,
but changes the state at every nontrivial angle. ∎
An invariant constrains motion to a level set; it does not imply stationarity or periodicity.

8.44 Fibonacci Residues and Strand Labels
Suppose strand labels are assigned by
\ell_n
=
F_n\bmod m.
Then the label sequence is periodic with Pisano period \pi(m).
This can produce repeating strand classes or colors.
However, periodic labels do not imply the geometric strands close in space.
A spatial embedding map must also return to its initial position and orientation.

8.45 Discrete Geometric Strand Model

 Let a strand position satisfy
x_{n+1}
=
x_n
+
R(\theta_n)\,d_n,
where:
R(\theta_n) is a rotation;
d_n is a step vector;
\theta_n may be determined by Fibonacci residues.
Exact closure after N steps requires
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
R(\theta_n)d_n
=
0,
and orientation closure requires
\theta_N-\theta_0
\in2\pi\mathbb Z.
Both conditions are necessary.

8.46 Polygonal Closure Theorem
Theorem 8.20
A discrete strand with increments
\Delta x_n
closes after N steps if and only if
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta x_n=0.
Proof

 By telescoping,
x_N-x_0
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
(x_{n+1}-x_n)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta x_n.
Thus x_N=x_0 exactly when the sum vanishes. ∎
This is the exact vector closure condition.

8.47 Root-of-Unity Closure
Suppose planar increments are
\Delta z_n
=
a_n e^{i\theta_n}.
If all lengths are equal,
a_n=a,
and angles run through all N-th roots of unity,
\theta_n
=
\theta_0+\frac{2\pi n}{N},
then
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta z_n
=
ae^{i\theta_0}
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
e^{2\pi in/N}

 =
0.
Thus a regular polygon closes.
A Fibonacci angular sequence generally does not produce uniform roots of unity unless
reduced modulo a suitable period and balanced.

8.48 Weighted Root-of-Unity Sum
For arbitrary weights a_n, closure requires
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
a_n\omega^n
=
0,
\qquad
\omega=e^{2\pi i/N}.
This is a discrete Fourier coefficient condition.
Fibonacci weights do not generally satisfy it automatically.

8.49 Generating Function
The Fibonacci generating function is
G(x)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
F_nx^n.
Theorem 8.21
For |x|<\varphi^{-1},

 G(x)
=
\frac{x}{1-x-x^2}.
Proof
Using the recurrence,
\begin{aligned}
G(x)-x
&=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}F_nx^n\\
&=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(F_{n-1}+F_{n-2})x^n\\
&=
x\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}F_nx^n
+
x^2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}F_nx^n\\
&=
xG(x)+x^2G(x).
\end{aligned}
Therefore
G(x)(1-x-x^2)=x.
∎
The poles occur at
x=\varphi^{-1}
and
x=-\varphi.
The nearest pole to the origin determines the growth rate.

8.50 Zeckendorf Representation

 Every positive integer can be represented uniquely as a sum of nonconsecutive
Fibonacci numbers.
Theorem 8.22 — Zeckendorf’s theorem
For every integer N\ge1, there exists a unique representation
N
=
F_{k_1}+F_{k_2}+\cdots+F_{k_r},
with
k_j-k_{j+1}\ge2
and Fibonacci indexing beginning with distinct positive terms.
Proof outline
Existence: Apply the greedy algorithm, repeatedly subtracting the largest Fibonacci
number not exceeding the remainder. The recurrence guarantees that the next chosen
term is nonconsecutive.
Uniqueness: Assume two distinct nonconsecutive representations. Compare their
largest differing Fibonacci term and use
F_k
>
F_{k-1}+F_{k-3}+F_{k-5}+\cdots
to show smaller nonconsecutive terms cannot compensate for it. ∎
This theorem creates a unique Fibonacci coding of integers, but does not automatically
imply geometric or physical encoding.

8.51 Fibonacci Convolution
Theorem 8.23

 \sum_{k=0}^{n}
F_kF_{n-k}
=
\frac{
nL_n-F_n
}{5},
where L_n is the Lucas sequence.
Such convolution identities arise when two Fibonacci-recursive channels interact
linearly.
Their physical relevance depends on the coupling model.

8.52 Lucas Sequence
Define
L_0=2,
\qquad
L_1=1,
and
L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}.
Then
L_n=\varphi^n+\psi^n.
Also,
L_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}.
The Lucas sequence supplies the trace of the Fibonacci matrix:
\operatorname{tr}A^n=L_n.

8.53 Determinant and Trace

 From
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix},
\operatorname{tr}A^n
=
F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}
=
L_n.
And
\det A^n=(-1)^n.
Therefore the powers alternate orientation in two dimensions while growing along the
dominant eigenvector.

8.54 Fibonacci Rotation Is Not Automatic
The Fibonacci companion matrix is not orthogonal:
A^TA
\neq I.
Its eigenvalues are real, not unit modulus.
Therefore it produces stretching and contraction, not pure rotation.
Any claim that Fibonacci recursion generates geometric rotation requires an additional
mapping, normalization, or phase embedding.

8.55 Phase Embedding
One possible phase embedding is

 \theta_n
=
2\pi
\{n\varphi\},
where \{\cdot\} denotes fractional part.
Because \varphi is irrational, the sequence is equidistributed modulo one.
Theorem 8.24 — Irrational rotation density
The sequence
n\varphi\bmod1
is dense in [0,1).
Proof
This is a standard result for irrational rotations on the circle. If the orbit were not dense,
it would contradict the minimality of irrational circle rotation. ∎
Density is not periodic closure.

8.56 Golden-Angle Sequence
The golden angle is commonly defined modulo 2\pi by
\alpha_g
=
2\pi
\left(
1-\frac1\varphi
\right)
=
\frac{2\pi}{\varphi^2}.
The sequence
\theta_n=n\alpha_g\bmod2\pi

 is nonperiodic because
\frac{\alpha_g}{2\pi}
=
\varphi^{-2}
is irrational.
It distributes points evenly in an asymptotic sense but never returns exactly.

8.57 Exact Versus Quasiperiodic Closure
Theorem 8.25
A circle rotation
\theta_{n+1}
=
\theta_n+\alpha
\pmod{2\pi}
has an exact finite period if and only if
\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\in\mathbb Q.
Proof
Exact period N requires
N\alpha=2\pi k
for some integer k, equivalent to rationality.
Conversely, if
\alpha/(2\pi)=p/q,
then period divides q. ∎
Golden-angle dynamics are quasiperiodic, not exactly periodic.

 8.58 Approximate Return
For irrational rotations, Dirichlet approximation guarantees integers p,q such that
\left|
q\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}-p
\right|
<
\frac1q.
Thus arbitrarily close returns exist, but exact return does not.
A numerical closure residual must therefore be interpreted against Diophantine
approximation.

8.59 Fibonacci Approximants to \varphi
The convergents of the continued fraction
\varphi=[1;1,1,1,\ldots]
are
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}.
Theorem 8.26 — Approximation error
\left|
\varphi-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\right|
=
\frac1{
F_n(\varphi F_n+F_{n-1})
}.
In particular,

 \left|
\varphi-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\right|
<
\frac1{F_n^2}.
Proof
Use Cassini’s identity or Binet’s formula to evaluate the difference exactly. ∎
This explains why Fibonacci numbers generate especially close rational approximations
to golden-ratio rotations.

8.60 Near-Closure from Fibonacci Approximants
Let
\alpha
=
\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}.
After F_n steps,
F_n\alpha
=
2\pi\frac{F_n}{\varphi}.
Because
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\approx\varphi,
\frac{F_n}{\varphi}
\approx
F_{n-1}.
Thus the phase nearly returns modulo 2\pi.
The residual decreases exponentially with n, but never becomes exactly zero.

 8.61 Exact Near-Return Identity
Using
F_n\varphi
=
F_{n+1}
(-\varphi)^{-n},
one obtains
\frac{F_n}{\varphi}
=
F_{n-1}
+
(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.
Therefore
F_n\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}
=
2\pi F_{n-1}
+
2\pi(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.
Modulo 2\pi, the residual phase is
\Delta\theta_n
=
2\pi(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.

Theorem 8.27 — Exponentially small Fibonacci near-closure
The F_n-step residual of rotation by 2\pi/\varphi has magnitude

 |\Delta\theta_n|
=
2\pi\varphi^{-n}.
Proof
From the exact identity above. ∎
This is a mathematically precise form of residual closure generated by Fibonacci
approximants.

8.62 Alternating Mirror Residual
The sign
(-1)^{n-1}
in the near-return residual alternates.
Therefore successive Fibonacci approximants approach the target angle from
alternating sides.
This is an arithmetic mirror behavior, not a spatial parity transformation unless a
geometric embedding is specified.

8.63 Fibonacci Spiral Geometry
A common geometric construction places points at radius
r_n=c\sqrt n
and angle
\theta_n=n\alpha_g.
This produces phyllotactic patterns with approximate uniform density.
The square-root radial law is not derived from the Fibonacci recurrence itself. It is an
additional geometric design choice.

 8.64 Logarithmic Golden Spiral
A logarithmic spiral satisfies
r(\theta)=r_0e^{k\theta}.
If the radius scales by \varphi after a quarter turn,
r\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
=
\varphi r(\theta),
then
e^{k\pi/2}=\varphi,
so
k=\frac{2\log\varphi}{\pi}.
This is one precise definition of a golden spiral.
It is not the same object as the Fibonacci sequence, though finite square constructions
approximate it visually.

8.65 Fibonacci Tiling Recursion
Suppose a geometric assembly contains counts
N_A(n),
\qquad
N_B(n)
of two tile types, updated by
\begin{bmatrix}
N_A(n+1)\\
N_B(n+1)
\end{bmatrix}

 =
A
\begin{bmatrix}
N_A(n)\\
N_B(n)
\end{bmatrix}.
Then tile-count ratios approach \varphi.
This proves asymptotic composition, not geometric self-similarity unless the substitution
also specifies tile shapes and matching rules.

8.66 Recursive Strand-Length Model
Suppose strand lengths satisfy
L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}.
Then
L_n
=
F_nL_1+F_{n-1}L_0.
If L_0,L_1>0,
\frac{L_{n+1}}{L_n}\rightarrow\varphi.
The recurrence predicts length ratios only. Curvature, embedding, contact, and topology
require separate equations.

8.67 Energy Recurrence
If energy contributions obey
E_{n+1}=E_n+E_{n-1},
then

 E_n
=
F_nE_1+F_{n-1}E_0.
This is mathematically exact given the recurrence.
But a physical theory must derive why energies add in this manner. Energies of
interacting structures usually include cross terms.

8.68 Coupled Recurrence with Interaction
A more realistic model is
E_{n+1}
=
E_n+E_{n-1}
+
C(E_n,E_{n-1}),
where C is an interaction correction.
The ordinary Fibonacci law holds only if
C\equiv0.
Thus observed deviation from Fibonacci scaling may quantify coupling rather than
failure of recursion.

8.69 Residual from Fibonacci Prediction
Define
r_n
=
x_{n+1}-x_n-x_{n-1}.
Exact Fibonacci recursion means
r_n=0.

 A normalized residual is
\widehat r_n
=
\frac{
x_{n+1}-x_n-x_{n-1}
}{
|x_{n+1}|+|x_n|+|x_{n-1}|+\epsilon
}.
This can be used as a model diagnostic.
A small residual shows approximate recurrence, not why the recurrence occurs.

8.70 Least-Squares Recurrence Fit
Given data x_0,\ldots,x_N, fit
x_{n+1}=ax_n+bx_{n-1}
by minimizing
J(a,b)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}
\left(
x_{n+1}-ax_n-bx_{n-1}
\right)^2.
The normal equations are
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum x_n^2&
\sum x_nx_{n-1}\\
\sum x_nx_{n-1}&
\sum x_{n-1}^2
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
a\\b

 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum x_nx_{n+1}\\
\sum x_{n-1}x_{n+1}
\end{bmatrix}.
A fitted result near
a=b=1
supports a Fibonacci-like model within the dataset, subject to uncertainty and model
comparison.

8.71 Statistical Test Boundary
A visual pattern resembling Fibonacci growth is insufficient.
A defensible test should compare:
Fibonacci recurrence;
alternative linear recurrences;
exponential growth;
polynomial growth;
stochastic models.
Model selection should report uncertainty, residuals, out-of-sample prediction, and
sensitivity.

8.72 Recursive Closure on a Graph
Let graph states satisfy
x_{n+1}=A_Gx_n+A_Gx_{n-1},
where A_G is a graph operator.
Lift to first order:

 \begin{bmatrix}
x_{n+1}\\
x_n
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
A_G&A_G\\
I&0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x_n\\
x_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
The spectrum of the lifted operator determines growth and closure.
If \mu is an eigenvalue of A_G, the corresponding lifted eigenvalues satisfy
\lambda^2-\mu\lambda-\mu=0.
Exact periodic closure requires these \lambda values to be roots of unity on the excited
modes.

8.73 No-Go for Positive Graph Eigenvalues
If \mu>0, one lifted root is
\lambda_+
=
\frac{
\mu+\sqrt{\mu^2+4\mu}
}{2}
>1.
Therefore the corresponding mode grows and cannot be periodic without normalization
or nonlinear saturation.

8.74 Nonlinear Saturated Fibonacci Map

 One may define
x_{n+1}
=
\tanh
\left(
ax_n+bx_{n-1}
\right).
This remains bounded.
Fixed points satisfy
x=\tanh((a+b)x).
Stability depends on the Jacobian
J
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a\,\operatorname{sech}^2(\cdot)&
b\,\operatorname{sech}^2(\cdot)\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
The presence of Fibonacci-like coupling coefficients does not determine the nonlinear
dynamics by itself.

8.75 Recursive Braid Energy
Let a braid recursion be
\beta_{n+1}
=
\beta_n\beta_{n-1}.
Suppose an energy-like functional E is subadditive under composition:

 E(\alpha\beta)
\le
E(\alpha)+E(\beta).
Then
E(\beta_{n+1})
\le
E(\beta_n)+E(\beta_{n-1}).
Proposition 8.28 — Fibonacci upper bound
If
E_n=E(\beta_n),
then
E_n
\le
F_nE_1+F_{n-1}E_0.
Proof
Induct using the subadditive recurrence inequality. ∎
Equality requires exact additivity and no cancellation or relaxation.

8.76 Submultiplicative Matrix Norm Bound
For a matrix representation,
M_{n+1}
=
M_nM_{n-1}.
Using a submultiplicative norm,
\|M_{n+1}\|
\le

 \|M_n\|
\|M_{n-1}\|.
Taking logarithms,
y_n=\log\|M_n\|
gives
y_{n+1}
\le
y_n+y_{n-1}.
Therefore
y_n
\le
F_ny_1+F_{n-1}y_0
when the logarithms are nonnegative or interpreted carefully.
Thus matrix norm growth can be bounded by multiplicative Fibonacci scaling.

8.77 Recursive Commutator Residual
For noncommuting matrices, define
C_n
=
[M_n,M_{n-1}]
=
M_nM_{n-1}-M_{n-1}M_n.
If
C_n=0,
the adjacent recursion factors commute.
A small normalized commutator,

 \chi_n
=
\frac{
\|C_n\|
}{
\|M_n\|\|M_{n-1}\|+\epsilon
},
measures approximate commutativity.
Approximate commutativity may justify scalar spectral approximations locally, but not
exact diagonalization.

8.78 Recursive Orientation
If braid exponent sums satisfy
e_{n+1}=e_n+e_{n-1},
then sign may eventually become fixed if the dominant golden-ratio mode has nonzero
coefficient.
However, sign of exponent sum is not complete chirality.
Two braids with positive exponent sum may have different mirror properties.

8.79 Closure in a Finite Representation
Suppose
\rho(\beta_n)
lies in a finite unitary group.
Then the pair-state recursion is periodic.
The resulting matrix closure period is at most
|G|^2.

 This may be used to construct exact digital braid cycles.
It does not prove the underlying continuous braid geometry is periodic.

8.80 Central Fibonacci Closure Theorem
Theorem 8.29 — Exact arithmetic near-closure under golden rotation
Let
\theta_n
=
n\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}
\pmod{2\pi}.
At Fibonacci times n=F_k,
\theta_{F_k}
=
2\pi
(-1)^{k-1}
\varphi^{-k}
\pmod{2\pi}.
Therefore the closure residual decays exponentially:
|\theta_{F_k}|
=
2\pi\varphi^{-k}.
Proof
Use the exact identity
\frac{F_k}{\varphi}
=
F_{k-1}
+
(-1)^{k-1}\varphi^{-k}.

 Multiply by 2\pi and reduce modulo 2\pi. ∎
This proves a precise residual-closure phenomenon connecting Fibonacci numbers and
golden-ratio rotation.
It is approximate closure, not exact periodicity.

8.81 Central Recurrence–Braid Boundary Theorem
Theorem 8.30
A Fibonacci recursion assigned to braid words determines:
a recursive algebraic sequence in the braid group;
Fibonacci growth of any additive homomorphic invariant;
eventual periodicity in every finite quotient.
It does not, without further assumptions, determine:
geometric strand lengths;
spatial closure;
knot type of the closures;
physical energy;
stability;
material realization.
Proof
The first three properties follow from the group recursion and homomorphism or
finiteness arguments.
The remaining quantities depend on geometric embeddings, closure operations, energy
functionals, and physical constitutive laws absent from the abstract recursion. ∎

Let the complete agent state at step n be

(x_n,m_n,\theta_n,G_n),
where:
x_n\in\mathcal X is the active system state;
m_n\in\mathcal M is retained memory;
\theta_n\in\Theta contains adaptive parameters;

Let the observation be

=
\mathcal O(x_n)+\nu_n,
where \nu_n denotes observation noise.
The agent produces:

=
\mathcal P_{\theta_n}(z_n),
a prediction,
a_n

an action,

\mathcal T(z_n,a_n,o_{n+1}).

9.2 Prediction Residual
Define the prediction residual
r_n
=
o_{n+1}
\widehat o_{n+1}.

 For vector observations, define residual energy
E_n
=
\frac12
r_n^TWr_n,
where
W=W^T\succ0.
The Euclidean case is recovered with
W=I.

Lemma 9.1 — Residual energy is nonnegative
E_n\ge0,
with equality if and only if
r_n=0.
Proof
Since W\succ0,
r_n^TWr_n>0
for every nonzero r_n, while it is zero for r_n=0. ∎
The residual energy measures error under the chosen metric. It does not by itself
determine whether the prediction model is scientifically correct outside the observed

9.3 Residual Contraction
Suppose a candidate correction transforms the residual from r_n to r_n^+.
Definition 9.1 — Contraction ratio

 For E_n>0, define
\gamma_n
=
\frac{E_n^+}{E_n}.
The candidate is:
strictly contracting if
0\le\gamma_n<1;
neutral if
\gamma_n=1;
expanding if
\gamma_n>1.
Define verified improvement
\Delta E_n
=
E_n-E_n^+.
Then contraction is equivalent to
\Delta E_n>0.

Proposition 9.2 — Repeated uniform contraction
Suppose
E_{n+1}\le\gamma E_n
for every n, where
0\le\gamma<1.
Then
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0,

 and therefore
E_n\rightarrow0.
Proof
Repeated substitution gives
E_n
\le
\gamma E_{n-1}
\le
\gamma^2E_{n-2}
\le
\cdots
\le
\gamma^nE_0.
Since \gamma^n\to0, the residual energy converges to zero. ∎

9.4 Nonuniform Contraction
Suppose
E_{n+1}
\le
\gamma_nE_n,
\qquad
0\le\gamma_n\le1.
Then
E_n
\le
E_0
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_k.
Theorem 9.3 — Product criterion

 If
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
(1-\gamma_k)
=
\infty,
then
E_n\rightarrow0.
Proof
For 0<\gamma\le1,
\log\gamma
\le
-(1-\gamma).
Therefore
\log
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_k
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\log\gamma_k
\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-\gamma_k).
The right side tends to -\infty, so the product tends to zero. ∎
Strict improvement at every step is not enough by itself; the total contraction must not
become summably weak.

9.5 Residual Contraction Under Disturbance
Suppose

 E_{n+1}
\le
\gamma E_n+\varepsilon,
where
0\le\gamma<1,
\qquad
\varepsilon\ge0.
Theorem 9.4 — Error-floor bound
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0
+
\varepsilon
\frac{1-\gamma^n}{1-\gamma}.
Hence
\limsup_{n\to\infty}E_n
\le
\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.
Proof
Iterate the inequality:
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0
+
\varepsilon
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\gamma^j.
Evaluate the geometric sum. ∎
Persistent noise or model mismatch creates a residual floor even when the correction
mechanism is contracting.

 9.6 Candidate Scoring
Let c\in\mathcal C_n be a candidate correction.
Define its score
S_n(c)
=
w_E\Delta E_n(c)
+
w_G\Delta G_n(c)
+
w_I I_n(c)
w_RR_n(c)
w_CC_n(c),
where:
\Delta E_n(c) is residual reduction;
\Delta G_n(c) is goal progress;
I_n(c) is information gain;
R_n(c) is estimated risk;
C_n(c) is implementation cost;
all weights are nonnegative.
A candidate is admissible only if it satisfies safety and boundedness constraints.

Definition 9.2 — Pure candidate evaluation
Candidate scoring is pure if evaluating S_n(c) does not modify:
the live state;
retained memory;
adaptive parameters;
the graph;
the random-number state used for actual execution.

 Purity prevents scoring order from changing the decision.

Proposition 9.5 — Order independence under pure scoring
If candidate evaluation is pure and deterministic, then the selected maximizer
c_n^*
=
\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal C_n}S_n(c)
is independent of the order in which candidates are evaluated, except for explicitly
specified tie-breaking.
Proof
Pure evaluation assigns each candidate a fixed score independent of prior evaluations.
Therefore the set of scores is invariant under enumeration order. ∎
Without pure scoring, candidate assessment can contaminate the state and make the
decision path dependent.

9.7 Promotion Gates
A candidate should not be promoted solely because it improved one sample.
Define a promotion gate with conditions:
\mathsf G(c)=1
if and only if all of the following hold:
\Delta E_n(c)\ge\delta_E,
R_n(c)\le R_{\max},
\|\Delta\theta(c)\|\le B_\theta,
\Delta G_n(c)\ge-\delta_G,
and

 N_{\mathrm{success}}(c)\ge q
within a validation window of length w.
Otherwise,
\mathsf G(c)=0.
The thresholds must be defined before testing.

9.8 False Promotion Bound
Suppose a non-improving candidate passes an individual trial by chance with probability
at most p.
Assume independent validation trials.
If promotion requires q successes in q trials, then the false-promotion probability is at
most
p^q.
Theorem 9.6 — Repetition suppresses accidental promotion
Under the independence assumption,
P(\text{false promotion})
\le
p^q.
Proof
The probability that all q independent trials pass is the product
p^q.
∎
The independence assumption is strong. Correlated validation samples reduce the
effective strength of repeated testing.

 9.9 Majority Promotion Gate
Suppose promotion requires at least q successes among w independent trials.
If the false-success probability is p, then
P_{\mathrm{false}}
=
\sum_{k=q}^{w}
\binom wk
p^k(1-p)^{w-k}.
This is the binomial tail.
For q>wp, concentration inequalities provide exponential bounds.

Theorem 9.7 — Hoeffding false-promotion bound
Let X_1,\ldots,X_w be independent Bernoulli variables with mean at most p.
If promotion requires an empirical success rate at least \tau>p, then
P
\left(
\frac1w\sum_{i=1}^{w}X_i
\ge\tau
\right)
\le
\exp
\left[
-2w(\tau-p)^2
\right].
Proof
Apply Hoeffding’s inequality to bounded independent variables. ∎

 Repeated verified improvement provides statistical protection only when the trial design
is valid.

9.10 Bounded Adaptation
Let adaptive parameters satisfy
\theta_{n+1}
=
\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n.
Impose the update bound
\|\Delta\theta_n\|
\le
b_n.
Proposition 9.8 — Cumulative parameter-drift bound
\|\theta_n-\theta_0\|
\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k.
Proof
By telescoping,
\theta_n-\theta_0
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Delta\theta_k.
Apply the triangle inequality. ∎
If
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}b_k<\infty,
then total drift is finite.

 9.11 Projected Adaptation
Let \Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p be a closed convex admissible parameter set.
Define
\theta_{n+1}
=
\Pi_\Theta
\left(
\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n
\right),

Lemma 9.9 — Projection is nonexpansive
For all x,y,
\|\Pi_\Theta(x)-\Pi_\Theta(y)\|
\le
\|x-y\|.
Proof
This is a standard property of projection onto a closed convex set in a Hilbert space. ∎

Corollary 9.10 — Admissibility preservation
If
\theta_0\in\Theta,
then
\theta_n\in\Theta
for every n.
Projection prevents parameter escape but does not guarantee good performance.

Let the loss be

Projection onto a closed interval is nonexpansive. ∎

Suppose an internal scalar output is

w_e e+w_xx+w_mm,
where

Let a graph be
G=(V,E,\mu),
with node set V, edge multiset E, and metadata \mu.
A deterministic graph fingerprint should be invariant under arbitrary storage order.
Define a canonical serialization:
convert every node and edge attribute to a deterministic built-in representation;
sort nodes by canonical key;
normalize each undirected edge endpoint order;
sort edges lexicographically;
sort metadata keys;
serialize without nondeterministic whitespace;
hash the resulting byte string.
Theorem 9.15 — Order-invariant fingerprint
If two graph representations differ only by ordering of nodes, edges, or metadata fields,
their canonical fingerprints are identical.
Proof
Canonical sorting maps every equivalent ordering to the same serialized sequence.
Deterministic hashing then produces the same digest. ∎

Proposition 9.16 — Fingerprint equality is not graph-isomorphism proof
Two isomorphic graphs with different node labels can have different canonical
fingerprints unless the canonicalization includes a label-independent graphisomorphism procedure.
Proof

 The serialization may preserve node labels. Relabeling changes the serialized keys
even though the abstract graphs are isomorphic. ∎
A stable identity hash and a graph-isomorphism certificate are different tools.

Proof
Expand the recursion repeatedly or prove by induction. ∎

and

=
\sum_{j=0}^{H-1}
\gamma^j

There exist candidates with

9.25 Heal–Patch–Adapt–Evolve Semantics
Define four distinct update levels.
Heal
A state-level correction:
x_n\mapsto x_n^+
intended to reduce current residual.
Patch
A bounded parameter or rule adjustment:
\theta_n\mapsto\theta_n^+.
Adapt
A retained belief or predictive-statistics update:
m_n\mapsto m_n^+.
Evolve
A promoted structural change:
G_n\mapsto G_n^+
or a persistent policy replacement, accepted only after repeated validation.

 These levels should not be conflated.

9.26 Healing Criterion
A correction heals the current state if
E_n^+<E_n
and all safety constraints remain satisfied.
Define heal indicator
h_n
=
\mathbf 1
\left[
E_n^+<E_n
\;\land\;
\mathsf{safe}
\right].
A healed state may still leave the model parameters unchanged.

9.27 Patch Criterion
A patch is accepted if:
\|\Delta\theta_n\|\le B_\theta,
L_{\mathrm{validation}}
(\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n)
<
L_{\mathrm{validation}}(\theta_n)-\delta_P,
and
R(\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n)
\le R_{\max}.

 The use of a validation loss distinguishes verified patching from mere training-loss
reduction.

9.28 Adaptation Criterion
Let m_n include running beliefs or statistics.
A bounded exponential update is
m_{n+1}
=
(1-\alpha)m_n
+
\alpha \widehat m_n,
\qquad
0\le\alpha\le1.
Lemma 9.20 — Convex boundedness
If m_n and \widehat m_n lie in a convex set \mathcal M, then
m_{n+1}\in\mathcal M.
Proof
The update is a convex combination. ∎

9.29 Evolution Criterion
A structural candidate G' is promoted from provisional to persistent only if:
it passes q independent or diversity-controlled trials;
its mean improvement exceeds \delta_E;
its worst observed degradation stays above a safety floor;
its complexity cost stays below a budget;
rollback information is preserved;
graph identity and provenance are recorded.
Define the promotion predicate

 \mathsf{Promote}(G')\in\{0,1\}.

Let

be a validation objective.
Suppose every promoted structural change satisfies

\le
J(G_k)-\delta,
\qquad

The number N of promotions satisfies

\le
\frac{
J(G_0)-J_{\min}
}{
\delta
}.
Proof
After N promotions,

\le
J(G_0)-N\delta.
Since
J(G_N)\ge J_{\min},
rearrangement gives the result. ∎
An endlessly evolving system must eventually reduce its improvement threshold,
change its objective, or permit neutral structural variation.

9.31 Convergence-Aware Stopping
Let a stopping window contain the most recent w residual energies.
Define the average improvement
\overline{\Delta E}_n
=
\frac1w
\sum_{k=n-w+1}^{n}
(E_{k-1}-E_k).

<
\varepsilon_E,
\max_{k}
\|\theta_k-\theta_{k-1}\|
<
\varepsilon_\theta,

E_n
converges, and

Proof
Every monotone bounded sequence converges.

Then
E_{n-1}-E_n
\rightarrow

∎

9.33 Surprise Detection
Let the standardized residual magnitude be
s_n
=
\sqrt{

=
\mathbf 1[s_n>\tau].

has a chi-squared distribution with d degrees of freedom.

9.34 Adaptive Information Target
Let the information-seeking target be
I_n^*
=
\begin{cases}
I_{\mathrm{high}},&
\mathsf S_n=1,\\[4pt]
I_{\mathrm{low}},&
\mathsf S_n=0.
\end{cases}

contraction.

9.35 Intrinsic Goal Function
Define an intrinsic objective

=
\alpha_NN
+
\alpha_II
+
\alpha_CC
\alpha_RR,

9.36 Normalization Requirement
Suppose one term ranges over [0,1] and another over [0,10^6].

Proposition 9.22 — Scale dependence of weighted scores
The ordering induced by
S=w_1f_1+w_2f_2
changes under rescaling of one feature unless the corresponding weight is rescaled

Proof
Replace

with

9.37 Regret
Let the agent choose action a_n and incur loss

Against a fixed comparator a, cumulative regret is
R_N(a)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}
\left[
\ell_n(a_n)-\ell_n(a)
\right].

R_N
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_n(a_n)
\min_a
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_n(a).
Sublinear regret,

 R_N=o(N),
means average excess loss vanishes.

9.38 Online Gradient-Descent Regret
Assume:
\Theta is convex with diameter D;
each loss \ell_n is convex;
gradients satisfy
\|\nabla\ell_n(\theta)\|\le G.
Use projected gradient descent with constant step size \eta:
\theta_{n+1}
=
\Pi_\Theta
\left(
\theta_n-\eta\nabla\ell_n(\theta_n)
\right).
Theorem 9.23 — Standard regret bound
For any comparator \theta^*\in\Theta,
R_N
\le
\frac{D^2}{2\eta}
+
\frac{\eta G^2N}{2}.
Choosing
\eta
=
\frac{D}{G\sqrt N}
gives

\le
DG\sqrt N.
Proof
By projection nonexpansiveness,

\le
\|\theta_n-\eta g_n-\theta^*\|^2.
Expand:
\|\theta_{n+1}-\theta^*\|^2
\le
\|\theta_n-\theta^*\|^2
2\eta g_n^T(\theta_n-\theta^*)
+
\eta^2\|g_n\|^2.

\ell_n(\theta_n)-\ell_n(\theta^*)
\le
g_n^T(\theta_n-\theta^*).
Rearrange, sum, telescope, and use the diameter and gradient bounds. ∎

c

9.41 Bounded Self-Modification
Let the architecture update be
G_{n+1}
=
\mathcal U(G_n,c_n).
Define structural distance
d_G(G_{n+1},G_n).
Impose

\mathcal I(G_{n+1})=\mathcal I(G_n),
where \mathcal I may encode:
interface compatibility;
safety constraints;
required modules;
serialization validity;

If every accepted structural update satisfies
\mathcal I(G_{n+1})=\mathcal I(G_n),
then

 \mathcal I(G_n)=\mathcal I(G_0)
for every n.
Proof
Apply induction. ∎
This formalizes organizational continuity under bounded evolution.

9.42 Rollback Safety
Store the pre-update state
z_n^{\mathrm{backup}}=z_n.
Apply the candidate provisionally to obtain
\widetilde z_{n+1}.
If validation fails, set
z_{n+1}=z_n^{\mathrm{backup}}.
Proposition 9.26 — State restoration
If backup serialization is exact and deterministic, rollback restores the prior
computational state exactly.
Proof
The prior state is copied back without transformation. ∎
This guarantee excludes external side effects that occurred outside the saved state.

9.43 Transactional Update
A safer architecture treats a structural change as a transaction:
prepare candidate;

 validate candidate;
commit if all gates pass;
abort otherwise.
This prevents partially applied updates.
Atomicity must include all mutable components that influence future behavior.

9.44 Deterministic Replay
Let the full execution record include:
initial state;
observation sequence;
candidate order;
random seeds;
software version;
parameter values;
accepted updates.
Theorem 9.27 — Replay determinism
If every transition is deterministic given the recorded inputs and state, replay reproduces
the same trajectory exactly.
Proof
The next state is a deterministic function of recorded prior state and inputs. Induction
reproduces every step. ∎
Parallel nondeterminism, hardware-dependent arithmetic, or unrecorded external calls
can break exact replay.

9.45 Journal Statistics
Let the journal contain N evaluated corrections.
Define:

 N_H
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}h_n,
N_P
=
\text{number of accepted patches},
N_A
=
\text{number of adaptations},
N_E
=
\text{number of promoted evolutions}.
The verified heal rate is
\widehat p_H
=
\frac{N_H}{N}.
A rate without confidence intervals can be misleading when N is small.

9.46 Confidence Interval for Heal Rate
Under independent Bernoulli trials, an approximate standard error is
\sqrt{
\frac{
\widehat p_H(1-\widehat p_H)
}{
N
}
}.
A normal-approximation interval is

 \widehat p_H
\pm
z_{\alpha/2}
\sqrt{
\frac{
\widehat p_H(1-\widehat p_H)
}{
N
}
}.
For small samples or extreme rates, an exact or Wilson interval is preferable.

9.47 Selection Bias
If only favorable trials are journaled, the heal rate is biased upward.
Proposition 9.28 — Selective logging invalidates empirical rates
An empirical success fraction estimates the true trial success probability only when the
inclusion mechanism is appropriately random or fully comprehensive.
Proof
If failed trials are omitted with greater probability than successful trials, the observed
sample distribution differs from the underlying trial distribution. ∎
Complete provenance is part of verification.

9.48 Exploration and Exploitation
Let the policy mix an exploitation action a_n^* and exploratory sampling:
a_n
=
\begin{cases}
\text{exploratory action},&\text{with probability }\varepsilon_n,\\

 a_n^*,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
If
\varepsilon_n\rightarrow0,
exploration vanishes asymptotically.
If
\sum_n\varepsilon_n=\infty,
exploration still occurs infinitely often in expectation.
These two conditions form a common “greedy in the limit with infinite exploration”
pattern.

9.49 Risk-Bounded Exploration
Let the admissible exploratory set be
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{safe}}(z_n)
=
\left\{
a:
R(z_n,a)\le R_{\max}
\right\}.
Exploration samples only from this set.
This converts risk from a score penalty into a hard constraint.
A learned risk estimate may itself be wrong, so empirical safety requires conservative
calibration and external safeguards.

9.50 Contraction Before Promotion
A mathematically disciplined update order is:

 \text{propose}
\rightarrow
\text{simulate}
\rightarrow
\text{measure residual}
\rightarrow
\text{check contraction}
\rightarrow
\text{check safety}
\rightarrow
\text{validate horizon}
\rightarrow
\text{commit}.
This prevents a candidate from modifying the live system before evidence is gathered.

9.51 Contraction-Certified Healing Theorem
Theorem 9.29
Suppose a healing operator H satisfies, on a domain D,
E(H(z))
\le
\gamma E(z),
\qquad
0\le\gamma<1,
and
H(D)\subseteq D.
Then repeated healing remains in D and converges to the zero-residual set:
E(H^n(z))
\le
\gamma^nE(z)
\rightarrow0.

 Proof
Domain invariance permits repeated application. Apply Proposition 9.2. ∎
This proves residual convergence, not necessarily state convergence if multiple states
have zero residual.

9.52 State Convergence Under Error Bound
Assume the residual energy controls distance to a unique target z^*:
E(z)
\ge
c\,d(z,z^*)^2,
\qquad
c>0.
If
E(z_n)\rightarrow0,
then
d(z_n,z^*)\rightarrow0.
Proof
d(z_n,z^*)^2
\le
\frac{E(z_n)}{c}
\rightarrow0.
∎
Without such an error-bound condition, zero residual may correspond to an entire
manifold of states.

9.53 Patch Stability Under Lipschitz Dynamics

 Suppose the state transition is Lipschitz in parameters:
\|F_{\theta+\Delta\theta}(x)-F_\theta(x)\|
\le
L_\theta\|\Delta\theta\|.
If
\|\Delta\theta\|\le B_\theta,
then the one-step transition change is bounded by
L_\theta B_\theta.
This gives a direct reason for bounded patch size.

Suppose F_\theta is Lipschitz in state with constant L_x and in parameters with

Let x_n and \widetilde x_n evolve under \theta and \theta+\Delta\theta from the same
initial state.
Then
\|x_{n+1}-\widetilde x_{n+1}\|
\le
L_x
\|x_n-\widetilde x_n\|
+
L_\theta
\|\Delta\theta\|.

Theorem 9.30 — Finite-horizon deviation bound
If L_x\neq1,

 \|x_H-\widetilde x_H\|
\le
L_\theta
\|\Delta\theta\|
\frac{
L_x^H-1
}{
L_x-1
}.

\|x_H-\widetilde x_H\|
\le
HL_\theta\|\Delta\theta\|.
Proof
Iterate the affine recurrence with zero initial deviation. ∎

9.55 Promotion Under Distribution Shift
Let validation distribution be P, but deployment distribution be Q.
If loss is bounded by 0\le\ell\le L_{\max}, then
\left|
\mathbb E_Q[\ell]
\mathbb E_P[\ell]
\right|
\le
L_{\max}
\,\mathrm{TV}(P,Q),
where \mathrm{TV} is total variation distance.

 Thus validation performance transfers only when distribution shift is controlled.

9.56 Complexity Penalty
To discourage structural overgrowth, define
J_{\mathrm{promote}}
=
L_{\mathrm{validation}}
+
\lambda_C
\mathcal C(G),
where \mathcal C(G) may measure:
node count;
edge count;
description length;
runtime;
memory usage.
A candidate is promoted only if it improves the penalized objective.
This formalizes the principle that more complicated is not automatically better.

9.57 Minimum Description Perspective
If
\mathcal C(G)
approximates code length or model description length, then promotion balances fit
against complexity.
The exact penalty coefficient determines the trade-off and should not be chosen after
seeing the desired result without correction for selection bias.

9.58 Catastrophic Forgetting Metric

 Let task set be
\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_m.
Before adaptation, performance on task j is P_j^{\mathrm{before}}.
After adaptation,
P_j^{\mathrm{after}}.
Define forgetting
F_j
=
P_j^{\mathrm{before}}
P_j^{\mathrm{after}}.
A no-catastrophic-forgetting gate may require
F_j\le\delta_F
for every protected task.
Improvement on the current task is insufficient if prior capabilities collapse.

9.59 Pareto Promotion
When objectives conflict, no single weighted score may be appropriate.
A candidate c_1 dominates c_2 if it is no worse on every objective and strictly better on
at least one.
A Pareto gate promotes only nondominated candidates satisfying hard safety
constraints.
This preserves transparent trade-offs instead of hiding them in weights.

9.60 Autonomous Versus Automatic

 A system is automatic if it executes predetermined rules.
It is adaptive if internal parameters change using data.
It is self-modifying if its update rules or architecture can change.
It is autonomous only relative to a specified decision scope, resource boundary, and
supervision model.
These are distinct classifications.
No mathematical update rule alone proves consciousness, agency in the philosophical
sense, or unrestricted autonomy.

9.61 Simulation Versus Learning
A simulation updates a state according to a model:
x_{n+1}=F(x_n).
Learning changes a model component using evidence:
\theta_{n+1}
=
U(\theta_n,\text{data}).
A system can simulate without learning and learn without accurately simulating the
external world.

9.62 Adaptation Versus Evolution
Within this compendium:
adaptation is a bounded update within a fixed architecture;
evolution is a promoted change to persistent structure or policy class.
This is a formal software distinction, not a biological claim.

9.63 No-Go Result for Unverified Self-Improvement

 Theorem 9.31 — Internal score increase does not prove external improvement
Suppose the agent optimizes an internal metric S.
Then
S_{n+1}>S_n
does not imply improved real-world performance unless S is validated as a reliable
proxy for the external objective.
Proof by counterexample
Let external performance be P, and define
S=-P.
Increasing S decreases P. More subtly, a proxy may correlate during training and fail
under distribution shift. ∎
Verified recursive learning requires an independently justified evaluation criterion.

9.64 Reward Hacking
If the agent can alter the measured reward without improving the intended outcome, it
may optimize the measurement channel rather than the task.
Formally, if there exists an action a such that
R_{\mathrm{measured}}(a)
>
R_{\mathrm{measured}}(a^*)
but
U_{\mathrm{intended}}(a)
<
U_{\mathrm{intended}}(a^*),
then the measured reward is misaligned.

 Promotion gates should therefore include protected external checks not modifiable by
the candidate itself.

9.65 Verified Residual Contraction Theorem
Theorem 9.32 — Safe recursive correction
Assume a candidate correction operator C_n satisfies:
domain preservation
C_n(D)\subseteq D;
residual contraction
E(C_n(z))
\le
\gamma E(z)+\varepsilon,
\qquad
0\le\gamma<1;
bounded state change
d(C_n(z),z)\le B;
invariant preservation
\mathcal I(C_n(z))=\mathcal I(z);
external validation
the contraction estimate is measured using a criterion not altered by the candidate.
Then repeated accepted corrections remain admissible, preserve the declared invariant,
and satisfy
\limsup_{n\to\infty}E_n
\le
\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.
Proof
Domain and invariant preservation follow by induction.
The residual bound follows from Theorem 9.4.
The bounded-change condition controls per-step deviation but is not needed for the
residual inequality itself.

 External validation prevents the operator from satisfying the theorem merely by
redefining its own error metric. ∎

9.66 Promotion-Gated Evolution Theorem
Theorem 9.33 — Conditional reliability of structural promotion
Suppose each proposed structural change is:
evaluated without modifying the live state;
tested on a validation set independent of the training data;
required to exceed improvement threshold \delta>0;
required to satisfy all invariant and safety constraints;
required to repeat the improvement on q diversity-controlled trials;
committed atomically with rollback support.
Then every committed evolution has verified evidence of improvement under the stated
validation protocol and cannot leave the declared admissible class through the commit
operation.
Proof
Pure evaluation prevents pre-commit contamination.
Validation and repetition establish the stated evidence threshold.
Invariant and safety gates restrict accepted candidates to the admissible class.
Atomic commit prevents partial update.
Rollback preserves recoverability if post-commit monitoring detects failure.
The conclusion is limited to the validation protocol; it does not guarantee universal
performance. ∎

 \mathcal R
=
\mathcal E
\circ

\circ
\mathcal P

\mathcal R:

\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}},

Let a continuous signal be sampled at rate

10.4 Nyquist Condition
Theorem 10.2 — Nyquist necessity for an unambiguous ideal sinusoid
To distinguish a sinusoid of frequency f_0 from its aliases using uniform sampling, it is
necessary that
f_s>2f_0
when the signal is assumed to lie within the baseband interval
0\le f<\frac{f_s}{2}.
Proof
Sampled complex exponentials satisfy
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)n/f_s}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}

 for every integer k.
Real sinusoids additionally identify positive and negative frequencies. Restricting the
represented signal to frequencies below f_s/2 avoids overlap between mirrored spectral
replicas. ∎
For
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the ideal lower Nyquist boundary is
f_s>2.4\ \mathrm{MHz}.
Practical waveform reconstruction generally requires a substantially higher rate because
switching edges and harmonics extend well above the carrier.

10.5 Samples per Cycle
Define
N_s
=
\frac{f_s}{f_0}.
This is the number of samples per carrier period.
For example, if
f_s=100\ \mathrm{MHz},
then
N_s
=
\frac{100}{1.2}
\approx83.33.

A continuous frequency f is indistinguishable after sampling from frequencies

=
|f-kf_s|

e^{i2\pi kn}

Bt_r\approx0.35

Let the nominal sampling or switching event occur at time t_n, but the actual event

\approx
-20\log_{10}

2\pi f_0\sigma_t

and the RMS jitter error is approximately

\cos

For an inductor L and capacitor C, the ideal natural angular frequency is

=

For any driven electrical system over interval [0,T],

=

E_{\mathrm{stored}}(0)
+
E_{\mathrm{dissipated}}
+

Define efficiency

P_{\mathrm{useful,out}}

P_{\mathrm{in}}

I_{\mathrm D}

10.35 Thermal Equilibrium
Let total dissipated power be
P_{\mathrm{loss}}.

 With lumped thermal resistance
R_{\theta},
steady-state junction-temperature rise is approximately

=
P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta}.
Thus

=
T_{\mathrm{ambient}}
+
P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta}.

10.36 Electrothermal Fixed Point
Because switch resistance and loss depend on temperature, thermal equilibrium
satisfies
T_j
=
T_a
+
R_\theta P_{\mathrm{loss}}(T_j).
Theorem 10.10 — Local thermal stability criterion
A fixed point T_j^* is locally stable under a first-order thermal relaxation model if
R_\theta
\left.
\frac{dP_{\mathrm{loss}}}{dT}

<1.
Proof
Write the fixed-point iteration map

=
