10.37 Dead Time
In a half bridge, dead time prevents simultaneous conduction of both switches.
If dead time is too short, cross-conduction risk increases.
If too long, reverse conduction and waveform distortion increase.
The ideal value depends on:
propagation delay;
turn-off time;
device variation;
temperature;
gate resistance;
layout parasitics.
No universal dead-time value follows from carrier frequency alone.

10.38 Parasitic Inductance

 A current transition produces parasitic voltage
V_L
=
L_p\frac{di}{dt}.
For rapid switching, even small L_p can create significant overshoot.
Similarly,
I_C
=
C_p\frac{dv}{dt}
describes displacement current through parasitic capacitance.
These relations explain why high-frequency power-stage behavior cannot be predicted
from ideal LC values alone.

10.39 Ringing Frequency
A parasitic inductance L_p and capacitance C_p may ring at
f_r
=
\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{L_pC_p}}.
This ringing may be mistaken for a designed resonance.

observed frequency follows the predicted sensitivity.

10.40 Resonance Identification Test
Suppose an observed spectral peak is claimed to arise from L and C.

C'\!=\alpha C.

 The ideal prediction is
f_0'
=
\frac{f_0}{\sqrt\alpha}.
Proposition 10.11 — Parameter-shift falsification test
If the measured peak does not shift consistently with the predicted relationship within
uncertainty, the simple LC model is incomplete or incorrect.
Proof
The frequency dependence follows directly from
f_0=(2\pi\sqrt{LC})^{-1}.
∎

10.41 Phase-Locked Loop Model
Let reference phase be
\theta_r(t)
and controlled-oscillator phase be
\theta_o(t).
Define phase error
\phi
=
\theta_r-\theta_o.
A simple first-order sinusoidal phase model is

=
\Delta\omega
K\sin\phi,
where
\Delta\omega
=
\omega_r-\omega_{\mathrm{free}}.

10.42 Locking Condition
Theorem 10.12 — Static phase lock
A stationary phase difference exists if and only if
|\Delta\omega|\le K.
Proof
At equilibrium,
0
=
\Delta\omega-K\sin\phi_*.
Thus
\sin\phi_*
=
\frac{\Delta\omega}{K}.
A real solution exists exactly when the magnitude of the right side does not exceed one.
∎
Inside the lock range,

=
\arcsin
\left(
\frac{\Delta\omega}{K}
\right)
for the stable branch.

10.43 Stability of the Locked Phase
Linearize around equilibrium:
\phi=\phi_*+\delta.
Then
\dot\delta
\approx
-K\cos\phi_*\,\delta.
Theorem 10.13 — Stable branch condition
The equilibrium is locally stable when
K\cos\phi_*>0.
For K>0, this requires
|\phi_*|<\frac{\pi}{2}.
Proof
The scalar linearized system decays when its coefficient is negative. ∎

10.44 Locking Time Constant
The small-signal phase-error decay rate is

=
K\cos\phi_*.
Therefore
\tau_{\mathrm{lock}}
=
\frac1{
K\cos\phi_*

so

10.45 Injection Locking
An oscillator weakly driven near its natural frequency can often be reduced to an Adlertype phase equation.

10.46 Harmonic Locking
Two frequencies are harmonically related if

\frac{f_1}{f_2}
=
\frac nm.

=

An oscillator may lock such that

=
\frac pq f_d,

10.48 Rational Frequency Ratio Versus Coherence
Proposition 10.14

Frequency ratio and phase coherence are distinct measurements.

10.49 Beat Frequency
For two close sinusoids,
\cos(2\pi f_1t)+\cos(2\pi f_2t)
=
2
\cos
\left[
\pi(f_1-f_2)t
\right]
\cos
\left[
\pi(f_1+f_2)t
\right].
The envelope varies at beat frequency
f_b=|f_1-f_2|.

 A slow amplitude envelope may therefore arise from ordinary superposition rather than
nonlinear energy transfer.

10.50 Intermodulation
A nonlinear system driven at f_1 and f_2 may generate frequencies
mf_1\pm nf_2.
Second-order terms produce
f_1+f_2,
\qquad
|f_1-f_2|,
\qquad
2f_1,
\qquad
2f_2.
Third-order terms produce components such as
2f_1-f_2.
A spectral line at a combination frequency is evidence of nonlinearity, not automatically
of a new fundamental resonance.

10.51 Amplitude Modulation
For carrier f_c and modulation f_m,
v(t)
=
A
\left[
1+\mu\cos(2\pi f_mt)
\right]
\cos(2\pi f_ct).

 Expanding,
v(t)
=
A\cos(2\pi f_ct)
+
\frac{A\mu}{2}
\cos[2\pi(f_c+f_m)t]
+
\frac{A\mu}{2}
\cos[2\pi(f_c-f_m)t].
The spectrum contains the carrier and two sidebands.
Sidebands do not require multiple independent oscillators.

10.52 Frequency Modulation
For
v(t)
=
A
\cos
\left[
2\pi f_ct+\beta\sin(2\pi f_mt)
\right],
the spectrum contains infinitely many sidebands
f_c\pm nf_m
with amplitudes determined by Bessel functions J_n(\beta).
Phase modulation can therefore produce a rich harmonic pattern from one carrier.

10.53 Spectral Resolution

 For a finite observation time T_{\mathrm{obs}}, Fourier-bin spacing is approximately
\Delta f
=
\frac1{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}.
To resolve two tones separated by
\delta f,
one generally needs
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\gtrsim
\frac1{\delta f}.
Window choice affects leakage and effective resolution.

10.54 Windowing
A finite record multiplies the time signal by a window w(t).
In frequency space, this convolves the true spectrum with the window spectrum.
Trade-offs include:
main-lobe width;
side-lobe suppression;
amplitude accuracy;
noise bandwidth.
A narrow spectral peak can be an artifact of window selection or insufficient record
length.

10.55 Coherent Sampling
Coherent sampling occurs when the record contains an integer number of cycles:
f_0T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\in\mathbb Z.

 Then an ideal tone aligns with a discrete Fourier bin, reducing spectral leakage.
For N samples,
\frac{f_0}{f_s}
=
\frac{k}{N}
for integer bin index k.

10.56 Spectral Leakage
If coherent sampling is not satisfied, the finite-record transform spreads tone energy
across neighboring bins.
Leakage can resemble phase noise or sidebands.
A frequency claim should therefore state:
sample rate;
record length;
window;
bin spacing;
interpolation method;
clock reference.
10.57 Frequency Estimation Uncertainty
Even with high sample rate, frequency uncertainty is limited by:
observation duration;
signal-to-noise ratio;
phase noise;
clock stability;
model assumptions.
Sample rate determines the representable bandwidth, not by itself the ultimate
frequency resolution.

 10.58 Clock Reference Error
If the sampling clock has fractional error
\epsilon_c,
then all measured frequencies inherit approximately the same fractional scale error:
\frac{\Delta f_{\mathrm{meas}}}{f_{\mathrm{meas}}}
\approx
\epsilon_c.
A frequency reported to many digits is not meaningful unless clock accuracy supports
those digits.

10.59 Allan Variance
For fractional-frequency samples y_k averaged over time \tau, Allan variance is
\sigma_y^2(\tau)
=
\frac12
\left\langle
(\overline y_{k+1}-\overline y_k)^2
\right\rangle.
It distinguishes types of oscillator instability across averaging times.
Standard deviation of repeated frequency estimates is not always an adequate stability
measure because oscillator noise may be time correlated.

10.60 Harmonic Energy Distribution
For a periodic voltage with Fourier coefficients V_n, Parseval’s identity gives
V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2
=

 \sum_n
|V_n|^2
under consistent coefficient normalization.
The total RMS energy cannot be inferred from the fundamental amplitude alone when
harmonics are significant.

10.61 Total Harmonic Distortion
For voltage harmonics,
\operatorname{THD}
=
\frac{
\sqrt{
V_2^2+V_3^2+\cdots
}
}{
V_1
}.
A phase-locked carrier may still have high distortion.
Coherence and waveform purity are independent metrics.

10.62 Resonant Voltage Magnification
In a series resonator at resonance,
I_{\mathrm{rms}}
=
\frac{
V_{\mathrm{source,rms}}
}{R}.
The inductor voltage magnitude is

 V_L
=
\omega_0LI
=
QV_{\mathrm{source}}.
Similarly,
V_C
=
QV_{\mathrm{source}}.
The reactive voltages may greatly exceed source voltage, while ideally canceling in the
series sum.
This is voltage magnification, not energy creation.

10.63 Resonant Current Magnification
In parallel resonance, branch currents may greatly exceed source current while
canceling at the input node.
Again, internal circulating reactive current does not imply excess output power.

10.64 Coupled Resonators
For two coupled modes with uncoupled frequency \omega_0, coupling can split the
resonance into two normal-mode frequencies.
A simple symmetric model is
\ddot x_1+\omega_0^2x_1+\kappa x_2=0,
\ddot x_2+\omega_0^2x_2+\kappa x_1=0.
Define normal coordinates
x_\pm=x_1\pm x_2.

 Then
\ddot x_\pm
+
(\omega_0^2\pm\kappa)x_\pm
=
0.
Thus
\omega_\pm
=
\sqrt{\omega_0^2\pm\kappa}.
A pair of nearby spectral peaks may therefore indicate mode splitting rather than two
independent source frequencies.

10.65 Stability of Coupled Modes
The symmetric coupled system is stable only if
\omega_0^2-|\kappa|>0.
If coupling magnitude exceeds the uncoupled stiffness, one normal-mode squared
frequency becomes negative and the equilibrium is unstable.
Coupling does not always increase coherence or stability.

10.66 Parametric Resonance
A parametrically modulated oscillator may satisfy
\ddot x
+
2\zeta\omega_0\dot x
+
\omega_0^2
\left[

 1+h\cos(\Omega t)
\right]
x
=
0.
Instability regions occur near
\Omega\approx\frac{2\omega_0}{n},
especially the principal region
\Omega\approx2\omega_0.
This is fundamentally different from ordinary forced resonance.

10.67 Parametric Threshold
Damping creates a nonzero modulation threshold for parametric growth.
The exact threshold depends on detuning and model normalization.
Therefore observing growth at a rational frequency relation does not prove lossless
amplification; input energy is supplied through the time-varying parameter.

10.68 Power-Balance Audit
A defensible experimental power audit should measure:
P_{\mathrm{DC,in}},
P_{\mathrm{gate}},
P_{\mathrm{aux}},
P_{\mathrm{load,out}},
P_{\mathrm{thermal}},
and stored-energy change

 \frac{dE_{\mathrm{stored}}}{dt}.
The residual balance is
R_P
=
P_{\mathrm{in,total}}
P_{\mathrm{out,total}}
\frac{dE_{\mathrm{stored}}}{dt}.
A correct accounting should give
R_P
consistent with measurement uncertainty.

10.69 Uncertainty Propagation for Power
If
P=VI
and voltage and current uncertainties are independent,
\left(
\frac{\sigma_P}{P}
\right)^2
\approx
\left(
\frac{\sigma_V}{V}
\right)^2
+
\left(
\frac{\sigma_I}{I}
\right)^2.
For AC power with phase,

 P=VI\cos\phi,
phase uncertainty contributes approximately
\left(
\frac{\sigma_P}{P}
\right)^2
\approx
\left(
\frac{\sigma_V}{V}
\right)^2
+
\left(
\frac{\sigma_I}{I}
\right)^2
+
\tan^2\phi\,\sigma_\phi^2.
Near
\phi=\frac{\pi}{2},
real-power estimation becomes highly sensitive to phase error.

10.70 Probe Delay Error
If voltage and current measurement channels have relative delay \Delta t, phase error at
frequency f is
\Delta\phi
=
2\pi f\Delta t.
At 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz}, a delay mismatch of 1\ \mathrm{ns} creates approximately
0.432^\circ
phase error.

 When reactive power is large, this can create substantial false real-power readings.

10.71 Energy per Switching Cycle
If average power is P at switching frequency f_s, then average energy transferred or
dissipated per cycle is
E_{\mathrm{cycle}}
=
\frac P{f_s}.
At megahertz frequency, modest average power corresponds to small energy per cycle
but a very large number of repeated events.
This makes per-cycle parasitic energy important.

10.72 Scaling of Switching Loss with Frequency
If per-transition energy is approximately constant,
E_{\mathrm{tr}},
and there are N_{\mathrm{tr}} transitions per cycle, then
P_{\mathrm{tr}}
=
N_{\mathrm{tr}}
E_{\mathrm{tr}}
f_s.
Thus switching loss grows linearly with frequency until waveform, temperature, or
device behavior changes.

10.73 Frequency Optimization
Let useful power scale as P_u(f) and loss as P_\ell(f).
Define net objective

 J(f)
=
P_u(f)-\lambda P_\ell(f).
An optimal carrier satisfies
J'(f_*)=0,
with
J''(f_*)<0
for a local maximum.
A chosen frequency is justified when it optimizes a clearly stated measured or modeled
objective under constraints.

10.74 Example Loss Trade-Off
Suppose
P_u(f)
=
af,
for low-frequency throughput, while
P_\ell(f)
=
bf+cf^2.
Then
J(f)
=
(a-\lambda b)f-\lambda cf^2.
The stationary frequency is

 f_*
=
\frac{
a-\lambda b
}{
2\lambda c
}
when the numerator is positive.
This illustrates how an interior optimum can arise from competing scaling laws.
The coefficients must come from measurement or a validated physical model.

10.75 Dimensional Analysis
A frequency cannot be derived from dimensionless numbers alone.
To produce units of inverse time, a model must contain at least one dimensional scale,
such as
\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},
\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},
\frac{v}{\ell},
or
\frac E{\hbar}.
Theorem 10.15 — Dimensional necessity
A formula constructed only from pure numbers cannot yield an absolute frequency.
Proof
Dimensionless inputs combined through algebraic operations remain dimensionless. A
dimensional output requires at least one dimensional input or unit-defining constant. ∎

 Therefore 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} cannot follow solely from geometric ratios such as 48,
\varphi, 4/3, or an angle.

10.76 Scaling Nonuniqueness
Suppose a frequency is derived as
f=\frac{v}{\ell}.
Scaling the length
\ell\mapsto a\ell
changes the frequency to
f\mapsto\frac fa.
Thus the same dimensionless geometry can support infinitely many absolute
frequencies at different physical scales.
A claim of a universal frequency requires a universal dimensional constant or
independently fixed scale.

10.77 Harmonic Coincidence
Given an observed frequency f_0, many reference frequencies can be chosen such that
f_0=nf_r,
or
f_0=\frac pq f_r.
Without a prior reason to select n,p,q, harmonic numerology is underdetermined.

Proposition 10.16 — Rational-fit nonuniqueness
For any positive frequencies f_0 and f_r, rational approximations can make

 f_0/f_r
arbitrarily close to p/q.
Proof
The rational numbers are dense in the real numbers. ∎
A near-rational ratio is not compelling evidence without uncertainty bounds and a
mechanism that predicts that specific ratio in advance.

10.78 Model-Selection Criterion for a Frequency
A selected carrier is scientifically supported when competing models are compared.
For models M_k predicting frequencies f_k(\theta_k), evaluate:
prediction error;
parameter count;
uncertainty;
out-of-sample tests;
sensitivity under controlled changes.
A model that predicts 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} only after fitting the same observation has not
independently predicted it.

10.79 Falsifiable Resonance Claim
A strong claim should take the form:
Given independently measured L,C,R, the system predicts a resonance at
f_*\pm\sigma_f. Altering C by a known amount shifts the peak according to the stated
derivative, while control configurations lacking the resonant path do not show the same
response.
This is testable.
A statement that 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} is a “root frequency” without a dimensional
derivation is not yet testable enough.

 10.80 Phase-Coherence Metric
For N measured phase channels,
Z_N
=
\frac1N
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
e^{i\theta_k}.
Define
r=|Z_N|.
Then:
0\le r\le1.
A value near one indicates phase concentration.
It does not directly measure:
power efficiency;
frequency accuracy;
waveform distortion;
causal coupling;
energy generation.
These require separate metrics.

10.81 Frequency-Lock Metric
For generalized harmonic phase
\phi_k(t)
=
m\theta_{1,k}(t)-n\theta_{2,k}(t),
define

 R_{m:n}
=
\left|
\frac1N
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
e^{i\phi_k}
\right|.
This tests m:n phase locking across observations.
A stable mean generalized phase and high R_{m:n} support synchronization.

10.82 Phase-Locking Value
For repeated trials,
\operatorname{PLV}
=
\left|
\frac1N
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
e^{i\Delta\theta_k}
\right|.
PLV can be high even when amplitudes are negligible or signals share a common
artifact.
Controls must address:
common clock;
filtering;
volume conduction or electrical crosstalk;
window overlap;
reference-channel leakage.
10.83 Causal Locking Boundary
Correlation or phase coherence does not establish direction of causality.

 Possible explanations include:
oscillator A drives B;
B drives A;
a third source drives both;
measurement channels share a clock;
analysis filtering induces apparent coherence.
Perturbation experiments are needed to distinguish these cases.

10.84 Frequency-Pulling Test
If oscillator A causally influences oscillator B, changing A’s free-running frequency may
pull B within a locking range.
The observed lock boundary can be compared with an Adler-type model.
A shared measurement artifact will not necessarily reproduce the predicted detuningdependent phase lag and unlocking behavior.

10.85 Central Carrier Engineering Theorem
Theorem 10.17 — Conditional engineering validity of a selected carrier
Let a system be designed around carrier f_0. Suppose:
a physical model predicts
f_0=f(\theta)
from independently measured parameters \theta;
uncertainty propagation predicts
f_0\pm\sigma_f;
measured spectral response agrees within uncertainty;
controlled parameter changes produce the predicted frequency shifts;
phase-locking remains stable under the derived detuning and jitter bounds;
complete power accounting satisfies conservation within measurement uncertainty;
thermal and switching losses remain within specified limits.
Then f_0 is a validated engineering operating point for that system and operating
regime.

 Proof
Conditions 1–4 validate the frequency model against independent parameter and
perturbation evidence.
Condition 5 validates synchronization performance.
Condition 6 excludes unsupported energy claims.
Condition 7 establishes feasibility under the specified hardware constraints.
The conclusion is limited to the tested system and regime. ∎

10.86 Fundamental-Frequency No-Go Theorem
Theorem 10.18 — No absolute frequency from dimensionless architecture alone
Let a proposed derivation use only dimensionless integers, ratios, angles, symmetry
counts, and algebraic constants.
Then it cannot uniquely derive an absolute frequency in hertz.
Proof
All inputs are dimensionless. Algebraic combinations of dimensionless inputs remain
dimensionless. Hertz has physical dimension
T^{-1}.
Therefore a dimensional scale is missing. ∎
This applies to attempts to derive 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} solely from:
48;
24+24;
\varphi;
4/3;
53.13^\circ;
Flower-of-Life angles;
braid counts.

 A dimensional mechanism must be supplied.

10.87 Central 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} Boundary Statement
The value
1.2\ \mathrm{MHz}
may legitimately be:
a selected switching frequency;
a measured resonance;
a control carrier;
a phase-lock reference;
an optimization result;
a system-specific eigenfrequency.
It is not established as:
a universal natural constant;
a geometry-only frequency;
evidence of energy surplus;
proof of a fundamental field theory;
a unique consequence of the number 48.
Those stronger claims require independent dimensional derivation and empirical
confirmation.

10.88 Proof Boundaries
This chapter establishes:
carrier period and phase relations;
sampling and aliasing conditions;
harmonic spectra;
timing-jitter and phase-noise relations;
ideal and damped resonance equations;
quality factor, bandwidth, and ring-down;
driven-oscillator amplitude and phase;

 stored-energy and complex-power relations;
semiconductor loss accounting;
thermal fixed-point stability;
parasitic ringing and falsifiable resonance shifts;
Adler phase locking;
harmonic and subharmonic synchronization;
beat, modulation, and intermodulation spectra;
spectral-resolution and coherent-sampling limits;

It does not determine whether a particular physical device is safe, efficient, compliant, or

11.1 Mechanical State
Consider a translational mechanical coordinate
x(t),
with velocity

For a body of mass m>0, kinetic energy is

For force F, infinitesimal work is
dW=F\,dx.
Instantaneous mechanical power is
P_m
=
F\dot x.

If
F\dot x>0,
the force supplies energy to the coordinate.
If
F\dot x<0,
the force extracts energy from the coordinate.
If
F\dot x=0,
the force transfers no instantaneous power.
Proof
Power is the time derivative of work:
P_m
=
\frac{dW}{dt}

F\dot x.

11.3 Linear Spring–Mass–Damper
Consider
m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=F_{\mathrm{ext}}(t),

Multiply by \dot x:
m\ddot x\dot x
+
c\dot x^2

kx\dot x

Recognize
m\ddot x\dot x
=
\frac{d}{dt}

F_{\mathrm{ext}}\dot x.

P_{\mathrm{ext}}

{R_c+R_L}.
And indeed,
P_{\mathrm{mech,ext}}
=
P_L+P_c.

11.13 Electrical Conversion Efficiency
Define instantaneous conversion efficiency from extracted mechanical power to useful
load power:
\eta_e
=
\frac{P_L}{P_L+P_c}.
Substituting,
\eta_e
=
\frac{R_L}{R_c+R_L}.
Proposition 11.8 — Resistive conversion efficiency

 \boxed{
\eta_e
=
\frac{R_L}{R_c+R_L}
}
Proof
Cancel the common factor
k_t^2v^2/(R_c+R_L)^2.
∎
Large R_L improves electrical efficiency but reduces current and mechanical damping.

11.14 Maximum Load Power for Prescribed Velocity
Assume the mechanical velocity v is externally prescribed and unaffected by electrical
loading.
Then
P_L(R_L)
=
\frac{k_t^2v^2R_L}
{(R_c+R_L)^2}.
Differentiate:
\frac{dP_L}{dR_L}
=
k_t^2v^2
\frac{
R_c-R_L
}{
(R_c+R_L)^3
}.

 Theorem 11.9 — Resistive impedance matching
For prescribed velocity, load power is maximized when
\boxed{R_L=R_c}.
At the optimum,
P_{L,\max}
=
\frac{k_t^2v^2}{4R_c}.
Proof
The derivative vanishes at R_L=R_c. It is positive below and negative above this value.
∎
At maximum electrical power transfer, half of the converted power is lost in the coil:
\eta_e=\frac12.

11.15 Why Maximum-Power Matching Can Fail in a Coupled Suspension
In a real harvester, velocity is not fixed independently of R_L.
Changing load resistance changes damping:
c_e(R_L)
=
\frac{k_t^2}{R_c+R_L},
which changes the mechanical response amplitude and therefore changes v.
Thus the actual optimization is
P_L(R_L)
=
\frac{k_t^2R_L}

 {(R_c+R_L)^2}
v(R_L)^2.
The optimum need not satisfy
R_L=R_c.

Proposition 11.10 — Coupled optimum depends on mechanical dynamics
When velocity depends on load,
\frac{dP_L}{dR_L}
contains both the direct electrical derivative and the derivative of v(R_L).
Proof
Apply the product rule:
\frac{dP_L}{dR_L}
=
\frac{\partial P_L}{\partial R_L}
+
\frac{\partial P_L}{\partial v}
\frac{dv}{dR_L}.
The second term generally does not vanish. ∎
Maximum-power transfer must be optimized on the coupled system.

11.16 Harmonic Base Excitation
Let
y(t)=Y\cos\omega t.
For the base-excited relative equation
m\ddot r+c_t\dot r+kr=-m\ddot y,

 where
c_t=c_m+c_e,
the forcing amplitude is
m\omega^2Y.
The steady-state relative-displacement amplitude is
R(\omega)
=
\frac{
m\omega^2Y
}{
\sqrt{
(k-m\omega^2)^2
+
(c_t\omega)^2
}
}.
Relative-velocity amplitude is
V_r=\omega R.

11.17 Mean Harvested Power Under Harmonic Motion
For sinusoidal relative velocity
v(t)=V_r\cos(\omega t-\phi),
the mean-square velocity is
\langle v^2\rangle
=
\frac{V_r^2}{2}.
The mean load power is

 \overline P_L
=
\frac12
\frac{
k_t^2R_L
}{
(R_c+R_L)^2
}
V_r^2.
Substituting V_r,
\overline P_L
=
\frac12
\frac{
k_t^2R_L
}{
(R_c+R_L)^2
}
\frac{
m^2\omega^6Y^2
}{
(k-m\omega^2)^2
+
(c_t\omega)^2
}.
This equation displays the central trade-off:
increasing electrical damping improves conversion coefficient;
but excessive damping reduces relative velocity.
11.18 Optimal Total Damping at Resonance
At mechanical resonance,
k=m\omega^2,

 so
V_r
=
\frac{m\omega^3Y}{c_t\omega}
=
\frac{m\omega^2Y}{c_t}.
The mean power extracted by electromagnetic damping is
\overline P_e
=
\frac12c_eV_r^2
=
\frac12
c_e
\frac{
m^2\omega^4Y^2
}{
(c_m+c_e)^2
}.
Treating c_m as fixed, maximize
f(c_e)
=
\frac{c_e}{(c_m+c_e)^2}.
Differentiate:
f'(c_e)
=
\frac{
c_m-c_e
}{
(c_m+c_e)^3
}.

 Theorem 11.11 — Damping match at ideal resonance
For a harmonically base-excited linear oscillator at exact resonance, total
electromagnetic extraction is maximized when
\boxed{c_e=c_m}.
Proof
The derivative changes from positive to negative at c_e=c_m. ∎
This is the mechanical analogue of matching loss channels.
Useful load power is lower than total electromagnetic extraction because coil losses
must be subtracted.

11.19 Suspension Comfort Versus Harvesting
In a vehicle, maximizing relative suspension velocity may conflict with ride comfort.
Representative objectives include:
sprung-mass acceleration;
suspension travel;
dynamic tire load;
harvested power.
Define a multi-objective cost
J
=
w_a
\int a_s^2dt
+
w_r
\int r^2dt
+
w_t
\int F_t^2dt
-

 w_p
\int P_Ldt.
The negative sign on harvested power rewards energy recovery.
Different weights produce different compromises.

Proposition 11.12 — No universal optimum without an objective
A damping law cannot be called globally optimal unless the performance functional,
constraints, excitation distribution, and operating regime are specified.
Proof
Different objectives can rank the same candidate controllers differently. ∎
Maximum energy harvesting and best ride quality are generally not identical goals.

11.20 Quarter-Car Suspension Model
Let:
m_s be sprung mass;
m_u be unsprung mass;
z_s be sprung displacement;
z_u be unsprung displacement;
z_r be road input;
k_s be suspension stiffness;
c_s be suspension damping;
k_t be tire stiffness.
The equations are
m_s\ddot z_s
=
-k_s(z_s-z_u)
-c_s(\dot z_s-\dot z_u)
+
F_a,

 m_u\ddot z_u
=
k_s(z_s-z_u)
+
c_s(\dot z_s-\dot z_u)
k_t(z_u-z_r)
F_a.
Here F_a is an actuator or regenerative force applied internally between the masses.

11.21 Internal Force Cancellation
Lemma 11.13 — Suspension actuator conserves total mechanical momentum
internally
Adding the two equations cancels F_a:
m_s\ddot z_s+m_u\ddot z_u
=
-k_t(z_u-z_r).
Proof
The actuator acts with equal and opposite forces on the two masses. ∎
An internal suspension actuator redistributes motion between sprung and unsprung
masses; it does not create net external momentum.

11.22 Quarter-Car Stored Energy
Define
E_q
=
\frac12m_s\dot z_s^2
+

 \frac12m_u\dot z_u^2
+
\frac12k_s(z_s-z_u)^2
+
\frac12k_t(z_u-z_r)^2.
Because the road coordinate is time varying, differentiating the tire energy introduces
road-input power.
Let
v_r=\dot z_s-\dot z_u.
The passive damper power is
-c_sv_r^2.
The actuator power transferred into the mechanical suspension is
P_a
=
F_av_r.

Theorem 11.14 — Quarter-car energy balance
\frac{dE_q}{dt}
=
-c_sv_r^2
+
F_av_r
k_t(z_u-z_r)\dot z_r.
Proof
Multiply each mass equation by its corresponding velocity, add, and differentiate the
spring energies. ∎
The road-input power is

 P_{\mathrm{road}}
=
-k_t(z_u-z_r)\dot z_r.
The actuator is regenerative when
F_av_r<0.

11.23 Regenerative Force Sign
Definition 11.2 — Instantaneously regenerative force
A suspension force is instantaneously regenerative if
P_a=F_av_r<0.
The extracted mechanical power is
P_{\mathrm{ext}}=-F_av_r>0.
A force may improve ride while consuming energy when
F_av_r>0.
Thus active control and regeneration are not synonymous.

11.24 Semi-Active Damping Constraint
A semi-active damper cannot supply net mechanical energy.
Its force must satisfy
F_{\mathrm{sa}}v_r\le0.
A variable-damping law has form
F_{\mathrm{sa}}
=
-c(t)v_r,

 with
c_{\min}\le c(t)\le c_{\max},
\qquad
c_{\min}\ge0.
Then
F_{\mathrm{sa}}v_r
=
-c(t)v_r^2
\le0.

Theorem 11.15 — Passivity of bounded variable damping
Any damping law
F=-c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x
with
c(t,x,\dot x)\ge0
is instantaneously dissipative.
Proof
F\dot x
=
-c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x^2
\le0.
∎
The coefficient may be nonlinear, state dependent, or time varying without violating
passivity, provided it remains nonnegative.

11.25 Skyhook Damping

 An ideal skyhook controller applies force approximately proportional to sprung-mass
absolute velocity:
F_{\mathrm{sky}}
=
-c_{\mathrm{sky}}\dot z_s.
A physical suspension actuator acts between the two masses, so the desired force is
implemented conditionally or approximately.
A common semi-active logic selects high damping when the available damper force
opposes sprung-mass motion:
\dot z_s
(\dot z_s-\dot z_u)>0.
Otherwise, low damping is selected.

11.26 Passivity Projection
Suppose an active controller requests force
F_d.
To enforce semi-active behavior, project it onto the dissipative force set.
For relative velocity v_r\neq0, require
Fv_r\le0.
With force bound |F|\le F_{\max}, the admissible interval is:
F\in[-F_{\max},0]
when v_r>0, and
F\in[0,F_{\max}]
when v_r<0.

 Proposition 11.16 — Closest passive force
The Euclidean projection of F_d onto the admissible interval gives the minimum-change
passive approximation.
Proof
Projection onto a closed convex interval uniquely minimizes squared distance to F_d. ∎
This provides a rigorous safety layer around an unconstrained controller.

11.27 Clipped-Optimal Regenerative Control
Suppose an unconstrained optimal-control law requests
F^*(t).
A regenerative implementation may use
F_{\mathrm{regen}}
=
\Pi_{\mathcal F(v_r)}
(F^*),
where
\mathcal F(v_r)
=
\{F:Fv_r\le0,\ |F|\le F_{\max}\}.
This preserves the requested force whenever it is already regenerative and clips it
otherwise.

11.28 Active Suspension Power
An active actuator may draw electrical power
P_{\mathrm{elec,in}}

 while delivering mechanical power
P_{\mathrm{mech}}
=
F_av_r.
Under motoring operation,
P_{\mathrm{mech}}>0.
Under regeneration,
P_{\mathrm{mech}}<0.
A bidirectional power converter can exchange energy with storage in both directions.

11.29 Bidirectional Efficiency
Let \eta_m be motoring efficiency and \eta_g be generating efficiency.
For motoring:
P_{\mathrm{elec,in}}
=
\frac{
P_{\mathrm{mech,out}}
}{
\eta_m
}.
For generation:
P_{\mathrm{elec,out}}
=
\eta_g
P_{\mathrm{mech,in}}.
Both satisfy
0<\eta_m,\eta_g\le1.

 Round-trip efficiency is
\eta_{\mathrm{rt}}
=
\eta_m\eta_g
before storage losses.

11.30 Net Energy Recovery
Over interval [0,T], define generated electrical energy
E_g
=
\int_0^T
\max(0,-F_av_r)\eta_g\,dt.
Define consumed actuator energy
E_c
=
\int_0^T
\frac{
\max(0,F_av_r)
}{
\eta_m
}
\,dt.
Auxiliary electronics consume energy E_{\mathrm{aux}}.
Net recovery is
E_{\mathrm{net}}
=
E_g-E_c-E_{\mathrm{aux}}.
A regenerative suspension can have positive gross generation but negative net energy
after actuation and electronics.

 11.31 Energy-Neutral Control
Definition 11.3 — Energy-neutral operating horizon
The controller is energy neutral over [0,T] if
E_g
\ge
E_c+E_{\mathrm{aux}}.
This is a horizon-based statement, not an instantaneous one.
A controller may consume energy during one event and recover it during another.

11.32 Storage Dynamics
Let storage energy be E_b.
A simplified model is
\dot E_b
=
\eta_cP_{\mathrm{charge}}
\frac{
P_{\mathrm{discharge}}
}{
\eta_d
}
P_{\mathrm{self}},
with bounds
E_{\min}
\le
E_b

 \le
E_{\max}.
A controller requesting regeneration when storage is full must divert or dissipate the
energy elsewhere.

11.33 State-of-Charge Constraint
Let normalized state of charge be
s=\frac{E_b-E_{\min}}{E_{\max}-E_{\min}}.
Then
0\le s\le1.
A constrained controller must satisfy forward invariance of this interval.
For example, at s=1,
\dot s\le0,
and at s=0,
\dot s\ge0.

Theorem 11.17 — Interval invariance condition
For scalar storage state s\in[0,1], if
f(0,u)\ge0
and
f(1,u)\le0
for every admissible boundary control, then solutions cannot leave the interval through
either boundary under standard uniqueness assumptions.
Proof

 At the lower boundary, the vector field does not point outward. At the upper boundary, it
also does not point outward. This is the one-dimensional tangent-cone condition for
invariance. ∎

11.34 Heave Natural Frequency
For a single sprung mass with effective suspension stiffness k_s,
\omega_h
=
\sqrt{\frac{k_s}{m_s}},
and
f_h
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\sqrt{\frac{k_s}{m_s}}.
This is the ideal undamped heave frequency.

11.35 Wheel-Hop Frequency
Ignoring coupling for a first approximation, unsprung wheel-hop frequency is
\omega_w
\approx
\sqrt{
\frac{k_t+k_s}{m_u}
}.
Because m_u\ll m_s and k_t is high, wheel-hop frequency is typically higher than body
heave frequency.
Exact normal frequencies follow from the coupled eigenvalue problem.

11.36 Quarter-Car Eigenvalue Problem

 For the undamped fixed-road system,
M\ddot q+Kq=0,
with
q
=
\begin{bmatrix}
z_s\\z_u
\end{bmatrix},
M
=
\begin{bmatrix}
m_s&0\\
0&m_u
\end{bmatrix},
and
K
=
\begin{bmatrix}
k_s&-k_s\\
-k_s&k_s+k_t
\end{bmatrix}.
Normal frequencies satisfy
\det(K-\omega^2M)=0.

Theorem 11.18 — Quarter-car characteristic equation
m_sm_u\omega^4
\left[
m_s(k_s+k_t)+m_uk_s
\right]\omega^2

 +
k_sk_t
=
0.
Proof
Compute the determinant:
\det
\begin{bmatrix}
k_s-m_s\omega^2&-k_s\\
-k_s&k_s+k_t-m_u\omega^2
\end{bmatrix}
=0.
Expanding and simplifying gives the polynomial. ∎
Its two positive roots correspond approximately to body heave and wheel hop.

11.37 Positivity of Quarter-Car Frequencies
Assume
m_s,m_u,k_s,k_t>0.
The quadratic in \lambda=\omega^2 has:
positive sum of roots;
positive product of roots.
Its discriminant is nonnegative because the generalized stiffness problem has real
eigenvalues.
Therefore both squared frequencies are positive.

11.38 Damped State-Space Model
Define state

 x
=
\begin{bmatrix}
z_s-z_u\\
z_u-z_r\\
\dot z_s\\
\dot z_u
\end{bmatrix}.
Then
\dot x=Ax+B_uu+B_rw,
where:
u=F_a;
w represents road velocity or acceleration, depending on state definition.
This form supports linear control, estimation, and optimization.
The exact matrices must be derived consistently from the chosen coordinates.

11.39 Controllability
For
\dot x=Ax+Bu,
the controllability matrix is
\mathcal C
=
\begin{bmatrix}
B&AB&A^2B&\cdots&A^{n-1}B
\end{bmatrix}.
The system is controllable if
\operatorname{rank}\mathcal C=n.

 A suspension actuator may fail to control a mode if its force direction is orthogonal to
that mode in generalized coordinates.

11.40 Observability
With measurements
y=Cx,
the observability matrix is
\mathcal O
=
\begin{bmatrix}
C\\
CA\\
CA^2\\
\vdots\\
CA^{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
The state is observable if
\operatorname{rank}\mathcal O=n.
A controller requiring unmeasured suspension velocity must use sensing, differentiation,
or an observer.

11.41 Linear Quadratic Control
For
\dot x=Ax+Bu,
define cost
J
=
\int_0^\infty

 \left(
x^TQx+u^TRu
\right)dt,
with
Q\succeq0,
\qquad
R\succ0.
The optimal state feedback is
u=-Kx,
where
K=R^{-1}B^TP
and P solves the algebraic Riccati equation
A^TP+PA-PBR^{-1}B^TP+Q=0.
This controller generally consumes energy and is not automatically regenerative.

11.42 Regeneration-Aware Optimal Control
Include electrical power or storage energy in the objective:
J
=
\int
\left[
x^TQx
+
u^TRu
\lambda P_{\mathrm{regen}}(x,u)
\right]dt.
Because

 P_{\mathrm{regen}}
=
-\min(0,uv_r)
is nonsmooth, practical formulations may introduce auxiliary variables or piecewise
models.
The resulting controller balances ride and energy recovery explicitly.

11.43 Passivity-Based Control
Let a mechanical system have storage function H(x) satisfying
\dot H
=
y^Tu
D(x),
\qquad
D(x)\ge0.
If feedback is
u=-Ky,
\qquad
K\succeq0,
then
\dot H
=
-y^TKy-D(x)
\le0.

Theorem 11.19 — Passive output feedback stability
If H is positive definite and radially unbounded, and the largest invariant set in

 \{\dot H=0\}
is the equilibrium, then the equilibrium is asymptotically stable.
Proof
The storage function is a Lyapunov function. Apply LaSalle’s invariance principle. ∎
This provides a strong route to safe damping control.

11.44 Port-Hamiltonian Form
An electromechanical suspension may be written
\dot z
=
[J(z)-R(z)]
\nabla H(z)
+
G(z)u,
where:
J^T=-J represents energy-conserving interconnection;
R\succeq0 represents dissipation;
H is stored energy;
u is external input.
Then
\dot H
=
-\nabla H^TR\nabla H
+
y^Tu,
with
y=G^T\nabla H.
This structure exposes conservation and dissipation directly.

 11.45 Skew-Symmetric Interconnection
Lemma 11.20
For any vector g and skew-symmetric matrix J,
g^TJg=0.
Proof
g^TJg
=
(g^TJg)^T
=
g^TJ^Tg
=
-g^TJg.
Therefore the scalar equals its negative and must be zero. ∎
The J-term redistributes energy but does not create or destroy it.

11.46 Mechanical Impedance
For harmonic motion with phasor velocity V, mechanical impedance is
Z_m(\omega)
=
\frac F V.
For a mass–spring–damper,
Z_m(\omega)
=
c
+
i
\left(

 \omega m-\frac{k}{\omega}
\right).
At resonance,
\omega m-\frac{k}{\omega}=0,
so the impedance is purely resistive:
Z_m=c.

11.47 Electrical Reflection into Mechanical Impedance
The transducer with electrical impedance
Z_e(\omega)
reflects a mechanical impedance
Z_{\mathrm{em}}(\omega)
=
\frac{k_t^2}{Z_e(\omega)}
under the chosen sign convention.
If
Z_e=R+iX,
then
Z_{\mathrm{em}}
=
k_t^2
\frac{R-iX}{R^2+X^2}.
Its real part gives damping:
c_e(\omega)
=

 k_t^2
\frac{R}{R^2+X^2}.
Its imaginary part modifies apparent stiffness or inertia.

11.48 Inductive Roll-Off
For
Z_e=R+i\omega L,
the reflected damping is
c_e(\omega)
=
\frac{k_t^2R}
{R^2+\omega^2L^2}.
At low frequency,
c_e\approx\frac{k_t^2}{R}.
At high frequency,
c_e\sim
\frac{k_t^2R}{\omega^2L^2}.
Thus coil inductance reduces high-frequency damping and harvesting.

11.49 Reactive Compensation
A capacitor can compensate coil inductance near a target frequency.
For series electrical impedance,
Z_e
=
R+i
\left(

 \omega L-\frac1{\omega C}
\right).
At electrical resonance,
\omega L=\frac1{\omega C},
so
Z_e=R
and reflected damping is maximized for that resistance.
Reactive compensation changes bandwidth and voltage stress and must be analyzed
with parasitics.

11.50 Adjustable Damping Through Power Electronics
A controlled converter can emulate an effective resistance
R_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)
at the generator terminals.
Then
c_e(t)
\approx
\frac{k_t^2}{R_c+R_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)}
in the quasi-static regime.
This enables semi-active damping without physically changing the transducer.
The converter still has switching and conduction losses.

11.51 Negative Resistance Boundary
If the converter emulates

 R_{\mathrm{eff}}<-R_c,
the denominator becomes negative and
c_e<0.
The transducer then injects mechanical energy rather than harvesting it.
This is active behavior and can destabilize the suspension.

Theorem 11.21 — Negative damping instability of a simple oscillator
For
m\ddot x+c_t +kx=0,
if
c_t<0,
the equilibrium is unstable.
Proof
The characteristic equation is
m\lambda^2+c_t\lambda+k=0.
The sum of roots is
-\frac{c_t}{m}>0.
Therefore at least one root has positive real part. ∎
Active negative damping requires additional stabilizing control.

11.52 Saturation

ẋ

Real regenerative force is bounded:

 |F_a|
\le
F_{\max}.
Generator current is bounded:
|i|
\le
I_{\max}.
Since
F_a=k_ti,
the current limit gives
|F_a|
\le
k_tI_{\max}.
Voltage limits also constrain force at high speed because
e=k_tv.

11.53 Voltage-Limited Regeneration
For a DC bus with allowable converter voltage V_{\max},
|k_tv-L\dot i-R_ci|
\le
V_{\max}.
At high velocity, back EMF may exceed converter voltage capability, limiting current
control.
Field weakening or alternative winding configurations may be needed, each with tradeoffs.

11.54 Force–Velocity Feasible Region

 A simple quasi-static electrical relation is
V
=
k_tv-R_ci.
With
F=k_ti,
V
=
k_tv-\frac{R_c}{k_t}F.
Voltage and current limits define a feasible region in the (v,F) plane.
A requested damping law outside this region cannot be realized.

11.55 Harvested Power Bound
Under current limit,
|i|\le I_{\max},
the instantaneous electrical conversion power satisfies
|P_{\mathrm{conv}}|
=
|k_tvi|
\le
k_t|v|I_{\max}.
Under force limit,
|F|\le F_{\max},
mechanical extraction obeys

 P_{\mathrm{ext}}
\le
F_{\max}|v|.
These are actuator-envelope bounds.

11.56 Cauchy–Schwarz Energy Bound
Over a horizon [0,T],
E_h
=
\int_0^T
c_e(t)v(t)^2dt.
If
0\le c_e(t)\le c_{\max},
then
E_h
\le
c_{\max}
\int_0^T v(t)^2dt.
Thus harvested mechanical energy is bounded by the velocity-energy content of
suspension motion.

11.57 Road-Input Upper Bound
From the energy balance,
E_{\mathrm{harvested}}
+
E_{\mathrm{other\,loss}}
=
E_{\mathrm{road\,input}}

 \Delta E_{\mathrm{stored}}
over a horizon.
Therefore
E_{\mathrm{harvested}}
\le
E_{\mathrm{road\,input}}
+
E_{\mathrm{initial\,stored}}
when final stored energy is nonnegative.
No passive suspension can harvest more energy than enters from excitation plus
released initial storage.

Theorem 11.22 — Passive harvesting upper bound
For a passive system beginning with stored energy E(0)\ge0,
E_{\mathrm{useful,out}}(T)
\le
E_{\mathrm{external,in}}(T)+E(0).
Proof
Integrate the total energy balance. All dissipative losses and final stored energy are
nonnegative. ∎
This excludes sustained energy-positive operation without a corresponding external
energy source.

11.58 Terrain Energy Source
A vehicle traversing rough terrain exchanges energy among:
propulsion system;

 vehicle kinetic energy;
gravitational potential;
suspension storage;
tire deformation;
terrain deformation;
thermal dissipation.
Harvesting suspension motion may slightly increase the propulsion energy required to
maintain speed because added damping resists motion induced by the terrain.
The full vehicle-energy balance must include this effect.

11.59 Constant-Speed Propulsion Penalty
If suspension harvesting adds mean resisting force projected along vehicle travel,
\overline F_{\mathrm{res}},
then maintaining speed V_x requires additional propulsion power approximately
P_{\mathrm{prop,extra}}
=
\overline F_{\mathrm{res}}V_x.
This quantity may exceed, equal, or be less than recovered electrical power depending
on the mechanical pathways and efficiency.
A suspension harvester can still be valuable for damping and recovering energy that
would otherwise become heat, but it cannot be evaluated from generator output alone.

11.60 Regeneration Versus Added Drag
Proposition 11.23
Positive electrical generation does not prove reduced total vehicle-energy consumption.
Proof

 The generator may increase mechanical resistance, causing the traction system to
supply additional energy. Net benefit requires comparing recovered energy with added
propulsion and conversion losses. ∎
The correct metric is vehicle-level net energy, not isolated generator output.

11.61 Random Road Input
Road profiles are often modeled as stochastic processes with power spectral density
S_r(\omega).
For a linear system with transfer function from road input to relative velocity
H_v(\omega),
the relative-velocity spectrum is
S_v(\omega)
=
|H_v(\omega)|^2S_r(\omega).
Mean-square velocity is
\mathbb E[v^2]
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
S_v(\omega)\,d\omega.

11.62 Mean Harvested Power Under Stationary Random Excitation
For constant effective damping c_e,
\overline P_e
=
c_e\mathbb E[v^2].
Therefore

 \overline P_e
=
\frac{c_e}{2\pi}
\int
|H_v(\omega;c_e)|^2
S_r(\omega)\,d\omega.
Because H_v depends on c_e, maximizing average power requires optimizing the full
integral.

11.63 Stochastic Optimization
Let road spectra vary with road class and speed.
Define expected objective
J(c_e)
=
\mathbb E_{\rho}
\left[
w_pP_h
w_aA_s
w_tT_d
\right],
where \rho indexes operating conditions.
A robust damping law maximizes expected or worst-case performance over a specified
distribution or uncertainty set.
A controller optimized on one road profile may perform poorly elsewhere.

11.64 Adaptive Damping
Let the damping coefficient be adjusted according to estimated state:

 c_e(t)
=
\pi(\hat x(t)).
To retain passivity, enforce
0\le c_e(t)\le c_{\max}.
Then instantaneous extracted mechanical power is
P_e=c_e(t)v_r^2\ge0.
The electrical useful output remains
P_L=\eta_e(t)P_e
after conversion loss.

11.65 Estimation Error
Suppose estimated relative velocity is
\hat v=v+\varepsilon_v.
A requested force
F=-c\hat v
has true mechanical power
P
=
Fv
=
-cv^2-c\varepsilon_vv.
The second term may be positive enough to violate passivity.

Theorem 11.24 — Robust passivity condition with bounded velocity error

 Assume
|\varepsilon_v|\le\bar\varepsilon.
For force
F=-c\hat v,
a sufficient condition for
Fv\le0
is
|\hat v|\ge\bar\varepsilon
and force sign chosen to oppose every true velocity consistent with the estimate.
Explanation
When the uncertainty interval for v includes both signs, no nonzero force based only on
\hat v can guarantee opposition to the true motion. A safe controller may set force to
zero or minimum damping in that region.

11.66 Passivity Observer
Define cumulative controller energy exchange
E_c(t)
=
\int_0^t
F_a(\tau)v_r(\tau)\,d\tau.
A passive controller should not allow cumulative supplied energy to exceed an allowed
energy tank.
A passivity observer tracks E_c, and a passivity controller modifies commands when the
energy budget would be violated.

11.67 Energy Tank

 Let E_T\ge0 be a virtual stored-energy state:
\dot E_T
=
-P_a-P_{\mathrm{loss}},
under a selected convention.
Active action is permitted only when sufficient tank energy exists.
Regenerative events refill the tank.

Theorem 11.25 — Passivity with a nonnegative energy tank
If:
total storage is
H_{\mathrm{tot}}=H_{\mathrm{plant}}+E_T;
the tank is constrained by
E_T\ge0;
active power is drawn only from E_T;
then the combined plant–controller system remains passive relative to external ports,
assuming all internal accounting is exact.
Proof
Active controller output decreases E_T by the same amount it increases plant energy.
Internal exchange cancels in the total storage derivative. Nonnegative dissipation
remains. ∎
This is a formal method for mixing active ride control with previously recovered energy.

11.68 Magnetic Spring Force
A nonlinear magnetic spring may have potential
U_m(x),
with force

 F_m(x)
=
-\frac{dU_m}{dx}.
Its tangent stiffness is
k_m(x)
=
\frac{d^2U_m}{dx^2}.
Local stability at equilibrium x_* requires
U_m'(x_*)=0
and
U_m''(x_*)>0.

11.69 Negative Stiffness
A magnetic arrangement may exhibit a region where
k_m(x)<0.
Negative stiffness can reduce effective suspension stiffness when combined with a
positive mechanical spring.
Total tangent stiffness is
k_{\mathrm{tot}}
=
k_s+k_m.
Local static stability requires
k_{\mathrm{tot}}>0.

Theorem 11.26 — Static instability under negative total stiffness
For potential U near equilibrium,

 U(x_*+\delta)
=
U(x_*)
+
\frac12k_{\mathrm{tot}}\delta^2
+
o(\delta^2).
If
k_{\mathrm{tot}}<0,
the equilibrium is not a local minimum.
Proof
Small nonzero \delta lowers the potential. ∎
Negative stiffness must be bounded and stabilized by positive stiffness or control.

11.70 Progressive Magnetic Spring
A progressive spring has increasing tangent stiffness:
\frac{dk_m}{dx}>0
over the operating range, or more generally stiffness magnitude grows with
displacement.
For a polynomial potential
U(x)
=
\frac12k_2x^2
+
\frac14k_4x^4,
\qquad
k_2,k_4>0,
force is

 F=-k_2x-k_4x^3,
and tangent stiffness is
k_{\mathrm{tan}}
=
k_2+3k_4x^2>0.
This yields soft central response and stronger end-stroke resistance.

11.71 Nonlinear Damping
A nonlinear damper may satisfy
F_d
=
-c_1v-c_3v^3,
with
c_1,c_3\ge0.
Power is
P_d
=
F_dv
=
-c_1v^2-c_3v^4
\le0.
Proposition 11.27 — Passivity of odd monotone damping
Any force law
F_d=-g(v)
with
vg(v)\ge0

 is dissipative.
Proof
F_dv=-vg(v)\le0.
∎

11.72 Hysteretic Damping
If force depends on internal hysteresis state h,
F=F(x,v,h),
instantaneous force–velocity sign may not always be nonpositive because energy can
be temporarily stored and returned.
Passivity must then be tested with an augmented storage function
H(x,h).
A loop area in the force–displacement plane represents net energy dissipated per cycle:
E_{\mathrm{cycle}}
=
\oint F\,dx.
The sign depends on the plotting convention.

11.73 Eddy-Current Damping
For a conductor moving through a magnetic field at sufficiently low speed, induced
current can produce approximately viscous force:
F_e=-cv.
At higher speed or frequency, skin effect, inductance, geometry, and field nonuniformity
make the damping frequency dependent.

 The electrical energy is primarily dissipated as heat unless the induced current is routed
into a useful load.
Eddy-current damping alone is not necessarily regenerative.

11.74 Piezoelectric Harvester Model
A simplified piezoelectric transducer can be written
F=kx+\theta v_p,
q=\theta x+C_pv_p,
where:
v_p is electrical voltage;
q is charge;
\theta is coupling coefficient;
C_p is capacitance.
The reciprocal coupling coefficient appears in both mechanical and electrical equations
under a consistent energy formulation.

11.75 Piezoelectric Stored Energy
A quadratic electromechanical energy may be written
H
=
\frac12kx^2
\theta xv_p
+
\frac12C_pv_p^2
under one choice of independent variables.
Positive definiteness requires

 k>0,
\qquad
C_p>0,
\qquad
kC_p-\theta^2>0.

Theorem 11.28 — Coupling stability condition
The quadratic form
\frac12
\begin{bmatrix}
x&v_p
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
k&-\theta\\
-\theta&C_p
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x\\v_p
\end{bmatrix}
is positive definite if and only if
k>0
and
kC_p-\theta^2>0.
Proof
Apply the positive-definite criterion for a symmetric 2\times2 matrix. ∎
Too-strong coupling relative to the selected uncoupled coefficients would make the
assumed quadratic energy unphysical.

11.76 Hydraulic Energy Recovery

 For hydraulic pressure p and volumetric flow Q,
P_h=pQ.
An accumulator stores energy through fluid compression.
A hydraulic motor–generator may convert this flow into electricity.
Losses include:
pressure drop;
leakage;
throttling;
pump/motor inefficiency;
generator loss;
accumulator hysteresis.
A throttling damper dissipates energy; a controlled hydraulic circuit may recover part of
it.

11.77 Rotary Conversion
A ball screw or rack mechanism may convert suspension velocity v into generator speed
\omega_g=Gv,
where G is a kinematic ratio with suitable units.
Generator torque \tau_g reflects mechanical force
F=G\tau_g
under ideal power preservation:
Fv=\tau_g\omega_g.
Friction, inertia, backlash, and screw efficiency modify these relations.

11.78 Reflected Inertia

 A rotary inertia J_g reflected through ratio G appears as translational inertia
m_{\mathrm{ref}}
=
J_gG^2.
Proof
Rotary kinetic energy is
\frac12J_g\omega_g^2
=
\frac12J_gG^2v^2.
Equate to
\frac12m_{\mathrm{ref}}v^2.
∎
High conversion ratios increase generator speed but also increase reflected inertia
quadratically.

11.79 Reflected Damping
A rotary damping torque
\tau=-b_g\omega_g
reflects as translational force
F=-G\tau
under sign convention, giving equivalent damping
c_{\mathrm{ref}}
=
b_gG^2.
Again, the ratio enters quadratically.

 11.80 Mechanical Backlash Boundary
Backlash creates a dead zone in which suspension motion does not transmit
continuously to the generator.
This introduces:
impact;
hysteresis;
noise;
delayed damping;
control nonlinearity.
A linear regenerative-damping model is invalid inside the backlash transition unless
augmented.

11.81 Fatigue and Harvesting
Energy recovery may increase force cycles or local stress.
For stress amplitude \sigma_a, fatigue life may be approximated by an S-N relation
\sigma_a^mN=C
over a limited material regime.
A design maximizing recovered power but sharply reducing fatigue life may be
unacceptable.
Structural durability must be part of the objective or constraints.

11.82 Thermal Limit of a Generator
Copper loss is
P_c=i_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R_c(T).
Resistance varies approximately as

 R_c(T)
=
R_0
\left[
1+\alpha(T-T_0)
\right].
Higher temperature increases loss, reducing allowable continuous current.
A transient high-power event may be feasible even when continuous operation is not.

11.83 Regenerative Damping Coefficient Under Thermal Drift
Because
c_e
=
\frac{k_t^2}{R_c(T)+R_L},
increasing coil resistance reduces effective damping for a fixed load.
Thus suspension behavior can drift with temperature unless compensated.

11.84 Fault Modes
A regenerative suspension should account for:
open circuit;
short circuit;
converter failure;
sensor failure;
overtemperature;
storage full;
storage disconnected;
communication loss;
mechanical jam.
Open circuit gives approximately

 i=0,
\qquad
c_e\approx0.
Short circuit gives high damping approximately
c_e\approx\frac{k_t^2}{R_c}
subject to inductance and current limits.
The safe mechanical behavior of both extremes must be evaluated.

11.85 Fail-Safe Passive Mode
A robust architecture may default to a passive damping path upon loss of control.
If the fallback force satisfies
Fv_r\le0
and remains within structural limits, loss of computation does not produce active
instability.
This is an architectural safety property rather than a performance guarantee.

11.86 Robust Stability with Damping Uncertainty
Consider
m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=0,
where
c\in[c_{\min},c_{\max}].
If
m>0,
\qquad
k>0,

 \qquad
c_{\min}>0,
then every member of the uncertainty family is asymptotically stable.
Proof
The characteristic polynomial
m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k
has positive coefficients for every admissible c. The Routh–Hurwitz criterion for a
second-order polynomial gives negative-real-part roots. ∎
If c_{\min}=0, the system may be neutrally stable but not asymptotically stable.

11.87 Time-Varying Damping
For
m\ddot x+c(t)\dot x+kx=0
with
c(t)\ge0,
energy satisfies
\dot E=-c(t)\dot x^2\le0.
Proposition 11.29 — Lyapunov stability under nonnegative time-varying damping
The origin is Lyapunov stable.
Proof
The total mechanical energy is positive definite and nonincreasing. ∎
Asymptotic convergence requires sufficient persistent damping; c(t) could vanish too
often to force decay.

 11.88 Persistent Damping Condition
Suppose there exist T>0 and \alpha>0 such that
\int_t^{t+T}c(\tau)\,d\tau
\ge\alpha
for every t.
Under suitable oscillator observability conditions, this persistent excitation of damping
can imply asymptotic or exponential decay.
The exact theorem depends on the time-varying system and cannot be inferred from c(t)
\ge0 alone.

11.89 Adaptive Damping Stability
Let
c(t)=c_0+\Delta c(t),
with
c_0>0
and
\Delta c(t)\ge-c_0.
Then total damping remains nonnegative.
If adaptation is additionally bounded,
|\Delta c(t)|\le B_c,
the force remains bounded by
|F_d|
\le
(c_0+B_c)|v|.

 This gives a simple robust passivity envelope.

11.90 Energy-Harvesting Controller Audit
A complete audit should report:
mechanical equations;
transducer equations;
force and EMF constants;
electrical impedance;
converter efficiency;
storage dynamics;
road-input model;
power-flow sign conventions;
suspension comfort metrics;
tire-load metrics;
actuator force, current, voltage, travel, and temperature limits;
net energy after auxiliary consumption;
sensitivity to speed and road class;
failure-mode behavior;
independent validation.
11.91 Gross Versus Net Harvested Energy
Define:
E_{\mathrm{gross}}
=
\int P_{\mathrm{generator,out}}dt.
Define total auxiliary and conversion cost:
E_{\mathrm{cost}}
=
E_{\mathrm{converter\,loss}}
+
E_{\mathrm{control}}
+

 E_{\mathrm{sensing}}
+
E_{\mathrm{storage\,loss}}.
Then
E_{\mathrm{net}}
=
E_{\mathrm{gross}}-E_{\mathrm{cost}}.
If an active suspension also consumes mechanical actuation energy, that must be
included separately.

11.92 Comparison with Conventional Damping
A regenerative damper should be compared with a baseline damper that would
otherwise dissipate
E_{\mathrm{baseline}}
=
\int c_bv_r^2dt.
Define recovery fraction
\eta_{\mathrm{rec}}
=
\frac{
E_{\mathrm{net}}
}{
E_{\mathrm{baseline}}
}.
This metric can exceed one only if the regenerative design also changes the motion so
that more mechanical energy enters the suspension than in the baseline. It would not
mean conversion efficiency above 100%.

11.93 Equivalent Damping Match

 To preserve comparable ride behavior, compare systems at equal effective damping or
equal comfort metrics.
Otherwise a harvester may appear to recover more energy merely because it allows
larger suspension motion or imposes harsher damping.
Fair benchmarking requires matched operating constraints.

11.94 Control-Barrier Constraint for Suspension Travel
Let suspension travel satisfy
|r|\le r_{\max}.
Define barrier function
h(r)=r_{\max}^2-r^2.
The safe set is
\mathcal S=\{r:h(r)\ge0\}.
A control-barrier condition may require
\dot h+\alpha h\ge0.
Since
\dot h=-2r\dot r,
the condition is
-2r\dot r
+
\alpha(r_{\max}^2-r^2)
\ge0.
Higher-order barrier methods are required when the control enters acceleration rather
than velocity directly.

 11.95 Tire-Contact Constraint
A simplified tire normal force is
F_t
=
F_{t0}
+
k_t(z_r-z_u)
under an appropriate reference convention.
Loss of contact occurs when
F_t\le0.
A controller optimizing harvested power must preserve
F_t>0
with an appropriate safety margin.
Maximum energy recovery is unacceptable if it causes wheel lift or severe tire-force
variation.

11.96 Peak Force Constraint
For damper force
F_d=-c_ev_r,
a force limit gives
c_e
\le
\frac{F_{\max}}{|v_r|}
when v_r\neq0.
Thus the maximum allowable damping coefficient decreases at high relative velocity.

 A constant high damping command may saturate during impacts.

11.97 Model Predictive Control
At each time step, solve
\min_{u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}}
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
\ell(x_k,u_k)
+
V_f(x_N)
subject to:
x_{k+1}=f(x_k,u_k,w_k),
u_kv_{r,k}\le0
for regenerative operation,
|u_k|\le F_{\max},
|r_k|\le r_{\max},
and storage constraints.
Only the first control input is applied, then the optimization is repeated.

11.98 Recursive Feasibility
A model-predictive controller is recursively feasible if feasibility at one step implies
feasibility at the next under the applied control and admissible disturbances.
This usually requires:
a terminal invariant set;
a backup control law;
disturbance margins.
Feasibility of one optimization instance alone does not ensure future feasibility.

 11.99 Stability of MPC
A common stability proof requires terminal cost V_f and terminal controller \kappa_f
satisfying
V_f(f(x,\kappa_f(x)))
V_f(x)
\le
-\ell(x,\kappa_f(x))
inside the terminal set.
Then the optimal finite-horizon value decreases along the closed-loop trajectory and
serves as a Lyapunov function.
Energy harvesting can be incorporated into \ell, but safety and positive-definite
regulation terms must remain sufficient for stability.

11.100 Central Electromechanical Conversion Theorem
Theorem 11.30 — Passive regenerative transduction
Consider a reciprocal linear transducer satisfying
F_{\mathrm{em}}=-k_ti,
e=k_tv,
and connected to a passive electrical network with stored energy E_e and dissipation
P_d\ge0.
Then the combined mechanical–electrical energy satisfies
\frac{d}{dt}
(E_m+E_e)
=
P_{\mathrm{external}}

 P_d
P_{\mathrm{other\,mechanical\,loss}}.
Consequently, electrical energy delivered to a load cannot exceed external mechanical
input plus released initial stored energy.
Proof
The electromechanical conversion terms are equal and opposite in the mechanical and
electrical energy balances and therefore cancel internally. The remaining terms are
external power and nonnegative losses. Integrate over time. ∎

11.101 Central Regenerative Suspension Bound
Theorem 11.31 — Net recovery bound
Let a suspension system begin with stored energy E(0), receive road and vehicle
mechanical input
E_{\mathrm{in}},
deliver useful electrical output
E_{\mathrm{out}},
and incur total nonnegative losses E_{\mathrm{loss}}.
Then
E_{\mathrm{out}}
=
E_{\mathrm{in}}
+
E(0)
E(T)

 E_{\mathrm{loss}},
and therefore
\boxed{
E_{\mathrm{out}}
\le
E_{\mathrm{in}}+E(0)
}.
Proof
Integrate the total energy balance from 0 to T. Since
E(T)\ge0
and
E_{\mathrm{loss}}\ge0,
the inequality follows. ∎

11.102 Central Semi-Active Stability Theorem
Theorem 11.32 — Stability under bounded regenerative damping
Consider
m\ddot x+kx+c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x=0
with
m>0,
\qquad
k>0,
\qquad
0<c_{\min}\le c(t,x,\dot x)\le c_{\max}.
Then the origin is globally asymptotically stable.

 Proof
Use
V(x,\dot x)
=
\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2.
Then
\dot V
=
-c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x^2
\le
-c_{\min}\dot x^2.
The derivative is nonpositive.
The set where
\dot V=0
is
\dot x=0.
For a trajectory to remain there, the equation requires
kx=0,
so
x=0.
By LaSalle’s invariance principle, the origin is globally asymptotically stable. ∎
The theorem applies to the isolated scalar mode. Vehicle safety requires the full coupled
model.

11.103 Central Harvesting–Comfort Trade-Off Theorem

 Theorem 11.33 — Added passive harvesting cannot increase mechanical energy
Let two systems have identical mass, stiffness, forcing, and initial conditions, but total
damping coefficients satisfy
c_2(t)\ge c_1(t)\ge0.
For each individual system,
\dot E_j
=
P_{\mathrm{in},j}
c_jv_j^2.
The larger damping coefficient guarantees greater instantaneous dissipation only for
equal velocity. It does not guarantee lower response energy, lower acceleration, or
greater harvested energy under coupled excitation because v_1 and v_2 differ.
Proof
The first statement follows directly from damping power at a common velocity.
The lack of a global ordering follows because damping changes phase and amplitude of
the response and therefore changes input power and velocity. Counterexamples occur
near and away from resonance. ∎
This theorem explains why damping must be optimized dynamically rather than
maximized blindly.

11.104 Engineering Validation Standard
A claim of useful regenerative suspension performance is supported only when the
following are demonstrated under matched conditions:
independently measured mechanical input;
full electrical output and loss accounting;
unchanged or improved ride and tire-contact constraints;
thermal feasibility;

 force, voltage, current, and travel compliance;
repeatability over road profiles and speeds;
comparison with passive and active baselines;
net, not merely gross, recovered energy;
uncertainty intervals;
failure-safe behavior.
11.105 Proof Boundaries
This chapter establishes:
mechanical work, energy, and power identities;
spring–mass–damper energy balance;
base-excitation power input;
electromagnetic reciprocity;
combined electromechanical conservation;
equivalent regenerative damping;
load-power and resistance-matching results;
coupled mechanical–electrical optimization boundaries;
harmonic and stochastic harvesting formulas;
quarter-car dynamics and modal frequencies;
semi-active passivity conditions;
passivity projection and energy-tank concepts;

storage constraints;

If the actual frequency differs by constant \Delta f, relative phase accumulates as

A reduced phase-error model is

A locked equilibrium requires

Adding an induction-harvesting coil changes the electromagnetic boundary conditions

Proof

13.30 Nonlinear Magnetic Inductance
In a magnetic circuit with saturation,
L=L(i,x).
The flux linkage is
\lambda(i,x).
Incremental inductance is
L_{\mathrm{inc}}
=
\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial i}.
Secant inductance is

 L_{\mathrm{sec}}
=
\frac{\lambda}{i}.
These are generally different.
The small-signal resonance should use the incremental inductance near the operating
point.

13.31 Resonance Shift Under Saturation
As a ferromagnetic core approaches saturation, incremental permeability falls, reducing
incremental inductance.
Because
f_r\propto L^{-1/2},
a decrease in L increases f_r.
Thus increasing drive amplitude can shift the resonance upward and invalidate a fixed
small-signal tuning calculation.

13.32 Skin and Proximity Effects
At megahertz frequency, conductor resistance exceeds its DC value because current
concentrates near conductor surfaces and is redistributed by nearby fields.
Let
R_{\mathrm{AC}}>R_{\mathrm{DC}}.
Then
Q_{\mathrm{actual}}
=
\frac{\omega L}{R_{\mathrm{AC}}}
<
\frac{\omega L}{R_{\mathrm{DC}}}.

+

\left\langle\dot x^2\right\rangle

rather than by maximizing damping without limit.

Theorem 13.17 — Resonant suspension energy bound

 For a periodic steady-state MAGPIE-type assembly with high-frequency drive power
P_d, mechanical disturbance power P_m, useful electrical output P_o, and nonnegative
loss P_\ell,
\boxed{
\overline P_o
=
\overline P_d
+
\overline P_m
\overline P_\ell.

Consequently,
\boxed{
\overline P_o
\le
\overline P_d+\overline P_m.

Proof
Integrate Poynting’s theorem and the mechanical energy balance over the complete

number of cycles is zero. Internal electromechanical conversion terms cancel, leaving
external inputs, useful output, and loss. ∎
This does not prevent useful net recovery of energy that would otherwise be dissipated.
It prevents unsupported creation of net energy.

14.1 The Original Insight
The original Howard Comma intuition was that ordinary geometry can omit something
structurally important.
Two objects may appear:
far apart in ordinary space but function as one tightly coupled unit;
close together in ordinary space but interact weakly;
geometrically aligned but operationally disconnected;
geometrically separated but connected through a strong intermediary or shared
pathway.
The first insight was therefore:
\text{visible distance}
\neq
\text{functional distance}.
The “comma” was conceived as the missing correction between those two descriptions.
That insight was useful, but it was not yet mathematically complete because the
following remained unspecified:
What exactly counts as interaction?
How is interaction converted into distance?
When is that distance mathematically valid?
How are different units normalized?
How is the residual tested across triples or networks?
How is the model prevented from fitting its desired conclusion circularly?
The perfected version answers each question explicitly.

14.2 Perfection Step One: Replace Metaphor with Measurable Inputs

 Let the entities be
x_1,\ldots,x_n.
For every pair (i,j), define measurable quantities:
C_{ij}
for contact or direct coupling,
A_{ij}
for accessibility, transmissibility, or pathway strength,
and
d_{ij}
for ordinary geometric separation.
The interaction kernel is defined as
\boxed{
K_{ij}
=
w_C C_{ij}
+
w_A A_{ij}
+
w_D\phi(d_{ij})
}
with
w_C,w_A,w_D\ge0,
and
w_C+w_A+w_D=1.
A standard geometric decay term is

 \boxed{
\phi(d)=e^{-d/L},
}
where L>0 is an interaction-length scale.
kingmaker_howard_comma_one_pager.pdf
This was the first major perfection: the Howard Comma was no longer defined by an
image or intuition alone. It was grounded in declared pairwise measurements.

14.3 Why the Weight Constraints Matter
The normalization
w_C+w_A+w_D=1
makes the kernel a convex combination of its components.
Proposition 14.1 — Convex boundedness
Suppose
0\le C_{ij},A_{ij},\phi(d_{ij})\le1.
Then
0\le K_{ij}\le1.
Proof
Because the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, K_{ij} is a convex combination of
three values in [0,1]. ∎
This provides a consistent numerical scale and prevents arbitrary coefficient inflation
from masquerading as stronger interaction.

14.4 Perfection Step Two: Require Symmetry

 The kernel is required to satisfy
K_{ij}=K_{ji}.
This means the basic perfected formulation describes reciprocal pairwise geometry.
If a system is direction dependent, one must either:
symmetrize the directional measurements;
construct separate forward and reverse kernels;
or use a directed-geometry extension.
The symmetric requirement was added because an ordinary Euclidean kernel distance
cannot generally be derived from an arbitrary nonsymmetric matrix.

14.5 Perfection Step Three: Require Positive Semidefiniteness
The decisive mathematical correction was the requirement
\boxed{
K\succeq0.
}
That means

THE MIRROR LEDGER
Invariant Reconstruction Theory for Knowledge Under Incomplete Observation
A challenge-complete architecture for evidence, uncertainty, inversion, contradiction,
history, universality, and prediction.

 CANONICAL PRINCIPLE
A claim should be accepted only to the degree that it survives every admissible
reconstruction and legitimate challenge permitted by the evidence.
Knowledge is not what fits one model. Evidence-stable knowledge is what remains
invariant across a declared class of evidence-compatible reconstructions, legitimate
mirror transformations, causal alternatives, historical countercases, and valid domain
translations.
I. NECESSARY CORRECTIONS
1. Replace “truth” with “evidence-stable knowledge.”
Let D be the available evidence and A(D) the declared set of admissible
reconstructions. A claim Q is stable when
Q(X) = q for every X in A(D).
This proves stability relative to A(D), not metaphysical certainty. Every result must
therefore carry its scope:
Q = Q[D, A, Θ, O],
where D is the evidence, A the admissible model class, Θ the assumptions, and O the
observation process.
2. Historical calculation is not automatically perfect reconstruction.
The past is fixed, but its surviving record may be incomplete:
D_historical = O(X_past) + ε + B − M.
Exact calculation does not imply complete historical recovery.
Past: fixed reality, incomplete reconstruction.
Future: unobserved reality, conditional projection.

 3. Not every inversion is legitimate.
A mirror M is admissible only when it preserves the relevant comparison structure and
gives the transformed claim a defined meaning. The mirror is a validation operation, not
a license to reverse everything arbitrarily.
4. Missingness must be modeled.
Missing data may be:
• missing completely at random,
• missing at random conditional on observed variables,
• missing not at random.
Only the third class directly makes absence part of the causal mechanism. Missingness
is potentially informative, not automatically informative.
5. Cross-domain recurrence does not establish universality.
Similar language ≠ similar mechanism ≠ shared invariant.
Universality requires an explicit translation T_j and preservation of the candidate
invariant under that translation.
II. FOUNDATIONAL OBJECT
The primary object is not a preferred model. It is the full evidence-compatible possibility
space:
A(D) = {X : X satisfies the evidence, constraints, and declared admissibility rules}.
For a target quantity Q, define its admissible image:
Q_set(D) = {Q(X) : X in A(D)}.
Three cases follow.

 Determined:
|Q_set(D)| = 1.
Bounded but unresolved:
Q_set(D) lies inside a meaningful interval or finite family.
Unidentified:
Q_set(D) is too broad, disconnected, or unbounded to support a useful conclusion.
This turns uncertainty from vague language into geometry.
III. THE EIGHT GOVERNING PRINCIPLES
1. Provenance Preservation
Every claim must retain a complete dependency chain:
source → transformation → derivation → inference → claim.
A claim record is:
C_k = (q_k, S_k, T_k, Θ_k, U_k, F_k),
where q_k is the claim, S_k its sources, T_k its transformations, Θ_k its assumptions,
U_k its uncertainty, and F_k its falsification conditions.
2. Category Separation
The ledger must preserve:
D0 ≠ D1 ≠ D2 ≠ D3 ≠ D4,
where:
D0 = unaltered record,
D1 = normalized record,

 D2 = exact derivation,
D3 = constrained inference,
D4 = interpretation or hypothesis.
No derived or inferred quantity may silently migrate backward and be treated as raw
observation.
3. Reconstruction Pluralism
When several models fit the record, preserve all materially distinct models:
A(D) = {X1, X2, …}.
Premature selection creates artificial certainty. Model disagreement is itself evidence:
U_Q = diameter{Q(X) : X in A(D)}.
The larger U_Q, the weaker the claim.
4. Legitimate Mirror Opposition
Every claim must face its strongest valid inversions:
• causal reversal,
• selection complement,
• observer inversion,
• category complement,
• temporal reversal where meaningful.
The mirror does not declare the inverse true. It measures dependence on framing.
Define mirror divergence:
Δ_M(Q) = distance between the direct result and the inverse-transformed mirrored
result.

 Small divergence indicates mirror stability. Large divergence indicates viewpoint
dependence that must remain visible.
5. Contradiction Preservation
Contradictions must not be averaged away before their cause is understood.
Construct a contradiction graph G_Γ = (V, E_Γ), where nodes are claims or
observations and edges encode conflict.
Contradiction clusters may reveal:
• observer-dependent frames,
• incompatible definitions,
• regime changes,
• manipulated reporting,
• geographic variation,
• temporal discontinuity,
• multiple latent populations.
A contradiction is both a defect candidate and a structural-signal candidate.
6. Historical Mechanism Testing
Historical analogy must compare generative mechanisms rather than imagery or
outcomes.
Represent a case as:
E_k = (actors, resources, institutions, technology, environment, information structure,
timescale, outcome).
Compare cases through a weighted mechanism distance. The corpus must include:
H+ supporting cases,
H− contrary cases,
H0 null cases,

 H? insufficiently documented cases.
Null cases are crucial because they reveal missing boundary conditions.
7. Domain Translation Discipline
A cross-domain claim must specify a translation:
T_j : S → S_j.
Each abstract object requires an operational counterpart. Only then can invariant
survival be tested:
I_j(T_j X) = I(X).
A proposed invariant fails when its meaning changes across domains, its measurement
changes without calibration, its translation depends on the desired conclusion, or
contradictory domains are excluded.
8. Prediction as Possibility Contraction
Prediction should not be represented as unjustified point certainty. Define the
admissible future set:
F_t(D) = {X(t) : X(t) is compatible with present evidence and admissible dynamics}.
New evidence or stronger constraints should contract this set:
F_t^(0) ⊇ F_t^(1) ⊇ F_t^(2).
Predictive power is the valid elimination of impossible futures, not confidence theater.
A useful contraction measure is:
Π_t = log[Volume(F_prior) / Volume(F_posterior)],

 or an analogous entropy, covering-number, credible-set, or width measure when
ordinary volume is unsuitable.
IV. CORE THEOREMS
Theorem 1 — Reconstruction Invariance
A unique evidence-determined answer exists if and only if Q is constant on A(D):
there exists q such that Q(X) = q for every X in A(D).
Proof.
If Q is constant, every admissible reconstruction yields q, so the evidence determines Q
relative to the model class. Conversely, if the evidence uniquely determines q, no
admissible reconstruction may yield another value. Therefore Q is constant on A(D). □
Theorem 2 — Non-Identifiability Witness
If there exist X1, X2 in A(D) such that Q(X1) ≠ Q(X2), then the available evidence does
not uniquely identify Q.
Proof.
Both reconstructions satisfy the declared evidence and admissibility rules, yet imply
different target values. The evidence therefore cannot select a unique value without
additional assumptions or information. □
Theorem 3 — Assumption Monotonicity
If A_Θ2(D) is a subset of A_Θ1(D) because Θ2 contains stronger assumptions, then
Q_set_Θ2(D) is a subset of Q_set_Θ1(D).
Adding assumptions contracts uncertainty. Contraction caused by assumptions must not
be mistaken for contraction caused by evidence.
Theorem 4 — Mirror Instability Witness

 If an admissible mirror produces divergence above tolerance,
Δ_M(Q) > ε,
then Q is not invariant under that legitimate change of frame. This does not
automatically refute Q; it proves that the conclusion depends on a frame or asymmetry
that must be identified and justified.
Theorem 5 — Prediction Non-Uniqueness
If two admissible evolutions agree for every time up to t0 but differ at some future time
t1, then the historical evidence alone does not uniquely determine the state at t1.
Proof.
Both futures are consistent with the complete available past. Since they diverge after t0,
the past record does not logically select one unique continuation. □
V. MASTER RECONSTRUCTION ENGINE
The framework should not select the model with merely the best fit. It should optimize a
multi-objective challenge space containing:
• evidence mismatch,
• provenance weakness,
• unresolved contradiction cost,
• mirror instability,
• historical mechanism inconsistency,
• cross-domain translation failure,
• unsupported assumption burden,
• model complexity.
Operationally:
J(X) = λ_E L_E + λ_P L_P + λ_C L_C + λ_M L_M + λ_H L_H + λ_U L_U + λ_A C_A +
λ_K C_K.

 The weight vector Λ must remain visible. Conclusions should be tested across
reasonable weight choices.
Sensitivity:
S_Λ(Q) = ||∂Q/∂Λ||.
Low sensitivity strengthens robustness.
VI. FINAL OUTPUT OBJECT
The engine should never emit only a narrative answer. Its proper output is:
Ω(D) = (K_s, K_b, K_c, K_m, K_a, K_f, K_u),
where:
K_s = stable knowledge,
K_b = bounded but unresolved quantities,
K_c = contested claims,
K_m = missing evidence,
K_a = assumption-dependent conclusions,
K_f = falsification conditions,
K_u = unknown or unidentified claims.
Each claim receives a ledger record containing:
• epistemic level,
• provenance,
• admissible value set,
• mirror divergence,
• sensitivity,
• falsification conditions,
• evidence needed for refinement.
VII. EPISTEMIC LEVELS

 L0 — Recorded
Directly present in a source.
L1 — Verified
Independently reproduced or corroborated.
L2 — Deductively Derived
Follows exactly from declared premises.
L3 — Identified Within Model Class
Invariant across all declared admissible reconstructions.
L4 — Bounded Inference
Not unique, but meaningfully constrained.
L5 — Hypothesis
Best current explanation but not reconstruction-invariant.
L6 — Unknown
The evidence does not meaningfully determine the claim.
VIII. FALSIFIABILITY REQUIREMENTS
The Mirror Ledger must be capable of failing. It requires revision when:
1. Its admissible-model construction systematically excludes later-confirmed
explanations.
2. Mirror testing increases complexity without improving calibration or error detection.
3. Stable claims perform no better than conventional single-model conclusions.
4. Independent analysts cannot reproduce the provenance ledger.
5. Cross-domain invariants depend on ambiguous mappings.
6. Uncertainty sets repeatedly exclude observed outcomes.
7. Results are excessively sensitive to arbitrary weights or admissibility rules.
The empirical test is:
Does the framework detect false certainty earlier and preserve valid certainty better?

 IX. BENCHMARK PROGRAM
Test the framework against cases involving:
• incomplete archives,
• survivorship bias,
• conflicting eyewitnesses,
• changing category definitions,
• failed forecasts,
• hidden confounding,
• engineering accidents,
• scientific reversals,
• manipulated datasets.
