Chapter 11
Formal Possibility Spaces
“The future is not a single destination. It is a structured
collection of attainable states constrained by the present.”

11.1 From Concept to Mathematics
In Volume II we introduced the idea of a possibility space as
the collection of attainable future states.
We now formalize that concept.
The objective is not to replace existing mathematical
frameworks, but to provide a common language for
describing attainable futures across dynamical systems,
control theory, optimization, computation, and engineering.

11.2 State-Dependent Possibility
Let
\Omega

 be the state space.
Given the current state
s
\in
\Omega,
define the possibility space
\mathcal P(s)
\subseteq
\Omega.
This set contains every state regarded as reachable under the
assumptions of the model.
The meaning of “reachable” depends entirely upon the
governing dynamics and constraints.

11.3 Reachability
Suppose
E
is an evolution operator.
The one-step reachable set is
R_1(s)
=
\{

 E(s)
\}.
The two-step reachable set is
R_2(s)
=
\{
E^2(s)
\}.
More generally,
R_n(s)
=
\{
E^n(s)
\}.
For deterministic systems, each set may contain a single
element.
For systems with controls or uncertainty, these sets may
contain many possible future states.

11.4 Constraint Operators
Possibility is never unlimited.
Introduce a constraint operator
C.

 The admissible possibility space becomes
\mathcal P_C(s)
=
\{
x\in\Omega
:
C(x)=\text{true}
\}.
Examples of constraints include:
• conservation laws,
• actuator limits,
• energy budgets,
• safety requirements,
• geometric boundaries,
• logical conditions.
Constraints define the boundary of possibility.

11.5 Controlled Possibility
Suppose a control input
u
belongs to an admissible control set
\mathcal U.
Evolution becomes

 s_{t+1}
=
E(s_t,u_t).
The possibility space expands to
\mathcal P(s)
=
\{
E(s,u)
:
u\in\mathcal U
\}.
Control theory studies how choosing different admissible
inputs changes the reachable future.

11.6 Probabilistic Possibility
Some systems evolve under uncertainty.
Rather than producing one reachable state,
they produce a probability distribution.
Represent this by
\mu_s
defined on
\mathcal P(s).

 The possibility space remains the same,
while probabilities describe how likely different attainable
states are under the adopted model.

11.7 Time-Dependent Possibility
Possibility evolves.
At time
t,
define
\mathcal P_t.
As the system changes,
\mathcal P_t
\neq
\mathcal P_{t+1}
in general.
Thus possibility becomes a dynamic mathematical object
rather than a static collection.

11.8 Nested Possibility
For many systems,
reachable sets satisfy

 R_1
\subseteq
R_2
\subseteq
R_3
\subseteq
\cdots.
Longer time horizons permit access to larger collections of
states.
Understanding the geometry of these nested reachable sets is
central to planning, robotics, and optimal control.

11.9 Geometry of Possibility
Possibility spaces possess mathematical structure.
Questions include:
Are they convex?
Connected?
Compact?
Differentiable?
Metric?
Topological?

 Different applications require different mathematical
assumptions.
The geometry of possibility often determines which
algorithms or analytical tools are appropriate.

11.10 Possibility Under Interaction
Suppose two systems interact.
Their joint possibility space becomes
\mathcal P(s_1,s_2).
Interaction may enlarge,
reduce,
or reshape the reachable future.
For example:
• cooperation can expand attainable outcomes,
• competition can restrict them,
• communication can coordinate them,
• constraints can prevent certain joint states.
The structure of interaction therefore directly influences the
structure of possibility.

11.11 Possibility Maps
A possibility map assigns a possibility space to every state.

 Formally,
\Pi:
\Omega
\rightarrow
2^\Omega,
where
2^\Omega
denotes the power set of
\Omega.
Thus,
\Pi(s)
=
\mathcal P(s).
This set-valued mapping provides a compact mathematical
description of attainable futures throughout the state space.

11.12 Possibility Across Disciplines
Discipline

Possibility Space

Reachable states

 Optimization

Economics

Different disciplines employ different terminology while

11.13 Why Formal Possibility
Matters
Formal possibility spaces separate two questions that are
often confused:
What can happen?
versus
What will happen?
The first concerns reachability.
The second concerns dynamics, optimization, probability, or
decision-making.
Maintaining this distinction improves both mathematical
clarity and scientific interpretation.

 11.14 Toward Selection Operators
Possibility identifies the attainable future.
The next question is how one—or several—of those
attainable states become realized.
To answer that question we introduce selection operators,
which formalize the mechanisms by which systems choose,
optimize, sample, or otherwise transition within possibility
spaces under explicitly stated assumptions.

Chapter 12
Selection Operators
“Possibility defines the landscape. Selection determines
the path.”

12.1 From Reachability to
Realization
The previous chapter defined the possibility space
\mathcal P(s),
the collection of states that are attainable from the current
state.
Possibility alone does not determine evolution.
A system must still transition from many attainable states
to one—or several—realized states.
The mathematical object that performs this role is the
selection operator.

 12.2 Formal Definition
Let
\mathcal P(s)
\subseteq
\Omega
be the possibility space.
A selection operator is written
\Sigma.
In its simplest form,
\Sigma:
\mathcal P(s)
\rightarrow
\Omega.
Given a possibility space,
the operator produces one realized successor state.
More general formulations may produce multiple states,
probability distributions, or sets of admissible choices.

12.3 Deterministic Selection
For deterministic systems,

 selection is unique.
If
\mathcal P(s)
=
\{x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n\},
then
\Sigma(\mathcal P)
=
x_k
for exactly one
x_k.
The governing equations uniquely determine the outcome.
Examples include:
• ideal rigid-body dynamics,
• deterministic algorithms,
• classical state-transition models under fixed
assumptions.

12.4 Probabilistic Selection
Many systems evolve probabilistically.
Instead of selecting one state directly,

 the operator assigns probabilities,
p_i
=
P(x_i).
Selection then becomes sampling from
\mathcal P(s)
according to an explicitly specified probability measure.
Examples include:
•
•
•
•

Markov processes,
stochastic simulations,
Bayesian inference,
randomized algorithms.

12.5 Optimization-Based Selection
Engineering frequently selects according to an objective.
Define
J(x)
as an objective function.
Selection becomes
\Sigma(\mathcal P)
=

 \arg\min_{x\in\mathcal P}
J(x),
or
\arg\max.
Examples include:
• shortest paths,
• minimum energy,
• maximum efficiency,
• least error,
• optimal control.
Optimization transforms possibility into purposeful
evolution.

12.6 Constraint-Based Selection
Some possibilities satisfy required conditions while others
do not.
Introduce constraints,
C_i(x).
Selection now occurs only within the admissible subset,
\mathcal P_C
=
\{

 x
\in
\mathcal P
:
C_i(x)
\text{ satisfied}
\}.
Constraint satisfaction is fundamental to:
•
•
•
•
•

robotics,
scheduling,
engineering design,
logistics,
verification.

12.7 Adaptive Selection
Selection mechanisms themselves may evolve.
Instead of
\Sigma,
consider
\Sigma_t.
Examples include:
Adaptive controllers.

 Learning algorithms.
Evolutionary computation.
Game-theoretic agents.
Machine learning.
Past experience modifies future selection.
The operator becomes dynamic.

12.8 Hierarchical Selection
Large systems often perform selection at multiple levels.
Examples include:
Mission planning.
↓
Path planning.
↓
Motor control.
Or
Corporate strategy.
↓
Department decisions.

 ↓
Individual actions.
Hierarchical selection allows complex systems to

12.9 Distributed Selection
In distributed systems,
no central selector exists.

Examples include:
Swarm robotics.
Ant colonies.
Distributed optimization.
Blockchain consensus.
Wireless sensor networks.

Graphs
Suppose
G=(V,E)

Each vertex performs
\Sigma_i.
The global selection operator becomes
\Sigma
=
(\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2,\ldots,\Sigma_N).

\hat{s},

 s.

Chapter 13
Formal Interaction Dynamics
“Selection determines what evolves. Interaction
determines how evolution becomes collective.”

13.1 From Individual Evolution to
Collective Evolution
Previous chapters introduced:
• state spaces,
• evolution operators,
• recursive dynamics,
• possibility spaces,
• selection operators.
These concepts describe how an individual system
evolves.

 Most scientific systems, however, are embedded within
larger collections of interacting systems.
No planet exists without gravity.
No neuron functions without neighboring neurons.
No robot operates without its environment.
No economy functions without exchange.
Interaction is therefore not an exception.
It is often the rule.

13.2 Joint State Spaces
Suppose two systems possess state spaces
\Omega_A
and
\Omega_B.
Their combined state space becomes
\Omega
=
\Omega_A
\times
\Omega_B.

 For
N
systems,
\Omega
=
\prod_{i=1}^{N}
\Omega_i.
Every point in this product space represents one complete
configuration of the coupled system.

13.3 Interaction Operators
Define the interaction operator
\mathcal{I}
:
\Omega
\rightarrow
\Omega.
Unlike ordinary evolution,
which advances one subsystem,
the interaction operator simultaneously updates multiple
components according to their relationships.
General evolution now becomes

 S_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{I}
\bigl(
S_t
\bigr).
The precise form of
\mathcal I
depends entirely upon the governing equations of the
system being modeled.

13.4 Pairwise Interaction
Many systems are well approximated by pairwise
interactions.
Represent
\mathcal I
=
\sum_{i<j}
\mathcal I_{ij},
where
\mathcal I_{ij}
describes interaction between systems

 i
and
j.
Examples include:
Mechanical contact.
Electrical coupling.
Chemical reactions.
Information exchange.
Network communication.
More complex models may require higher-order
interactions involving three or more components
simultaneously.

13.5 Coupling Functions
Suppose
s_i
denotes subsystem
i.
Its evolution may be written

 s_i(t+1)
=
F_i
\!\left(
s_i,
\sum_j
w_{ij}
H(s_i,s_j)
\right),
where
• H is the interaction function,
• w_{ij} is the coupling weight,
• F_i describes local evolution.
This form encompasses many models used in control
theory, network dynamics, and coupled oscillators.

13.6 Interaction Graphs
The interaction network is naturally represented by
G=(V,E).
Vertices correspond to subsystems.

Graph topology influences:
• information flow,

 • synchronization,
• robustness,
• stability,
• resilience,
• collective behavior.

13.7 Dynamic Networks
Interactions need not remain fixed.
Instead,
the graph becomes
G(t).

disappear,
or change weight.
Examples include:
Social networks.
Wireless communication.
Adaptive robotics.
Biological development.

 Transportation systems.

In many physical systems,

E_{\text{total}}

E_{\text{internal}}
+

• binding,
• coupling,

 Interactions may also exchange information.

13.10 Locality
Many interaction models satisfy locality.

\mathcal N(i).

s_i(t+1)
=
F_i

 \left(
s_i,

Chapter 14
Persistent Interaction Operators
“An interaction ends in an instant. Its consequences may
endure for years.”

14.1 Beyond Instantaneous
Interaction
An interaction is often represented mathematically as a
single transformation,

 S_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{I}(S_t).
This representation is sufficient for many problems.
However, numerous scientific and engineering systems
exhibit interactions whose consequences persist beyond
the moment of exchange.
Examples include:
• plastic deformation after loading,
• synaptic modification after learning,
• adaptive controller parameter updates,
• accumulated fatigue in structures,
• long-term ecological change,
• persistent changes in software or databases.
To represent these systems, interaction itself must possess
memory.

14.2 Persistent Interaction State
Introduce a persistent interaction variable,
M_t,
representing retained consequences relevant to future
evolution.
The complete system state becomes

 \hat{S}_t
=
(S_t,M_t).
The variable M_t is intentionally general. Depending on
the application, it may represent accumulated stress,
learned parameters, historical summaries, controller
states, or any other retained quantity justified by the
model.

14.3 Persistent Interaction Operator
Define the persistent interaction operator
\mathcal{I}_P,
acting on the augmented state,
\mathcal{I}_P:
(\Omega,\mathcal{M})
\rightarrow
(\Omega,\mathcal{M}).
Evolution becomes
\hat{S}_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{I}_P(\hat{S}_t).
Expanding,

 \begin{aligned}
S_{t+1}&=F(S_t,M_t),\\
M_{t+1}&=G(S_t,M_t).
\end{aligned}
The functions F and G describe the evolution of the
observable system and its retained interaction variables.

14.4 Interaction Accumulation
Many interactions accumulate gradually.
One common representation is
M_{t+1}
=
M_t
+
\Delta M_t,
where
\Delta M_t
represents the incremental contribution of the current
interaction.
Examples include:
• cumulative material fatigue,
• incremental learning,

 • gradual adaptation,
• long-term resource accumulation.

14.5 Decaying Persistence
Not every retained consequence lasts indefinitely.
A simple decay model is
M_{t+1}
=
\lambda M_t
+
\Delta M_t,
where
0<\lambda<1.
This representation appears in many fields:
• adaptive filtering,
• reinforcement learning,
• signal processing,
• biological adaptation,
• recursive estimation.
The decay coefficient controls the influence of older
interactions.

14.6 Saturation

 Many persistent variables possess natural limits.
Introduce a bounded update,
M_{t+1}
=
\operatorname{clip}
(M_t+\Delta M_t),
or more generally,
M_{t+1}
=
H(M_t,\Delta M_t),
where
H
enforces application-specific constraints.
Examples include:
•
•
•
•

actuator limits,
biological saturation,
storage capacity,
bounded controller gains.

14.7 Coupled Persistence
Persistent variables themselves may interact.
Suppose

 M_i
and
M_j
represent neighboring subsystems.
Then
M_i(t+1)
=
G_i
\left(
M_i,
\sum_j
w_{ij}
M_j
\right).
Persistent information therefore becomes part of the
interaction network rather than remaining isolated within
individual subsystems.

14.8 Structural Persistence
Some interactions modify the interaction network itself.
Instead of changing only subsystem states,
they alter

 G=(V,E).
Examples include:
• neural plasticity,
• adaptive communication networks,
• evolving transportation systems,
• social-network formation,
• rewiring in distributed robotics.
The graph evolves together with the states.

14.9 Persistence Kernels
Rather than storing complete histories,
many systems compress previous interactions through a
kernel,
K.
A general representation is
M_t
=
\sum_{k=0}^{t}
K(t-k)\,
\Delta M_k.
Different kernels emphasize different temporal scales.
Examples include:

 • exponential kernels,
• finite-memory windows,
• weighted averages,
• Gaussian kernels.
The choice of kernel depends on the assumptions of the
model.

14.10 Stability of Persistent
Interaction
Persistence improves some systems while destabilizing
others.
Beneficial examples include:
• adaptive flight control,
• predictive maintenance,
• machine learning,
• biological memory.
Potentially destabilizing examples include:
• runaway reinforcement,
• uncontrolled adaptation,
• excessive parameter drift,
• cascading accumulation.
Persistence therefore requires the same stability analysis
applied to other dynamical systems.

 14.11 Observability
Persistent variables may not be measured directly.
Instead,
observations satisfy
Y_t
=
O(S_t,M_t).
Estimating hidden persistent variables from observations
is central to:
•
•
•
•

Kalman filtering,
Bayesian estimation,
observer design,
hidden-state modeling.

\hat{S}_t

\hat{S}_{t+1}

M_{t+1}

15.5 Recursive Memory Kernels
Persistence need not depend only upon the immediately

M_t
=

K(t-k)\,
H(S_k),

15.6 Fixed Persistent Structures
A persistent equilibrium satisfies
\mathcal R(\hat S^*)
=
\hat S^*.
Thus,
\begin{aligned}
S^*
&=
F(S^*,M^*),\\
M^*
&=
G(S^*,M^*).
\end{aligned}

 15.7 Stability
Suppose two augmented states satisfy
\hat S
=
(S,M),
and
\hat T
=
(T,N).
A natural question is whether repeated recursion

When they do not hold, richer behaviors—including

 \mathcal R_G

16.1 Beyond Individual States
Previous chapters developed recursive evolution through
augmented states,
\hat S=(S,M),
where retained variables influence future dynamics.
We now shift perspective.
Rather than studying individual trajectories,
we study how persistence reshapes the mathematical
structure of the entire possibility landscape.
Persistence becomes an operator acting upon sets of

16.2 Persistence Mapping
Let

 \mathcal P(S)
denote the possibility space associated with state
S.
Define the Persistence Mapping
\mathcal M_P:
\mathcal P(S)
\rightarrow
\mathcal P(S').
Rather than advancing only the present state,
the mapping transforms the collection of attainable future
states.
Different retained variables may therefore produce different
future possibility spaces even when the observable state is
identical.

16.3 State-Dependent Evolution of
Possibility
The previous chapter introduced
\hat S=(S,M).
Possibility therefore becomes
\mathcal P(\hat S).

 Two systems satisfying
S_1=S_2
but
M_1\neq M_2
need not possess identical reachable futures.
Persistence influences attainable evolution.

16.4 Invariant Persistence
Structures
Certain properties of possibility spaces remain unchanged
despite recursive evolution.
Let
\Phi
be a structural property.
If
\Phi(\mathcal P_t)
=
\Phi(\mathcal P_{t+1}),
then
\Phi

 is called a Persistence Invariant under the specified
persistence mapping.
The specific invariant depends on the mathematical setting
and assumptions.
Examples might include connectivity, dimensionality,
symmetry, or preserved constraints.

16.5 Closure Under Persistence
A persistence mapping is closed if
\mathcal M_P(\mathcal P)
\subseteq
\mathcal P.
Closure guarantees that recursive evolution remains inside
the admissible mathematical framework.
Closure does not imply convergence.
It only ensures that evolution never leaves the defined
possibility domain.

16.6 Nested Persistence
Many systems generate nested possibility structures,
\mathcal P_0
\supseteq

 \mathcal P_1

\mathcal P_2

\mathcal P_0
\subseteq
\mathcal P_1

\mathcal P_2
\subseteq

 • connected?

A structural fixed point satisfies
\mathcal M_P(\mathcal P^*)
=
\mathcal P^*.

17.1 Why Metrics Matter
The previous chapters introduced persistence mappings

17.2 Metric Spaces
Let
X
be a set.

 A metric is a function

1. 1.
d(x,y)\ge0
(non-negativity)
2. 2.
d(x,y)=0
\iff
x=y
(identity)
3. 3.
d(x,y)=d(y,x)
(symmetry)
4. 4.
d(x,z)
\le
d(x,y)+d(y,z)
(triangle inequality)
These four properties provide the mathematical
foundation for measuring similarity and difference.

2.1 Why Spectral Theory Matters
In the previous chapter, operators were elevated from

What intrinsic properties of an operator remain
unchanged regardless of how we describe it?
The answer lies in its spectrum.

analytical frameworks in modern mathematics.

2.2 Eigenvectors
Suppose
T:V\rightarrow V
is a linear operator.
An eigenvector satisfies
Tv
=
\lambda v,
where
v\neq0.

 The transformation changes only the magnitude (or sign
and direction) of the vector.
Its orientation remains unchanged.
Such vectors reveal the intrinsic directions preserved by
the operator.

2.3 Eigenvalues
The scalar
\lambda
is called an eigenvalue.
It measures the scaling associated with the corresponding
eigenvector.
Interpretation:
|\lambda|>1

|\lambda|<1
Contraction
|\lambda|=1
Magnitude preserved

 \lambda=0
Collapse onto a lower-dimensional subspace
Complex eigenvalues often correspond to oscillatory or
rotational behavior.

2.4 Characteristic Equation
For finite-dimensional operators represented by matrices,
eigenvalues satisfy
\det(T-\lambda I)=0.
The roots of this characteristic polynomial form the
spectrum of the matrix.
For infinite-dimensional operators, more general spectral
definitions are required.

2.5 Eigenspaces
All vectors satisfying
Tv=\lambda v
form the eigenspace
E_\lambda.

 This space may possess dimension greater than one.
The collection of eigenspaces reveals how the operator
decomposes the underlying vector space.

If sufficiently many independent eigenvectors exist,
the operator may be written
T
=
PDP^{-1},
where
• D is diagonal,
• P contains eigenvectors.
Diagonalization transforms complicated repeated
computations into simple powers of diagonal matrices,
making recursive evolution easier to analyze.

2.7 Spectral Decomposition
More generally,
many operators admit decompositions into simpler
spectral components.

 Conceptually,
T
=
\sum_i
\lambda_i
P_i,
where
P_i
are projection operators onto invariant subspaces.
The precise form depends upon the class of operators
being considered.

2.8 Invariant Subspaces
A subspace
W\subseteq V
is invariant if
T(W)
\subseteq
W.
Rather than studying the entire system simultaneously,

 analysis may proceed independently on each invariant
component.
Invariant subspaces provide one of the central
organizational principles of operator theory.

2.9 Spectral Radius
The spectral radius,
\rho(T),
is defined by
\rho(T)
=
\max
|\lambda_i|
for finite-dimensional operators.

behavior.
Repeated application satisfies
T^n.
When
\rho(T)<1,

under appropriate assumptions.

x_{n+1}
=
Tx_n.

Many important mathematical models, however, cannot
be described by finitely many coordinates.
Examples include:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

temperature distributions,
fluid velocity fields,
electromagnetic fields,
quantum wavefunctions,
probability densities,
continuous-time signals,
solutions of differential equations.

 These systems naturally inhabit infinite-dimensional
spaces.
Functional analysis provides the mathematical language
for studying them.

3.2 Functions as Points
Instead of viewing a point as
(x,y,z),
functional analysis often treats an entire function as a
single point.
For example,
f(x)
=
\sin x
is one element of an infinite-dimensional space.
Another element might be
g(x)
=
e^{-x^2}.
Entire functions become the fundamental objects.

 3.3 Vector Spaces of Functions
Functions may be added,
(f+g)(x)
=
f(x)+g(x),
and multiplied by scalars,
(cf)(x)
=
cf(x).
Therefore many collections of functions satisfy the
axioms of vector spaces.
Examples include:
•
•
•
•

continuous functions,
differentiable functions,
square-integrable functions,
polynomial spaces.

3.4 Normed Spaces
To discuss convergence, approximation, and stability,
we require a notion of size.
A norm satisfies

 \|f\|
\ge
0.
Examples include
Maximum norm
\|f\|_\infty
=
\sup_x
|f(x)|.
Energy norm
\|f\|_2
=
\left(
\int
|f(x)|^2dx
\right)^{1/2}.
Different norms emphasize different aspects of a function.

3.5 Banach Spaces
A Banach space is a complete normed vector space.
Completeness means every Cauchy sequence converges
to a point already inside the space.

 This seemingly technical property underlies many
existence and convergence theorems.
Examples include:
• continuous functions with the maximum norm,
• L^p spaces under appropriate conditions,
• sequence spaces.

3.6 Hilbert Spaces
A Hilbert space is a Banach space equipped with an inner
product.
The inner product
\langle
f,g
\rangle
defines notions of:
• angle,
• orthogonality,
• projection,
• distance.
Hilbert spaces generalize Euclidean geometry to infinitely
many dimensions.
They are foundational in quantum mechanics, signal
processing, and approximation theory.

 3.7 Orthogonality
Two functions are orthogonal if
\langle
f,g
\rangle
=
0.
Orthogonality allows complicated functions to be
decomposed into simpler independent components.
Examples include:
Fourier series.
Wavelets.
Principal component methods.
Orthogonal polynomials.

3.8 Bases
Finite-dimensional spaces possess finite bases.
Infinite-dimensional spaces may possess countably
infinite bases.
Examples include

 1,
\sin x,
\cos x,
\sin 2x,
\cos 2x,
\ldots
Every sufficiently regular periodic function may be
represented through an infinite series under appropriate
assumptions.

3.9 Linear Operators on Function
Spaces
Operators now act upon functions,
T
:
V
\rightarrow
V.
Examples include:
Differentiation
Tf
=
f'.

 Integration
Tf
=
\int
f.
Convolution.
Projection.
Integral transforms.
The operator itself becomes the primary mathematical
object.

3.10 Bounded Operators
A bounded operator satisfies
\|Tf\|
\le
C
\|f\|
for some constant
C.
Boundedness ensures continuity.
Many analytical results rely upon this property.

 Unbounded operators also arise naturally, particularly in
differential equations and quantum theory, but require
additional mathematical care.

3.11 Weak Convergence
Infinite-dimensional spaces admit multiple notions of
convergence.
Strong convergence requires
\|f_n-f\|
\rightarrow
0.
Weak convergence is more subtle.
Instead of requiring norms to converge,
only inner products with every test function converge.
Weak convergence often provides existence results where
strong convergence fails.

3.12 Compact Operators
Compact operators play a role analogous to finitedimensional matrices.
Although acting on infinite-dimensional spaces,

 they often possess discrete spectral properties resembling
matrix eigenvalue problems.
Applications include:
•
•
•
•

Fredholm integral equations,
numerical approximation,
spectral analysis,
inverse problems.

3.13 Infinite-Dimensional Dynamics
Recursive evolution now becomes
f_{n+1}
=
T(f_n).
Instead of evolving vectors,
the system evolves entire functions.
Examples include:
• iterative solution of differential equations,
• adaptive filtering,
• recursive estimation,
• function-space optimization.
The same recursive principles introduced in earlier
volumes remain applicable, but the underlying spaces are
far richer.

 3.14 Functional Perspective on
Persistence
Within the persistence framework,
possibility mappings and persistence operators may, in
some applications, act naturally on function spaces rather
than finite-dimensional vectors.
For example, one might model evolving probability
distributions, fields, or continuous state descriptions.
Developing rigorous infinite-dimensional persistence
theory would require additional assumptions concerning
topology, continuity, compactness, and well-posedness,
and remains an area for future mathematical research.

 Volume IV
Chapter 4
Differential Geometry of State
Spaces
“Dynamics describe motion. Geometry describes the
space through which motion occurs.”

4.1 From Flat Spaces to Curved
Spaces
Previous chapters treated the state space
\Omega
as an abstract mathematical set.
For many applications, this is sufficient.
However, numerous systems evolve on spaces possessing
intrinsic geometric structure.
Examples include:
• planetary motion on curved manifolds,
• robotic orientation on rotation groups,
• constrained mechanical systems,

 • relativistic spacetime,
• nonlinear optimization landscapes,
• configuration spaces of articulated mechanisms.
Differential geometry provides the mathematical language
for describing such spaces.

4.2 Manifolds
A manifold is a mathematical space that locally
resembles Euclidean space but may possess global
curvature or topology.
Examples include:
• the surface of a sphere,
• a torus,
• rotation groups,
• configuration spaces,
• smooth surfaces.
Although curved globally,
each sufficiently small neighborhood behaves like
ordinary Euclidean coordinates.

4.3 Local Coordinates
Around every point
p\in M,

 there exists a coordinate chart
\phi:U\rightarrow\mathbb R^n,
where
U
is a neighborhood of
p.
Calculus can therefore be performed locally while
respecting the global geometry of the manifold.

4.4 Tangent Spaces
At each point
p,
there exists a tangent space,
T_pM.
This vector space contains all possible instantaneous
directions in which a trajectory may pass through
p.
Although the manifold itself may be curved,
its tangent space is linear.

 Many differential equations evolve naturally within
tangent spaces.

4.5 Tangent Vectors
A tangent vector may be interpreted as the instantaneous
velocity of a curve,
\gamma(t),
passing through
p.
Formally,
\gamma(0)=p,
and
\gamma'(0)
\in
T_pM.
Dynamics therefore become vector fields defined across
the manifold.

4.6 Vector Fields
A vector field assigns a tangent vector to every point,

 X:M\rightarrow TM.
Evolution equations become
\frac{dx}{dt}
=
X(x).
The geometry of the manifold influences every trajectory.

4.7 Riemannian Metrics
To measure lengths and angles,
the manifold is equipped with a Riemannian metric,
g.
The metric defines
• distance,
• angle,
• area,
• volume,
• energy.
Unlike Euclidean geometry,
the metric may vary continuously from point to point.

4.8 Geodesics

 The shortest path between nearby points is called a
geodesic.
Geodesics satisfy equations determined by the metric.
Examples include:
Straight lines in Euclidean space.
Great circles on spheres.
Free-fall trajectories in general relativity (under
appropriate formulations).
Optimal paths on curved surfaces.
Geodesics generalize the concept of “straightness.”

4.9 Curvature
Curvature measures how a manifold departs from flat
Euclidean geometry.
Several forms of curvature exist:
• sectional curvature,
• Ricci curvature,
• scalar curvature,
• Gaussian curvature (in two dimensions).
Curvature influences:
• geodesic behavior,

 •
•
•
•

stability,
diffusion,
optimization,
physical models.

4.10 Differential Forms
Geometry also studies quantities integrated over curves,
surfaces, and volumes.
Differential forms provide a coordinate-independent
framework for:
• work,
• flux,
• circulation,
• conservation laws.
The exterior derivative
d
generalizes gradient,
curl,
and divergence.

4.11 Lie Derivatives
Suppose

 X
is a vector field.
The Lie derivative
measures how geometric objects evolve along the flow
generated by
X.
Lie derivatives provide a powerful coordinate-free
description of continuous evolution.

4.12 Geometry of Persistence
Within the persistence framework,
possibility spaces may themselves be modeled as
geometric objects.
Persistence mappings can then be interpreted as
transformations acting on manifolds,
while recursive evolution traces curves through these
geometric structures.
The choice of manifold, metric, and smoothness
assumptions depends on the application and should be
specified explicitly.

 4.13 Geometric Flows
Some systems evolve not only on a manifold,
but alter the manifold itself.
Examples include:
• Ricci flow,
• mean curvature flow,
• evolving surfaces,
• adaptive geometric optimization.
Such flows change the geometry while simultaneously
influencing future dynamics.
This idea conceptually parallels evolving interaction
structures discussed in earlier volumes, though the
mathematical settings are distinct.

4.14 Toward Information Geometry
Geometry need not describe only physical space.
Probability distributions themselves may form curved
manifolds.
The next chapter develops information geometry,
introducing statistical manifolds, Fisher information
metrics, geodesics in probability space, and geometric
approaches to learning and inference.

 These tools provide a bridge between differential
geometry and modern statistics, optimization, and
machine learning.

Volume IV
Chapter 5
Information Geometry
“Information has shape. Learning is movement across
that shape.”

5.1 Beyond Physical Geometry
The previous chapter introduced manifolds describing
physical and abstract state spaces.

 Geometry, however, extends beyond physical position.
Probability distributions themselves possess geometric
structure.
A statistical model may therefore be viewed as a curved
manifold whose points represent probability distributions
rather than locations in space.
This perspective forms the foundation of Information
Geometry.
Applications include:
•
•
•
•
•
•

statistical inference,
machine learning,
signal processing,
Bayesian estimation,
optimization,
data science.

5.2 Statistical Manifolds
Let
\Theta
denote a parameter space.
Each parameter

 \theta
\in
\Theta
defines a probability distribution
p(x;\theta).
The collection
\mathcal M
=
\{
p(x;\theta)
\}
forms a statistical manifold.
Each point corresponds to an entire probability
distribution.
Learning becomes motion through this manifold.

5.3 Parameters as Coordinates
Parameters serve as local coordinates.
For example,
a Gaussian distribution is determined by
(\mu,\sigma).

 Every pair
(\mu,\sigma)
defines a unique point on the manifold.
Optimization algorithms therefore trace curves across
parameter space.

5.4 Fisher Information Metric
To measure distance on a statistical manifold,
information geometry introduces the Fisher Information
Metric
g_{ij}
=
\mathbb E
\!\left[
\frac{\partial\log p}{\partial\theta_i}
\frac{\partial\log p}{\partial\theta_j}
\right].
Unlike Euclidean distance,
this metric measures distinguishability between nearby
probability distributions under the assumptions of the
statistical model.

 5.5 Information Distance
Nearby probability distributions need not be equally
distinguishable.
The Fisher metric defines infinitesimal distance,
while other measures such as the Kullback–Leibler
divergence quantify directional differences between
distributions.
Each measure serves different analytical purposes.

5.6 Geodesics in Probability Space
The shortest paths with respect to the Fisher metric are
called information geodesics.
These curves represent the most direct transitions between
probability distributions according to the chosen
geometry.
Information geodesics appear in:
•
•
•
•

statistical inference,
Bayesian updating,
optimization,
thermodynamics.

5.7 Divergence Measures

 Unlike ordinary distance,
many information measures are not symmetric.
Examples include:
Kullback–Leibler divergence
D_{KL}(P\|Q).
Jensen–Shannon divergence.
Rényi divergence.
Wasserstein distance.
Each captures different aspects of probabilistic similarity
and should be selected according to the modeling
assumptions and objectives.

5.8 Natural Gradient
Standard gradient descent assumes Euclidean geometry.
Information geometry instead introduces the natural
gradient
\tilde\nabla
=
G^{-1}
\nabla,
where

 G
is the Fisher information matrix.
Natural gradients account for the curvature of parameter
space and often improve optimization efficiency in
appropriate settings.

5.9 Entropy Surfaces
Every probability distribution possesses entropy,
H(P).
Entropy defines scalar fields across statistical manifolds.
Optimization may therefore be interpreted geometrically
as movement across entropy landscapes.
Different regions correspond to different levels of
uncertainty or information content.

5.10 Bayesian Geometry
Bayesian inference updates probability distributions in
response to observations.
Geometrically,
each observation moves the current estimate to a new
point on the statistical manifold.

 The trajectory depends upon:
• prior assumptions,
• likelihood functions,
• observed data.
Thus Bayesian learning becomes geometric evolution.

5.11 Information Flow
Information itself evolves dynamically.
Represent this abstractly as
P_t
\rightarrow
P_{t+1}.
Repeated updating generates trajectories through
probability space.
The geometry of the manifold influences convergence,
stability, and sensitivity to observations.

5.12 Connections to Persistence
Within the persistence framework,
retained variables may represent probability distributions
rather than deterministic quantities.

 Persistence mappings can therefore be interpreted as
transformations acting on statistical manifolds.
Such interpretations require explicit probabilistic
assumptions and remain one possible specialization of the
general framework.

Although the terminology differs, the underlying
mathematics shares a common geometric foundation.

Mathematics

Many physical and mathematical systems evolve by

 Volume IV
Chapter 6
Calculus of Variations and Optimal
Evolution
“Nature often appears not to choose a path at random,
but from among admissible paths according to a
governing principle. The calculus of variations provides a
mathematical framework for studying such principles.”

6.1 Beyond States
Previous chapters described:
• state spaces,
• operators,
• manifolds,
• statistical geometry.
Those frameworks study individual states and their
evolution.
The calculus of variations studies something different:
entire trajectories.
Instead of asking

 “Where is the system?”
we ask
“Which admissible path satisfies the chosen mathematical
criterion?”

6.2 Curves as Mathematical Objects
Let
\gamma:[a,b]\rightarrow M
be a smooth curve on a manifold
M.
The entire curve—not merely its endpoints—is the object
of study.
Different curves connecting the same endpoints may have
different lengths, energies, costs, or other mathematical
properties.

6.3 Functionals
Unlike ordinary functions,
which map numbers to numbers,
a functional maps functions (or curves) to real numbers.

 Write
\mathcal J[\gamma].
Examples include:
• total length,
• accumulated energy,
• travel time,
• action,
• integrated cost.
Optimization now concerns curves rather than points.

6.4 An Example Functional
A common example is
\mathcal J[y]
=
\int_a^b
L(x,y,y')
\,dx,
where
L
is called the Lagrangian.
The Lagrangian specifies how each infinitesimal segment
contributes to the total functional.

 Different choices of L model different mathematical or
physical systems.

6.5 Variations
Suppose
y(x)
is a candidate curve.
Introduce a small perturbation
y_\varepsilon(x)
=
y(x)
+
\varepsilon\eta(x),
where
• \varepsilon is a small parameter,
• \eta(x) is a smooth perturbation satisfying appropriate
boundary conditions.
A minimizing curve should be insensitive to first-order
perturbations.

6.6 Stationary Curves
A curve is stationary if

 \left.
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}
\mathcal J[y_\varepsilon]
\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
=
0.
Stationary does not necessarily mean minimum.
It may correspond to:
• minimum,
• maximum,
• saddle point.
Additional analysis determines which case applies.

6.7 Euler–Lagrange Equation
Under appropriate smoothness assumptions,
stationary curves satisfy the classical Euler–Lagrange
equation
\frac{d}{dx}
\left(
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}
\right)
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}

 =
0.
This equation is one of the foundational results of the
calculus of variations.
Many differential equations arise naturally from it.

6.8 Boundary Conditions
Solutions depend not only upon the functional,
but also upon boundary conditions.
Examples include:
Fixed endpoints.
Free endpoints.
Periodic boundaries.
Mixed conditions.
The choice of boundary conditions is part of the
mathematical model and influences the resulting
solutions.

6.9 Geodesics Revisited
From the previous chapter,

 geodesics were introduced as shortest paths.
They now appear naturally as stationary curves of the
length functional.
Thus geometry and variational analysis become unified.

6.10 Hamilton’s Principle
In classical mechanics,
many systems are modeled by Hamilton’s Principle,
which states that trajectories satisfy a stationary action
principle under specified assumptions.
The action functional is
S[q]
=
\int_{t_1}^{t_2}
L(q,\dot q,t)
\,dt.
Applying the Euler–Lagrange equation yields the
equations of motion.
This provides a variational formulation of many classical
mechanical systems.

6.11 Constrained Optimization

 Real systems frequently evolve under constraints.
Suppose
g(y)=0.
One classical method introduces a Lagrange multiplier
\lambda,
forming an augmented functional
\mathcal J
+
\lambda g.
This allows constraints to be incorporated directly into the
optimization problem.

6.12 Numerical Variational Methods
Many variational problems cannot be solved analytically.
Numerical techniques include:
• finite elements,
• finite differences,
• collocation methods,
• direct transcription,
• gradient-based optimization.
These methods approximate stationary curves while
respecting the chosen mathematical formulation.

 6.13 Variational Perspectives on
Persistence
Within the persistence framework,
one possible extension is to define functionals that
measure properties of evolving possibility structures or
recursive trajectories.
For example, a researcher might study trajectories that
minimize an application-specific cost while satisfying
persistence constraints.
Such formulations would require explicit definitions of
the functional and admissible trajectory space and remain
a direction for future development rather than a
consequence of the framework itself.

 building directly upon the variational principles

Volume IV
Chapter 7
Optimal Control Theory
“Optimization identifies an ideal path. Control
determines how to follow it.”

7.1 From Passive Evolution to
Active Decision
The calculus of variations studies optimal trajectories
once a mathematical criterion has been chosen.
Control theory introduces a new element:

 decision.
Instead of allowing the system to evolve without
intervention,
we introduce inputs that influence future evolution.
The mathematical question becomes:
How should those inputs be chosen to achieve a
specified objective under stated assumptions and
constraints?

7.2 State Equations
Let the system state be
x(t)\in\Omega.
Introduce a control input
u(t)\in\mathcal U,
where
\mathcal U
is the admissible control set.
The evolution equation becomes

 \dot{x}
=
f(x,u,t).
The function
f
must be specified by the particular application.

7.3 Control Constraints
Real systems cannot apply arbitrary controls.
Examples include:
• actuator limits,
• maximum voltage,
• bounded thrust,
• steering limits,
• fuel constraints,
• safety requirements.
Mathematically,
u(t)\in\mathcal U,
where
\mathcal U
represents the admissible control set.

 These constraints define which actions are feasible.

7.4 Performance Functionals
Control seeks to optimize an objective.
Introduce the performance functional
J[u]
=
\Phi(x(T))
+
\int_{t_0}^{T}
L(x,u,t)\,dt.
Here,
• \Phi is a terminal cost,
• L is a running cost.
Different applications choose different objective
functions.
Examples include:
•
•
•
•
•

minimum energy,
minimum travel time,
maximum efficiency,
minimum error,
balanced trade-offs among competing goals.

 7.5 Open-Loop Control
An open-loop controller computes
u(t)
in advance.
Execution does not depend upon subsequent observations.
Advantages include:
• simplicity,
• low computational cost.
Limitations include sensitivity to disturbances and
modeling errors.

7.6 Feedback Control
A feedback controller continuously measures the system
and updates the control law.
Write
u
=
K(x),
where
K

 is the feedback policy.
Advantages include:
• disturbance rejection,
• adaptation,
• improved robustness.
Feedback is one of the central ideas in modern
engineering.

7.7 Stability
A principal objective of feedback is stability.
For an equilibrium
x^*,
one seeks conditions under which nearby trajectories
remain close or converge toward
x^*.
Classical tools include:
• Lyapunov methods,
• linearization,
• eigenvalue analysis,
• invariant sets.
The appropriate method depends on the mathematical
properties of the system.

 7.8 Controllability
A system is controllable if admissible control inputs can
drive it between desired states under the assumptions of
the model.
Controllability depends on:
• system dynamics,
• control inputs,
• constraints,
• time horizon.
In linear systems, algebraic criteria such as Kalman’s
controllability test provide practical tools.
More general systems require different analyses.

7.9 Observability
Control also depends upon measurement.
Suppose observations satisfy
y
=
h(x).

 A system is observable if the available observations
contain sufficient information to infer the relevant internal
state under appropriate assumptions.
Observers and state estimators are often used when not
every variable can be measured directly.

7.10 Pontryagin’s Maximum
Principle
A foundational result in optimal control is Pontryagin’s
Maximum Principle.
It introduces:
• state equations,
• costate equations,
• the Hamiltonian,
• stationarity conditions.
Together these provide necessary conditions for
optimality under the stated assumptions.
The principle greatly extends the calculus of variations to
systems with explicit control inputs.

7.11 Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman
Theory

 Dynamic programming provides another formulation.
Define the value function
V(x,t),
representing the optimal achievable performance from
state
x
at time
t.
Under suitable assumptions, the value function satisfies
the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation.
Solving the HJB equation yields an optimal feedback
policy, although exact solutions are often computationally
difficult.

7.12 Numerical Optimal Control
Many practical problems require numerical methods.
Common approaches include:
•
•
•
•

shooting methods,
collocation,
direct transcription,
model predictive control,

 • sequential quadratic programming.
Each balances computational cost, accuracy, and
robustness according to the application.

7.13 Control and the Persistence
Framework
Within the persistence framework, control policies may
influence both observable states and retained variables.
For example,
\hat{x}
=
(x,m),
where
• x is the observable state,
• m represents retained variables.
A controller may therefore optimize trajectories in the
augmented state space.
Such formulations require explicit definitions of the
dynamics, constraints, and objectives for the application
being studied.

 7.14 Toward Computational
Realization
Optimal control provides mathematical policies.
Implementing those policies requires efficient numerical
algorithms.

“A mathematical theory becomes computational when its
equations can be approximated with controlled
accuracy.”

8.1 From Continuous Mathematics
to Computation
Many mathematical models describe continuous
evolution.
Computers, however, operate through discrete
computations.
Numerical analysis provides the mathematical bridge
between exact equations and finite computation.
Rather than replacing mathematics,
numerical methods approximate mathematical solutions
while providing tools for analyzing approximation error,
stability, and convergence.

 8.2 Initial Value Problems
Many dynamical systems begin with an equation of the
form
\frac{dx}{dt}
=
f(x,t),
together with an initial condition
x(t_0)
=
x_0.
The objective is to approximate
x(t)
for future times.
Analytical solutions are not always available.
Numerical methods provide practical approximations.

8.3 Time Discretization
Choose a timestep
h.
Define

 t_n
=
t_0
+
nh.
Continuous evolution becomes a sequence
x_0,
x_1,
x_2,
\ldots
The choice of timestep influences both computational cost
and numerical accuracy.

8.4 Euler’s Method
The simplest integration scheme is the forward Euler
method,
x_{n+1}
=
x_n
+
h\,f(x_n,t_n).
Advantages include:
• conceptual simplicity,

 • low computational cost.
Limitations include:
• first-order accuracy,
• sensitivity to timestep,
• potential instability for stiff systems.

8.5 Improved Euler (Heun’s
Method)
A more accurate second-order method computes an
intermediate prediction before averaging the slope.
Conceptually,
1. Predict the next state.
2. Evaluate the slope again.
3. Average the two slopes.
This often reduces numerical error while remaining
computationally efficient.

8.6 Runge–Kutta Methods
Higher-order Runge–Kutta methods evaluate multiple
intermediate slopes within each timestep.
The classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) method is
widely used because it provides an excellent balance

 between accuracy and computational effort for many
problems.
The choice of integration method should reflect the
properties of the underlying system.

8.7 Adaptive Step Size
Not every region of a trajectory requires the same
timestep.
Adaptive methods estimate local error and adjust
h
automatically.
When dynamics change rapidly,
smaller steps improve accuracy.
When evolution is smooth,
larger steps improve efficiency.
Adaptive integration is especially valuable for systems
exhibiting multiple time scales.

8.8 Stability of Numerical Schemes

 A numerical method should not introduce behavior absent
from the mathematical model.
Stability analysis studies whether numerical errors remain
controlled during repeated computation.
An unstable numerical scheme may diverge even when
the underlying differential equation possesses stable
solutions.
The stability region depends upon both the integration
method and the problem being solved.

8.9 Convergence
A numerical method is convergent if its approximation
approaches the exact solution as the timestep decreases.
Consistency and stability together often imply
convergence under appropriate assumptions, a
relationship formalized by classical results such as the
Lax Equivalence Theorem for suitable classes of
problems.

8.10 Error Analysis
Numerical error generally consists of several components.
Local truncation error

 The error introduced during one timestep.
Global error
The accumulated error across many timesteps.
Round-off error
Finite-precision arithmetic performed by digital
computers.
Understanding these sources helps guide the selection of
algorithms and step sizes.

8.11 Stiff Systems
Some systems contain both very fast and very slow
dynamics.
Such systems are called stiff.
Explicit methods may require extremely small timesteps
to remain stable.
Implicit methods often provide better stability for stiff
problems, though at increased computational cost.
The choice between explicit and implicit methods
depends upon the mathematical properties of the model.

8.12 Numerical Linear Algebra

 Large simulations frequently require solving systems of
linear equations,
computing eigenvalues,
or performing matrix factorizations.
Representative tools include:
• LU decomposition,
• QR factorization,
• conjugate gradient methods,
• Krylov subspace methods,
• sparse matrix algorithms.
Efficient linear algebra is fundamental to modern
scientific computing.

8.13 Simulation of Persistent
Systems
Within the persistence framework,
recursive evolution may be represented computationally
as
\hat{x}_{n+1}
=
\mathcal{R}(\hat{x}_n),
where

 \hat{x}
=
(x,m,G)
contains observable state,
retained variables,
and interaction structure.
Numerical simulation provides one way to explore the
behavior of such models under explicitly defined
assumptions.
Simulation can illustrate the consequences of a model, but
it does not establish mathematical proof or empirical
validity by itself.

8.14 Toward Large-Scale Scientific
Computing
Modern mathematical models frequently involve:
• millions of variables,
• distributed computation,
• adaptive meshes,
• parallel algorithms,
• uncertainty quantification.
The next chapter extends numerical analysis into
Scientific Computing, where advanced computational

 architectures, high-performance algorithms, and largescale simulation environments support the study of
complex dynamical systems.

 9.1 From Equations to

Many scientific problems exceed the capabilities of a

Suppose a computation can be divided into independent

 T

9.5 Sparse Representations
Large matrices often contain mostly zero entries.
Rather than storing every element,

Advantages include:

9.7 Uncertainty Quantification
Model predictions are rarely exact.

• measurement error,
• parameter uncertainty,
• numerical approximation,
• incomplete models.
Uncertainty quantification seeks to characterize how these

 Methods include sensitivity analysis, probabilistic

9.8 Verification and Validation
Scientific computing distinguishes two complementary
questions.
Verification
“Was the mathematical model implemented correctly?”
Validation
“Does the model adequately represent the system it is
intended to describe for the stated purpose?”
Verification concerns correctness of implementation.
Validation concerns agreement with observations or
experimental evidence where applicable.
Both are necessary in computational science.

9.9 Reproducibility
A computational result should be reproducible.
A reproducible workflow documents:
• governing equations,

 • numerical methods,
• parameter values,
• software versions,
• random seeds (when relevant),
• datasets,
• computational environment.
Reproducibility enables independent verification and
builds confidence in computational studies.

9.10 Performance Metrics
Computational algorithms are evaluated using measures

• execution time,
• memory consumption,
• scalability,
• numerical accuracy,
• communication overhead,
• energy efficiency.
No single metric is universally optimal.
Trade-offs depend upon the goals of the application.

9.11 Adaptive Simulation
Modern simulations often adapt during execution.

 Examples include:

• adaptive optimization.
Adaptation allocates computational resources where they
are most beneficial according to predefined criteria.

Formal Verification and MachineAssisted Mathematics

 “A proof convinces the human mind. Formal verification
convinces a precisely defined logical system.”

10.1 Why Formal Verification?
As mathematics grows in complexity,
so does the possibility of unnoticed error.
Modern proofs may span hundreds of pages.
Large engineering systems may contain millions of lines
of code.
Formal verification provides mathematical techniques that
allow logical arguments and algorithms to be checked
against explicitly specified rules.
Rather than replacing human reasoning,
formal verification complements it by reducing ambiguity
and improving confidence in correctness.

10.2 Formal Systems
A formal verification system begins with:
• a formal language,
• logical rules,
• axioms,

 • inference rules.
Every proof becomes a sequence of explicitly justified
logical steps.
Nothing is accepted merely because it appears plausible.

10.3 Proof Assistants
A proof assistant is software that helps construct
formally verified proofs.
Examples include:
• Lean
• Coq
• Isabelle/HOL
• HOL Light
These systems verify that each logical step follows from
previously established definitions, axioms, or theorems.
They assist mathematicians—they do not independently
invent mathematical truth.

10.4 Formal Specifications
Before verification can begin,
the intended behavior of a mathematical object or
algorithm must be specified precisely.

 A specification defines:
• inputs,
• outputs,
• assumptions,
• required properties,
• constraints.
A program cannot be proven correct without first defining
what “correct” means.

10.5 Correctness
Formal verification distinguishes several notions of
correctness.

Logical Correctness
The proof follows valid inference rules.

Algorithmic Correctness
The algorithm satisfies its specification.

Implementation Correctness
The software faithfully implements the intended
algorithm.
Each level addresses a different source of potential error.

 10.6 Soundness
A verification system is sound if it never proves false
statements within its formal logic.
Soundness is one of the foundational requirements of
trustworthy proof systems.
Without soundness,
formal verification would lose its value.

10.7 Completeness
Some logical systems are complete for particular classes
of statements.
Others are intentionally incomplete but computationally
practical.
As discussed in earlier volumes,
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems place important limits
on sufficiently expressive formal systems under
appropriate assumptions.
Formal verification works within these well-understood
logical boundaries.

 10.8 Verified Algorithms
Algorithms themselves may be formally verified.
Examples include:
• sorting algorithms,
• graph algorithms,
• numerical methods,
• cryptographic protocols,
• control software,
• communication protocols.
Verification demonstrates that the implementation
satisfies the mathematical specification—not that the
specification itself necessarily models reality.

10.9 Certified Numerical
Computation
Numerical computation introduces approximation.
Formal methods can sometimes provide rigorous error
bounds.
Examples include:
• interval arithmetic,
• certified optimization,
• verified integration,

 • validated eigenvalue computation.
These techniques combine numerical analysis with formal
guarantees under explicitly stated assumptions.

10.10 Formal Models and Physical
Systems
A formally verified model is mathematically correct with
respect to its specification.
Whether that specification accurately represents a
physical system remains a separate empirical question.
It is therefore useful to distinguish:
• mathematical correctness,
• implementation correctness,
• empirical adequacy.
Each requires different methods of evaluation.

10.11 Verification Workflows
A disciplined verification workflow often includes:
1. Define mathematical objects.
2. State assumptions explicitly.
3. Specify desired properties.
4. Construct proofs.

 5. Verify computational implementations.
6. Test numerical behavior.
7. Compare with experimental or observational
evidence where applicable.
Each stage strengthens confidence in different aspects of
the overall framework.

10.12 Formal Verification and the
Persistence Framework
The persistence framework developed throughout these
volumes may itself be formalized.
Possible verification tasks include:
• checking definitions for internal consistency,
• verifying theorem statements under stated
assumptions,
• confirming recursive algorithms satisfy specified
properties,
• validating computational implementations against
their mathematical formulations.
Such verification does not establish new mathematics
automatically, but it helps ensure that the framework is
expressed consistently and implemented faithfully.

 10.13 Machine Assistance in
Modern Mathematics
Machine-assisted mathematics is increasingly used to:
• verify long proofs,
• explore conjectures,
• search for counterexamples,
• automate routine reasoning,
• certify computations.
Human creativity remains central to choosing definitions,
framing problems, and interpreting results.
Machine assistance provides additional rigor and
scalability.

10.14 Toward Integrated
Mathematical Systems
Formal verification naturally complements:
• operator theory,
• numerical analysis,
• optimization,
• dynamical systems,
• scientific computing.
Together they form an integrated methodology:

 1. Build a mathematical model.
2. Analyze it theoretically.
3. Implement it computationally.
4. Verify the implementation.
5. Validate applications where appropriate.
This synthesis represents one of the defining
characteristics of modern computational mathematics.

“Every mathematical model is a conversation between

 19.1 Why Mathematical Models
Exist
The world is extraordinarily complex.
No mathematical model captures every detail.
Instead,
models isolate the features relevant to a particular
question while deliberately omitting others.
A useful model therefore balances:
• simplicity,
• explanatory power,
• computational tractability,
• predictive capability within its intended domain.
The quality of a model depends not on its complexity, but
on how well it serves its stated purpose.

19.2 Abstraction
Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while preserving
essential mathematical structure.
Examples include:
Representing a planet as a point mass.

 Representing a communication network as a graph.
Representing uncertainty through probability
distributions.
Representing motion by differential equations.
Different abstractions may be appropriate for different
questions.

19.3 Assumptions
Every mathematical model begins with assumptions.
Examples include:
• continuity,
• differentiability,
• independence,
• conservation,
• boundedness,
• symmetry,
• stationarity.
Assumptions determine both the power and the
limitations of a model.
Explicit assumptions make models easier to understand,
test, and revise.

19.4 Scope

 Every model has a domain of applicability.
Questions to consider include:
• Which systems does the model represent?
• Under what conditions?
• Which phenomena are intentionally excluded?
• Which variables are treated as external inputs?
A model should not be expected to answer questions
beyond its intended scope.

19.5 Parameters
Models often contain parameters,
\theta.
Parameters may be:
• measured,
• estimated,
• calibrated,
• inferred.
Parameter uncertainty should be acknowledged explicitly,
particularly when predictions depend sensitively upon
their values.

19.6 Validation

 Validation asks:
Does the model adequately represent the system it is
intended to describe for the stated purpose?
Validation methods may include:
• comparison with observations,
• experimental testing,
• benchmark problems,
• cross-validation,
• sensitivity analysis.
Validation is distinct from mathematical proof.
A mathematically correct model may still fail to represent
a particular physical system adequately.

19.7 Verification
Verification asks:
Has the mathematical model been implemented correctly?
Verification concerns:
• equations,
• algorithms,
• software,
• numerical methods.
Validation concerns correspondence with the intended
application.

 Both are essential.

19.8 Uncertainty
No model is free from uncertainty.
Representative sources include:
• measurement error,
• parameter uncertainty,
• numerical approximation,
• incomplete knowledge,
• stochastic variability.
Quantifying uncertainty improves interpretation and
decision-making.

19.9 Model Comparison
Multiple mathematical models may describe the same
phenomenon.
Useful comparison criteria include:
•
•
•
•
•
•

predictive accuracy,
computational efficiency,
interpretability,
robustness,
theoretical consistency,
empirical support within the intended domain.

 Different applications may prioritize these criteria
differently.

19.10 Simplicity and Complexity
A more complicated model is not necessarily a better
model.
Increasing complexity may improve fidelity,
but can also introduce:
• overfitting,
• computational cost,
• parameter sensitivity,
• interpretability challenges.
Choosing an appropriate level of complexity is an
important modeling decision.

19.11 Iterative Refinement
Model development is often iterative.
A typical process is:
Observe
↓
Model
↓

 Analyze
↓
Simulate
↓
Compare
↓
Revise
↓
Repeat

Each cycle improves understanding by incorporating new
evidence, correcting deficiencies, or refining assumptions.

19.13 Responsible Modeling
Responsible mathematical modeling includes:
• stating assumptions explicitly,
• distinguishing proven results from conjectures,
• separating simulation from empirical evidence,
• documenting limitations,
• reporting uncertainty,
• enabling reproducibility.
These practices strengthen both scientific rigor and public
trust.

Part I — Residual Coherence:

1. Phase Space and Gauge Reduction
Let
\Theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_9)\in\mathbb T^9,
\qquad
\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z).
The common phase action is
\Theta\mapsto \Theta+\alpha\mathbf 1,
\qquad
\mathbf 1=(1,\ldots,1)^T.
Define
P_8=I_9-\frac19\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T.

Lemma 1.1 — Centering-projector properties
The matrix P_8 is the orthogonal projector onto

 \mathbf 1^\perp
=
\{v\in\mathbb R^9:\mathbf 1^Tv=0\}.
It satisfies
P_8^T=P_8,
\qquad
P_8^2=P_8,
\qquad
P_8\mathbf 1=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}P_8=8.

Proof
Symmetry follows immediately:
P_8^T
=
I_9-\frac19(\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T)^T
=
P_8.
For idempotence,
\begin{aligned}
P_8^2
&=
\left(I-\frac19\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T\right)^2\\
&=
I-\frac29\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T

 +\frac1{81}\mathbf 1(\mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1)\mathbf 1^T.
\end{aligned}
Since \mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1=9,
P_8^2
=
I-\frac29\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T
+\frac19\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T
=
P_8.
Also,
P_8\mathbf 1
=
\mathbf 1-\frac19\mathbf 1(\mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1)
=
\mathbf 1-\mathbf 1
=
0.
Hence \ker P_8=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}. Rank–
nullity gives
\operatorname{rank}P_8=9-1=8.
Because P_8 is symmetric and idempotent, it is the
orthogonal projector onto \mathbf 1^\perp. ∎

2. Explicit Relative-Phase Coordinates

 Define
B=
\begin{bmatrix}
e_1-e_9\\
e_2-e_9\\
\vdots\\
e_8-e_9
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb Z^{8\times 9}.
Then
x=B\Theta,
\qquad
x_j=\theta_j-\theta_9.

Lemma 2.1 — Rank and gauge annihilation
B\mathbf 1=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}B=8.

Proof
Each row has one +1, one -1, and otherwise zero entries, so
every row sums to zero. Hence B\mathbf 1=0.
Suppose
\sum_{j=1}^{8}c_j(e_j-e_9)=0.

 The first eight components give c_j=0 for every j. Thus the
rows are independent and \operatorname{rank}B=8. ∎

Theorem 2.2 — Quotient-coordinate completeness
The map
[\Theta]\in\mathbb T^9/U(1)
\longmapsto
B\Theta\in\mathbb T^8
is well-defined and bijective.

Proof
Well-definedness. If
\Theta'=\Theta+\alpha\mathbf 1,
then
B\Theta'
=
B\Theta+\alpha B\mathbf 1
=
B\Theta.
Injectivity. Suppose
B\Theta=B\Theta'.
Then for j=1,\ldots,8,

 \theta_j-\theta_9
=
\theta_j'-\theta_9'
\pmod{2\pi}.
Therefore
\theta_j'-\theta_j
=
\theta_9'-\theta_9
\pmod{2\pi}
for every j, so \Theta' differs from \Theta by one common
phase.
Surjectivity. Given any x=(x_1,\ldots,x_8)\in\mathbb T^8,
choose
\Theta=(x_1,\ldots,x_8,0).
Then B\Theta=x. ∎
This proves that the physical compact phase space is exactly
an eight-torus,
\mathbb T^9/U(1)\cong\mathbb T^8,
rather than merely “approximately eight-dimensional.” This
construction is already outlined in the source manuscript.

Let the channel phases be
\Psi_c(u)=r_c^Tu-\phi_c,
\qquad

where u\in\mathbb T^8, r_c^T is row c of a channel matrix
R\in\mathbb R^{48\times 8}, and \phi_c is an offset.
Define
Z_{48}(u)
=
\frac1{48}
\sum_{c=1}^{48}e^{i\Psi_c(u)},
and
\beta^2(u)
=
1-|Z_{48}(u)|^2.

Theorem 3.1 — Pressure-null equivalence
For every u,
0\le \beta(u)\le 1.
Moreover,

 \beta(u)=0
if and only if
\Psi_1(u)\equiv\Psi_2(u)\equiv\cdots\equiv\Psi_{48}(u)
\pmod{2\pi}.

Proof
Every term has unit modulus:
|e^{i\Psi_c}|=1.
By the triangle inequality,
|Z_{48}|
\le
\frac1{48}
\sum_{c=1}^{48}|e^{i\Psi_c}|
=
1.
Thus
0\le 1-|Z_{48}|^2\le1,
and therefore 0\le\beta\le1.
Now \beta=0 precisely when |Z_{48}|=1. Equality in the
triangle inequality for nonzero complex numbers occurs

e^{i\Psi_c}=e^{i\Psi_d}

\Psi_c-\Psi_d\in2\pi\mathbb Z.

2.1 Formal Setting
Let
\Omega
be a nonempty state space.
Let
\mathcal U
be a set of admissible inputs or controls.
Let
\mathcal M

 be a retained-state space.
The complete state is
z=(x,m)\in\mathcal Z,
\qquad
\mathcal Z=\Omega\times\mathcal M.
Here:
• x\in\Omega is the active or externally modeled state;
• m\in\mathcal M is the retained consequence relevant to
future evolution.
Define the recursive transition map
T:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal U\rightarrow\mathcal Z.
Write its components as
T((x,m),u)
=
\bigl(F(x,m,u),\,G(x,m,u)\bigr).
Thus,
x_{n+1}=F(x_n,m_n,u_n),
m_{n+1}=G(x_n,m_n,u_n).
This is the minimal formal architecture for a system in which
retained consequence can influence later evolution.

2.2 One-Step Possibility Mapping

 For each augmented state z=(x,m), define the one-step
possibility set
\Pi_1(z)
=
\left\{
T(z,u):u\in\mathcal U
\right\}.
If only the active state is of interest, define the projected
possibility set
\Pi_1^x(x,m)
=
\left\{
F(x,m,u):u\in\mathcal U
\right\}.
This distinguishes the complete future state from its
observable or active projection.

Definition 2.1 — Future-active retained
consequence
A retained state m is future-active at x if there exists another
retained state \tilde m\in\mathcal M such that
\Pi_1^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_1^x(x,\tilde m).

 Thus retention is not defined merely by storage. It is defined
by future influence.

2.3 Retained-State Relevance
Proposition 2.1 — Equivalent tests for onestep relevance
For fixed x, the following are equivalent:
1. m is future-active relative to some \tilde m.
2. There exists u\in\mathcal U such that
F(x,m,u)\neq F(x,\tilde m,u).
3. The maps
F_{x,m}:u\mapsto F(x,m,u)
and
F_{x,\tilde m}:u\mapsto F(x,\tilde m,u)
are not identical.
4. The projected one-step possibility sets differ for at least
one common admissible-input model.

Proof
If statement 2 holds, then at least one output under the same
admissible input differs, so the two input-to-state maps are
not identical; hence 3 follows.
If the maps differ, there exists some input at which their
outputs differ, so 3 implies 2.

 If 2 holds, then the systems possess different active-state
successors under that input. Under the common-input
interpretation of the possibility map, their one-step future
structures differ, giving 1.
Conversely, if the possibility sets differ, then some successor
belongs to one set but not the other. Therefore the underlying
maps cannot agree on every admissible input, establishing 2.
∎

2.4 Inert Storage
Definition 2.2 — Dynamically inert retained
state
A retained variable is dynamically inert over a domain
D\subseteq\Omega if
F(x,m,u)=F(x,\tilde m,u)
for all
x\in D,
\qquad
m,\tilde m\in\mathcal M,
\qquad
u\in\mathcal U.
In this case, the active dynamics are independent of retained
state on D.

 Theorem 2.2 — Inert-storage elimination
If m is dynamically inert over D, then the active-state
dynamics reduce to a memory-independent map
x_{n+1}
=
\bar F(x_n,u_n)
for trajectories remaining in D.

Proof
Because F is independent of the retained-state argument on
D, choose any fixed m_0\in\mathcal M and define
\bar F(x,u)=F(x,m_0,u).
For every m,
F(x,m,u)=F(x,m_0,u)=\bar F(x,u).
Therefore the active-state recursion is
x_{n+1}=\bar F(x_n,u_n).
The retained variable may continue to evolve internally, but
it does not influence the active trajectory while the state
remains in D. ∎
This theorem formalizes the difference between stored
history and future-active memory.

Define the n-step reachable set recursively:
\Pi_0(z)=\{z\},
and
\Pi_{n+1}(z)
=
\bigcup_{y\in\Pi_n(z)}
\left\{
T(y,u):u\in\mathcal U
\right\}.
The active-state projection is
\Pi_n^x(z)
=
\operatorname{pr}_\Omega\Pi_n(z).
The total reachable set is
\Pi_\infty(z)
=
\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\Pi_n(z).

Definition 2.3 — n-step retained influence
Two retained states m,\tilde m have distinguishable n-step
influence at active state x if

 \Pi_n^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_n^x(x,\tilde m).

finite-horizon influence

\Pi_1^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_1^x(x,\tilde m),

Proof
The result holds immediately with horizon n=1. ∎
The reverse need not hold. Two retained states may produce
identical one-step active outcomes but differ later because

Every deterministic system with finite memory length r can

z_n

\|A\|^n\|m_0\|
\le
\rho^n\|m_0\|.
Since 0\le\rho<1, \rho^n\to0. ∎

Theorem 2.13 — Bounded-input boundedmemory result
Suppose
\|A\|\le\rho<1
and
\|b_n\|\le B.
Then
\|m_n\|
\le

 \rho^n\|m_0\|
+
\frac{B(1-\rho^n)}{1-\rho},
and therefore
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|m_n\|
\le
\frac{B}{1-\rho}.

Proof
Using the exact decomposition,
\begin{aligned}
\|m_n\|
&\le
\|A^nm_0\|
+
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
\|A^{n-1-k}b_k\|\\
&\le
\rho^n\|m_0\|
+
B\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^j\\
&=
\rho^n\|m_0\|
+
B\frac{1-\rho^n}{1-\rho}.
\end{aligned}

 Taking the limit superior gives the result. ∎
This theorem formalizes a balance between reinforcement
and decay.

2.16 Persistence Threshold Model
Consider the scalar model
\dot w
=
D_+(t)-D_-(t)-\delta w+\eta(t),
\qquad
\delta>0.
Here:
• D_+ is constructive drive;
• D_- is destructive drive;
• \delta w is proportional decay;
• \eta is disturbance.
Assume constants
D_+(t)\ge d_+,
\qquad
D_-(t)\le d_-,
\qquad
\eta(t)\ge-\varepsilon.
Then

 \dot w
\ge
d_+-d_--\varepsilon-\delta w.
Define
w_{\mathrm{eq}}
=
\frac{d_+-d_--\varepsilon}{\delta}.

Theorem 2.14 — Lower persistence bound
If d_+-d_--\varepsilon>0, then
w(t)
\ge
w_{\mathrm{eq}}
+
\bigl(w(0)-w_{\mathrm{eq}}\bigr)e^{-\delta t}.

Proof
Compare w with the solution y of
\dot y
=
d_+-d_--\varepsilon-\delta y,
\qquad
y(0)=w(0).
The explicit solution is

 y(t)
=
w_{\mathrm{eq}}
+
\bigl(w(0)-w_{\mathrm{eq}}\bigr)e^{-\delta t}.
Since
\dot w+\delta w
\ge
\dot y+\delta y
and w(0)=y(0), the comparison principle yields
w(t)\ge y(t).
∎

Corollary 2.15 — Threshold persistence
Let w_c>0 be a required persistence threshold. If
w_{\mathrm{eq}}>w_c
and
w(0)\ge w_c,
then
w(t)\ge w_c
for all t\ge0.

 Proof
The lower comparison solution is a convex combination of
w(0) and w_{\mathrm{eq}}:
y(t)
=
e^{-\delta t}w(0)
+
(1-e^{-\delta t})w_{\mathrm{eq}}.
Both terms are at least w_c, so y(t)\ge w_c. Since w(t)\ge
y(t), the result follows. ∎
This gives a precise sufficient condition for persistence
above a threshold.

2.17 Interaction Quality Model
Consider
\dot w_{ij}
=
q_{ij}\chi_{ij}I_{ij}
\delta_{ij}w_{ij}
+
\eta_{ij},
with

 q_{ij}\in[-1,1],
\qquad
\chi_{ij}\ge0,
\qquad
I_{ij}\ge0,
\qquad
\delta_{ij}>0.
Assume these quantities are constant and \eta_{ij}=0.

Proposition 2.16 — Exact coupling trajectory
w_{ij}(t)
=
w_{ij}^*
+
\left(
w_{ij}(0)-w_{ij}^*
\right)e^{-\delta_{ij}t},
where
w_{ij}^*
=
\frac{q_{ij}\chi_{ij}I_{ij}}{\delta_{ij}}.

Proof
This is a linear first-order differential equation:
\dot w+\delta w=q\chi I.

 Solving by the integrating-factor method gives the stated
formula. ∎

Corollary 2.17 — Sign of long-term coupling
If
\chi_{ij}I_{ij}>0,
then the sign of the equilibrium coupling equals the sign of
q_{ij}.
Thus constructive and destructive interactions can be
formally distinguished by the sign of the quality factor in this

2.18 Feedback as Retained-State
Dependence
A system possesses feedback when future transitions depend
on a consequence of previous transitions.
Let
m_{n+1}=G(m_n,A_n)
and
A_{n+1}=H(x_{n+1},m_{n+1}).

 Theorem 2.18 — Minimal feedback criterion
If there exist m,\tilde m and an active state x such that
H(x,m)\neq H(x,\tilde m),
then retained state participates in the generation of future
interaction.

Proof
The same active state x produces different future interactions
when paired with different retained states. Therefore the
retained state is causally represented in the transition rule of
the model. ∎
This is a formal criterion inside the model. Empirical
causality requires additional experimental identification.

2.19 Feedback Isomorphism
Let two closed recursive systems be
S_1=(\Omega_1,T_1,K_1,C_1)
and
S_2=(\Omega_2,T_2,K_2,C_2).
Suppose there exists a bijection
\phi:\Omega_1\rightarrow\Omega_2

 such that
\phi\circ T_1=T_2\circ\phi
and a constraint-space bijection
\psi:K_1\rightarrow K_2
such that
C_2\circ\phi=\psi\circ C_1.

Theorem 2.19 — Trajectory conjugacy
For every n\ge0,
\phi\circ T_1^n
=
T_2^n\circ\phi.

Proof
Proceed by induction.
For n=0,
\phi\circ I=I\circ\phi.
Assume
\phi\circ T_1^n
=
T_2^n\circ\phi.
Then

 \begin{aligned}
\phi\circ T_1^{n+1}
&=
\phi\circ T_1\circ T_1^n\\
&=
T_2\circ\phi\circ T_1^n\\
&=
T_2\circ T_2^n\circ\phi\\
&=
T_2^{n+1}\circ\phi.
\end{aligned}
Therefore the result holds for all n. ∎

Corollary 2.20 — Constraint preservation
along trajectories
For every initial state x\in\Omega_1,
C_2\bigl(T_2^n(\phi(x))\bigr)
=
\psi\left(
C_1(T_1^n(x))
\right).

Proof
Using trajectory conjugacy,

 T_2^n(\phi(x))
=
\phi(T_1^n(x)).
Then
C_2(T_2^n(\phi(x)))
=
C_2(\phi(T_1^n(x)))
=
\psi(C_1(T_1^n(x))).
∎
This proves preservation of abstract recursive architecture
under conjugacy. It does not establish material or physical
identity.

2.20 Organizational Identity as an
Equivalence Class
Let
\mathcal Q:\mathcal Z\rightarrow\mathcal Y
extract the organizational features regarded as identityrelevant.
Define
z\sim_{\mathcal Q}\tilde z

 if
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\tilde z).

Lemma 2.21 — Identity relation
The relation \sim_{\mathcal Q} is an equivalence relation.

Proof
Reflexivity:
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(z),
so z\sim_{\mathcal Q}z.
Symmetry: If
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\tilde z),
then
\mathcal Q(\tilde z)=\mathcal Q(z).
Transitivity: If
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\tilde z)
and
\mathcal Q(\tilde z)=\mathcal Q(\hat z),
then
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\hat z).

 Thus \sim_{\mathcal Q} is an equivalence relation. ∎
The identity of the modeled system is then represented by the
equivalence class
[z]_{\mathcal Q}.

2.21 Identity Preservation Under
Dynamics
Definition 2.5 — Exact organizational
identity preservation
A transition T preserves organizational identity if
\mathcal Q(T(z))=\mathcal Q(z)
for every admissible state z.

Theorem 2.22 — Orbit identity preservation
If T preserves \mathcal Q, then
\mathcal Q(T^n(z))=\mathcal Q(z)
for all n\ge0.

Proof
Induction gives

 \mathcal Q(T^{n+1}(z))
=
\mathcal Q(T(T^n(z)))
=
\mathcal Q(T^n(z)).
Beginning with \mathcal Q(T(z))=\mathcal Q(z), repeated
application yields the result. ∎

2.22 Approximate Identity
Preservation
Exact invariance is often too strong.
Let d_{\mathcal Y} be a metric on organizational feature
space.
Define identity drift over one step by
\Delta_{\mathcal Q}(z)
=
d_{\mathcal Y}
\left(
\mathcal Q(T(z)),
\mathcal Q(z)
\right).
If
\Delta_{\mathcal Q}(z)\le\varepsilon,

 identity is preserved within tolerance \varepsilon for that
step.

Proposition 2.23 — Cumulative drift bound
Suppose
d_{\mathcal Y}
\left(
\mathcal Q(z_{k+1}),
\mathcal Q(z_k)
\right)
\le
\varepsilon_k.
Then
d_{\mathcal Y}
\left(
\mathcal Q(z_n),
\mathcal Q(z_0)
\right)
\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.

Proof
Apply the triangle inequality repeatedly:
\begin{aligned}
d(\mathcal Q(z_n),\mathcal Q(z_0))

 &\le
d(\mathcal Q(z_n),\mathcal Q(z_{n-1}))\\
&\quad+
d(\mathcal Q(z_{n-1}),\mathcal Q(z_{n-2}))
+\cdots\\
&\quad+
d(\mathcal Q(z_1),\mathcal Q(z_0))\\
&\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.
\end{aligned}
∎
Small local drift does not necessarily imply indefinite
identity preservation unless the accumulated drift remains
bounded.

2.23 Progress as Possibility
Improvement
A possibility space needs an ordering before “improvement”
can be formalized.
Let
V:\mathcal P(\Omega)\rightarrow\mathbb R
be a viability or opportunity functional.
Define progress by

 V(\mathcal P_{n+1})>V(\mathcal P_n).

Definition 2.6 — Retention-mediated

An interaction produces retention-mediated progress if

and
V(\Pi_1(x_{n+1},m_{n+1}))
>
V(\Pi_1(x_n,m_n)).
This definition makes explicit that “expanded possibility”
depends on a chosen and justified functional V.

Proposition 2.24 — Progress is not equivalent
to set enlargement
It is possible for
\mathcal P_{n+1}\not\supseteq\mathcal P_n
while
V(\mathcal P_{n+1})>V(\mathcal P_n).

Proof by example
Let

 \mathcal P_n=\{1,100\}
and
\mathcal P_{n+1}=\{50,60\}.
Neither set contains the other.
Define
V(\mathcal P)
=
\min_{x\in\mathcal P}x.
Then
V(\mathcal P_n)=1,
\qquad
V(\mathcal P_{n+1})=50.
Thus opportunity can improve according to a selected
criterion without simple set inclusion. ∎
Therefore progress always requires a value structure, not
merely a larger number of reachable states.

2.24 Communication as Coupled
Memory Update
Let two systems have states

\qquad
z_2=(x_2,m_2).
A communication event is represented by

\mapsto

\neq

Proof
Before communication, input u produces

After communication, the same input produces
F(x_2,m_2',u).
By assumption these differ, so the receiver’s future inputstate relation has changed. ∎

>
V\bigl(\Pi_1(x,m)\bigr).

 A response may also preserve value while reorganizing
possibilities.

2.27 Central Theorem of Retained
Consequence
Theorem 2.26 — Retained consequence
changes future possibility under sensitivity
Let
z_n=(x_n,m_n)
undergo an interaction producing
z_{n+1}=(x_{n+1},m_{n+1}).
Suppose there exists a counterfactual retained state \tilde
m_{n+1} associated with the same active state x_{n+1} such
