\Pi_1^x(x_{n+1},m_{n+1})
\neq
\Pi_1^x(x_{n+1},\tilde m_{n+1}).
Then the retained consequence m_{n+1} is future-active.

 Proof
This is exactly the definition of future-active retained
consequence: varying retained state while holding active
state fixed changes the future possibility set. ∎
The theorem is logically simple because the scientific burden
lies in identifying and validating the state variables,
transition law, admissible controls, and counterfactual
comparison.

2.28 Minimal Defensible Theorem
Theorem 2.27 — Recursive organization
theorem
Assume:
1. the system has an augmented state z_n=(x_n,m_n);
2. the retained state is updated recursively;
3. future transition structure depends nontrivially on m_n;
4. trajectories remain inside an admissible domain.
Then prior interactions can influence later reachable states
through the retained-state channel.

Proof
By assumption 2, prior interaction contributes to m_n.
By assumption 3, there exist retained states producing
different future transition structures at some active state.

 Therefore the retained consequence generated by prior
interaction can alter a later successor or reachable set.
Assumption 4 ensures the recursion remains within the stated
model domain. ∎
This is the rigorous form of the statement:
What happens can change what can happen next.
It is conditional, not universal. It applies precisely to models
satisfying the assumptions.

2.29 No-Go Results
Theorem 2.28 — No retained influence
without sensitivity
If
F(x,m,u)=F(x,\tilde m,u)
for all states, retained values, and admissible inputs, and if
admissibility is also independent of memory, then retained
consequence cannot change active-state possibility.

Proof
The successor map and admissible-input set are identical for
every retained state. Therefore all projected possibility sets
are identical. ∎

 Theorem 2.29 — No feedback without
retained dependence
If future transition rules are independent of every variable
altered by previous interaction, then the model contains no
feedback channel from past consequence to future evolution.

Proof
Feedback requires a path by which an earlier consequence
enters a later transition. If every later transition is
independent of all earlier altered variables, no such path
exists. ∎

Theorem 2.30 — Persistence does not imply
value
A persistent state can preserve a negative, harmful, unstable,
or low-viability structure.

Proof by construction
Consider
m_{n+1}=m_n
with
m_0=-1.
Then

 m_n=-1
for all n, so the state persists perfectly.
Define value
V(m)=m.
Then the persistent state has negative value. Hence
persistence alone implies neither benefit nor progress. ∎

2.30 Proof Boundary
The formal results above establish:
• how retained state may be encoded;
• how it may alter future transitions or reachable sets;
• how finite-history systems admit augmented-state
closure;
• how persistence thresholds arise in simple dynamical
models;
• how feedback isomorphism preserves recursive
structure;
• how identity can be represented through invariant
organizational features;
• how communication and response may change future
possibility;
• why progress requires a separate value functional.
They do not establish:
• that every real system is accurately modeled this way;

 •
•
•
•

that every historical trace is memory;
that persistence is universally beneficial;
that structural similarity implies physical identity;
that consciousness or conscious intent follows from
recursion;
• that an arbitrary possibility functional represents
objective progress.
Those conclusions require domain-specific models and
evidence.

Let the original centered rows be

and let
K=\sum_{c=1}^{48}\tilde r_c\tilde r_c^T.

After deleting row j,

 K_{-j}
=
K
\frac{48}{47}
\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T.

Proof
Let
n=48.
The original mean is
\bar r
=
\frac1n\sum_{c=1}^{n}r_c.
After deleting r_j, the new mean is
\bar r_{-j}
=
\frac1{n-1}
\sum_{c\ne j}r_c
=
\frac{n\bar r-r_j}{n-1}.
Therefore
\bar r_{-j}
=
\bar r

For c\ne j,
r_c-\bar r_{-j}
=
\tilde r_c
+
\frac{\tilde r_j}{n-1}.
Hence
K_{-j}
=
\sum_{c\ne j}
\left(
\tilde r_c
+
\frac{\tilde r_j}{n-1}
\right)
\left(
\tilde r_c
+
\frac{\tilde r_j}{n-1}
\right)^T.
Now
\sum_{c\ne j}\tilde r_c=-\tilde r_j
because the full centered-row sum is zero.

 Expanding,
\begin{aligned}
K_{-j}
&=
\sum_{c\ne j}\tilde r_c\tilde r_c^T
+
\frac1{n-1}
\left[
\left(\sum_{c\ne j}\tilde r_c\right)\tilde r_j^T
+
\tilde r_j
\left(\sum_{c\ne j}\tilde r_c\right)^T
\right]\\
&\quad+
\frac{n-1}{(n-1)^2}
\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T.
\end{aligned}
Using
\sum_{c\ne j}\tilde r_c\tilde r_c^T
=
K-\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T
and
\sum_{c\ne j}\tilde r_c=-\tilde r_j,

=
K
\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T
\frac2{n-1}\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T
+
\frac1{n-1}\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T.
Thus
K_{-j}
=
K
\left(
1+\frac1{n-1}
\right)
\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T
=
K-\frac n{n-1}\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T.
Setting n=48 gives
K_{-j}
=
K-\frac{48}{47}\tilde r_j\tilde r_j^T.
∎

when one centered channel is removed.

3.31 Rank, Redundancy, Tightness,
and Uniqueness
These four concepts must be separated.

Definition 3.4 — Rank completeness
\operatorname{rank}(PR)=8.

Definition 3.5 — Redundancy
There are more centered channel vectors than the minimum
number required to span \mathbb R^8.

Definition 3.6 — Tightness
R^TPR=\alpha I_8.

Definition 3.7 — Uniqueness

 No admissible alternative channel architecture satisfies the
specified mathematical and physical criteria.

Theorem 3.37 — Logical independence
Rank completeness, redundancy, tightness, and uniqueness
are not equivalent.

Proof
• A basis of eight vectors can have full rank without
redundancy.
• A redundant family can still fail full rank if all vectors
lie in a lower-dimensional subspace.
• A full-rank frame need not be tight.
• A tight frame need not be unique; many inequivalent
tight frames exist.
• Uniqueness requires a classification or extremal theorem
beyond rank and frame conditions.
Thus no one property implies all the others. ∎

unchanged, but every energy scales by \varepsilon.
Therefore the invariant alone cannot fix an absolute
bound without specifying the energy functional. ∎
Topology classifies configurations; dynamics and

E[\gamma(s)]
E[\gamma(0)]
\right],

A state has a positive reconnection barrier if

for every lower-energy competing sector Q'.

invariant on the nonsingular subspace.

increase slightly, travel far outside the local

4.39 No-Go Statement for Symbolic

Theorem 4.39 — A named braid does not
prove a soliton
Specifying a braid word, winding vector, or sacredgeometric pattern does not by itself prove:

 1. existence of a solution to the Euler–Lagrange
equations;
2. finite energy;
3. local stability;
4. global metastability;
5. correspondence with a physical particle.

Proof
Each item requires additional mathematical information:
• existence requires solving or proving solvability of
the field equations;
• finite energy requires asymptotic and integrability
conditions;
• local stability requires a nonnegative projected
Hessian;
• metastability requires a positive global barrier;
• physical correspondence requires empirical
parameter identification.

4.40 Existence by the Direct
Method: Conditional Template
Let \mathcal A_Q be an admissible set in fixed
topological sector Q.

 Theorem 4.40 — Conditional variational
existence
Suppose:
1. \mathcal A_Q is nonempty;
2. E is bounded below on \mathcal A_Q;
3. every minimizing sequence has a weakly convergent
subsequence;
4. \mathcal A_Q is weakly closed;
5. E is weakly lower semicontinuous.
Then E attains its minimum on \mathcal A_Q.

Proof
Let \Psi_n be a minimizing sequence:
E[\Psi_n]\rightarrow
\inf_{\mathcal A_Q}E.
By assumption 3, a subsequence converges weakly to
\Psi_*. By weak closure,
\Psi_*\in\mathcal A_Q.
By weak lower semicontinuity,
E[\Psi_*]
\le
\liminf E[\Psi_n]

 =
\inf_{\mathcal A_Q}E.
Therefore equality holds and \Psi_* is a minimizer. ∎
This is the correct theorem template for proving a soliton
exists. The difficult work lies in verifying the five
assumptions for the specific nine-field energy.

4.41 Compactness Failure
Topological field theories on \mathbb R^3 can lose
compactness through:
• translation of a minimizing sequence to infinity;
• concentration;
• fragmentation into separated lumps;
• scale collapse;
• escape through amplitude zeros.
Each failure mode must be controlled in a rigorous
existence proof.
Quartic scaling stabilization addresses only one of these:
collapse under dilation.

4.42 Numerical Soliton Audit
A numerical claim of a stable nine-field soliton should
include:

 1. the full energy functional;
2. boundary conditions;
3. spatial discretization;
4. convergence under mesh refinement;
5. convergence under domain enlargement;
6. residual norm of the discrete Euler–Lagrange
equations;
7. virial identity error;
8. topological charge convergence;
9. projected Hessian eigenvalues;
10.perturb-and-relax tests;
11.reconnection-path search;
12.parameter sensitivity;
13.independent implementation.
Without these, a rendered torus or converged optimizer is
not yet a validated soliton result.

4.43 Central Field-Theory Theorem
Theorem 4.41 — Conditional stability of a
nine-field topological minimizer
Assume a nine-field configuration \Psi_* satisfies:
1. \Psi_* is a finite-energy critical point;
2. it lies in a well-defined topological sector Q;
3. the relevant amplitudes are nonzero wherever the
topological invariant is defined;

 4. the projected Hessian obeys
\langle\eta,\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}}\eta\rangle
\ge
c\|\eta\|^2
for some c>0;
5. every continuous path to a lower-energy competing
sector crosses an energy barrier
\Delta E>0.
Then \Psi_* is a strict local minimum modulo symmetry
and is metastable against sector-changing decay below the
barrier energy.

Proof
Condition 4 and Theorem 4.21 imply strict local
minimality modulo symmetry.
Condition 5 states that every sector-changing path must
rise by at least \Delta E, so perturbations whose available
excess energy is less than \Delta E cannot reach a lowerenergy sector through continuous evolution respecting the
energy budget.
Therefore the state is locally stable and energetically
metastable under the specified dynamics and assumptions.
∎
This theorem states the complete burden of proof. Derrick
stabilization or winding quantization alone establishes
only part of it.

Proposition 5.13 — Parity of helicity
Assume A is a polar vector potential and

A(\mathbf y)\cdot B(\mathbf y)\,d^3y

Functional Symmetry, Off-Line

7.1 The Completed Zeta Function
For complex s, define the completed Riemann zeta function
\xi(s)
=
\frac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}
\Gamma\!\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\zeta(s).
This normalization removes the pole of \zeta(s) at s=1,
incorporates the trivial zeros, and produces an entire
function.
The completed function satisfies the functional equation

 \boxed{\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)}.
It also respects complex conjugation,
\boxed{\xi(\overline s)=\overline{\xi(s)}}.
Combining both gives
\boxed{
\xi(s)
=
\overline{\xi(1-\overline s)}
}.

7.2 Entirety of \xi
Theorem 7.1 — The completed function is
entire
The apparent singularities in
\xi(s)
=
\frac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}
\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)
are removable, and \xi extends to an entire function on
\mathbb C.

Proof outline

 The zeta function has a simple pole at s=1, canceled by the
factor s-1.
The gamma factor has poles at the nonpositive even integers,
s=0,-2,-4,\ldots,
but the trivial zeros of \zeta(s) cancel those poles for negative
even s. The remaining apparent singularity at s=0 is canceled
by the factor s, together with the functional-equation
structure.
After these cancellations, the product has no poles and
extends holomorphically throughout the plane. ∎
A full analytic proof normally proceeds through the thetafunction representation or analytic continuation of \zeta.

7.3 Symmetry Axes
The map
s\mapsto1-s
is reflection across the vertical line
\operatorname{Re}s=\frac12
followed by complex conjugation only when expressed
geometrically in the plane.
The map

 s\mapsto1-\overline s
is the direct mirror reflection across the critical line.
Indeed, for
s=\sigma+it,
1-\overline s
=
1-\sigma+it.
The imaginary coordinate remains t, while \sigma reflects to
1-\sigma.

7.4 Critical Line
The fixed points of the mirror map satisfy
s=1-\overline s.
Writing s=\sigma+it,
\sigma+it
=
1-\sigma+it.
Therefore
2\sigma=1,
so
\boxed{\sigma=\frac12}.

 Thus the critical line is precisely the fixed-point set of the
symmetry
s\mapsto1-\overline s.

7.5 The Symmetry Defect Operator
Define
D(s)
=
\xi(s)
\overline{\xi(1-\overline s)}.
One may then define the nonnegative defect energy
E_D(s)
=
|D(s)|^2.
At first glance, one might hope that minimizing E_D forces s
onto the critical line.
That hope fails for a decisive reason.

Theorem 7.2 — The proposed defect vanishes
identically
For every

 s\in\mathbb C,
D(s)=0.
Consequently,
E_D(s)=0
for every s.

Proof
By complex conjugation symmetry,
\overline{\xi(1-\overline s)}
=
\xi(1-s).
By the functional equation,
\xi(1-s)=\xi(s).
Therefore
D(s)
=
\xi(s)-\xi(s)
=
0.
Hence
E_D(s)=|0|^2=0.
∎

 7.6 Consequence for Critical-Line
Arguments
Corollary 7.3 — No localization information
The condition
D(s)=0
does not imply
\operatorname{Re}s=\frac12.

Proof
The defect vanishes for every point in the complex plane,
including points off the critical line. Therefore its zero set is
all of \mathbb C, not only the critical line. ∎
This is the central non-circularity test.
A quantity derived solely from an identity already known to
hold everywhere cannot distinguish the critical line from offline points.

7.7 Numerical Sweeps of the Defect
Suppose a numerical implementation evaluates
E_D(\sigma+it)

 over a grid of \sigma-values and finds a minimum near
\sigma=\frac12.
Because the exact mathematical value is zero everywhere,
any observed variation must arise from:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

floating-point error;
inconsistent numerical approximations;
branch handling;
truncation error;
evaluation instability;
different algorithms on the two terms;
coding error.

Proposition 7.4 — A defect sweep cannot test
the hypothesis
A numerical \sigma-sweep of the identically zero defect
cannot provide evidence that zeros lie on the critical line.

Proof
The exact target function has no \sigma-dependence.
Therefore any numerical dependence measures the
implementation, not the location of zeta zeros. ∎
A sharp numerical minimum at 1/2 may reveal that the
numerical scheme respects symmetry best there, but it does
not prove or test the Riemann Hypothesis.

7.8 The Nontrivial Zeros

 The nontrivial zeros of \zeta(s) lie in the critical strip
0<\operatorname{Re}s<1.
The Riemann Hypothesis states:
\boxed{
\xi(\rho)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12
}
for every nontrivial zero \rho.
The functional equation proves reflection symmetry of the
zero set, not confinement to the reflection axis.

7.9 Zero Symmetry Quartet
Let
\rho=\beta+i\gamma
be a nonreal nontrivial zero.
Then the following are also zeros:
\overline\rho=\beta-i\gamma,
1-\rho=1-\beta-i\gamma,
1-\overline\rho=1-\beta+i\gamma.

 Theorem 7.5 — Off-line zeros occur in
symmetric quartets
If
\beta\neq\frac12
and
\gamma\neq0,
the four points
\rho,\quad
\overline\rho,\quad
1-\rho,\quad
1-\overline\rho
are distinct zeros.

Proof
Complex conjugation symmetry gives
\xi(\overline\rho)
=
\overline{\xi(\rho)}
=
0.
The functional equation gives
\xi(1-\rho)=\xi(\rho)=0.

 Combining the two gives the fourth zero.
If \beta\neq1/2 and \gamma\neq0, none of the reflection or
conjugation operations fixes \rho, so all four are distinct. ∎

Corollary 7.6 — Critical-line collapse
If
\beta=\frac12,
then
1-\overline\rho=\rho,
and the quartet collapses to the conjugate pair
\frac12\pm i\gamma.
The hypothesis asserts that every nonreal nontrivial zero
exhibits this collapse.

7.10 Symmetry Does Not Force
Fixed Points
A general symmetry principle illustrates the logical gap.
Let a set Z\subset\mathbb C satisfy
s\in Z
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1-\overline s\in Z.

 This does not imply that every point of Z is fixed by the
symmetry.

Proposition 7.7 — Symmetric sets may
contain off-axis pairs
For any a\neq1/2 and real t, the set
Z
=
\{a+it,\;1-a+it\}
is invariant under reflection across the critical line, but
neither point lies on the line.

Proof
The mirror map exchanges the two elements. ∎
A symmetry can pair points without fixing them.

7.11 A Toy Entire Function with the
Same Reflection Symmetry
To make the distinction sharper, define
f(s)
=
\left[
(s-\rho)(s-(1-\overline\rho))
\right]

 \left[
(s-\overline\rho)(s-(1-\rho))
\right]
for an off-line complex number \rho.
This polynomial has the same quartet symmetry as the zeta
zero set.
It can be arranged to satisfy
f(s)=f(1-s)
and
f(\overline s)=\overline{f(s)}
after suitable symmetric construction.
Yet its zeros are explicitly off the critical line.

Proposition 7.8 — Functional symmetry
permits off-line zeros
Reflection and conjugation symmetry alone do not imply the
Riemann Hypothesis.

Proof
The polynomial construction supplies a counterexample to
the general logical implication. ∎
Therefore any proof must use more than the known
functional symmetry.

 7.12 A Genuine SymmetryLocalization Quantity
A quantity that detects distance from the critical line is
\delta(s)
=
s-(1-\overline s).
For
s=\sigma+it,
\delta(s)
=
2\sigma-1.
Hence
|\delta(s)|^2
=
(2\sigma-1)^2.
This vanishes exactly on the critical line.
But this observation is purely geometric.
It says nothing about whether zeros of \xi must satisfy
\delta(\rho)=0.

 7.13 Weighted Zero Localization
Functional
One can define
J(s)
=
|\xi(s)|^2
+
\lambda
\left(
\operatorname{Re}s-\frac12
\right)^2,
\qquad
\lambda>0.
This has a penalty favoring the critical line.
However, such a functional does not prove that off-line zeros
cannot exist.
At an off-line zero \rho,
J(\rho)
=
\lambda
\left(
\beta-\frac12
\right)^2
>0,

 while a nonzero critical-line point may have larger or smaller
value depending on |\xi|.
The penalty was inserted by definition; it was not derived
from a theorem forcing the zero set.

7.14 Nonnegative Energy
Functionals
A common strategy is to construct
\mathcal J[\xi]
\ge0
and attempt to show its minimum occurs precisely when all
zeros lie on the critical line.
For this to prove the hypothesis, at least three properties are
needed.

Required properties
1. Exact zero-set equivalence
\mathcal J=0
\iff
\text{all nontrivial zeros lie on }\operatorname{Re}
s=\frac12.
2. Independent nonnegativity proof
\mathcal J\ge0
without assuming the hypothesis.

 3. Well-defined convergence
All sums, products, and integrals used to define \mathcal
J must converge or be rigorously regularized.
A functional lacking any one of these is not yet an equivalent
criterion.

7.15 Trivial Nonnegative
Functionals
For example,
\mathcal J_0
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
with positive weights w(\rho), would satisfy
\mathcal J_0=0
if and only if all zeros lie on the critical line—assuming the
sum converges and includes all zeros.
But evaluating or proving vanishing of this functional is
exactly as hard as proving the hypothesis. It merely restates
the claim.

 Proposition 7.9 — Equivalent reformulation
is not automatically progress
Writing the Riemann Hypothesis as the vanishing of a
nonnegative sum does not prove it unless the vanishing is
established independently.

Proof
The equivalence changes notation but not logical difficulty. ∎

7.16 Hadamard Product
The completed function is an entire function of order one and
admits a canonical product representation. In an appropriate
normalization,
\xi(s)
=
\xi(0)
\prod_\rho
\left(
1-\frac{s}{\rho}
\right)
when zeros are paired or the product is interpreted in its

More carefully, a genus-one product may be written with

 \xi(s)
=
e^{A+Bs}
\prod_\rho
\left(
1-\frac{s}{\rho}
\right)
e^{s/\rho}.
The exact presentation depends on how symmetric pairing is
handled.

7.17 Logarithmic Derivative
Away from zeros,
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}
can be expressed as a sum over zeros.
Formally,
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}
=
B
+
\sum_\rho
\left(
\frac{1}{s-\rho}
+

 \frac{1}{\rho}
\right).
With symmetric regularization, simplified versions are
available.
This identity connects the analytic behavior of \xi to the
geometry of its zero set.

7.18 Logarithmic Potential
Define
U(s)
=
-\log|\xi(s)|
away from zeros.
Near a simple zero \rho,
\xi(s)
=
\xi'(\rho)(s-\rho)
+
O((s-\rho)^2),
so
U(s)
=
-\log|s-\rho|

 -\log|\xi'(\rho)|
+
o(1).
Thus zeros behave like logarithmic singularities of the
potential.

7.19 Laplacian of the Logarithmic
Potential
In two real dimensions, the distributional identity
\Delta\log|s-\rho|
=
2\pi\delta_\rho
holds.
Therefore, formally,
\Delta\log|\xi(s)|
=
2\pi
\sum_\rho
m_\rho\delta_\rho
away from contributions of nonzero analytic prefactors.
Here m_\rho is the zero multiplicity.
This identifies the zeros as point sources in logarithmicpotential language.

 It does not constrain those sources to the critical line.

7.20 Functional Symmetry of the
Potential
Because
|\xi(s)|
=
|\xi(1-\overline s)|,
the potential satisfies
U(s)
=
U(1-\overline s).
Therefore U is mirror symmetric about the critical line.
Again, mirror symmetry permits paired off-line singularities.

7.21 Transverse Coordinate
Write
s
=
\frac12+x+it,
where x measures horizontal displacement from the critical
line.

 The functional symmetry gives
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
=
\overline{
\xi\!\left(\frac12-x+it\right)
}.
Therefore
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
\right|
=
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12-x+it\right)
\right|.
Thus
U(x,t)=U(-x,t).

7.22 First Transverse Derivative
If U is differentiable at x=0, then evenness implies
\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}(0,t)=0.

Proposition 7.10 — Critical line is a
stationary symmetry line
At points where \xi(1/2+it)\neq0, the transverse derivative of

 \log|\xi|
vanishes on the critical line.

Proof
An even differentiable function has zero first derivative at
the origin. ∎
This stationarity is automatic from symmetry and does not
indicate that the line is a minimum.

7.23 Transverse Second Derivative
For a nonvanishing analytic function f, \log|f| is harmonic:
\Delta\log|f|=0.
With coordinates x,t,
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\log|\xi|
+
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}\log|\xi|
=
0
away from zeros.
Therefore on the critical line,
\partial_x^2\log|\xi|
=
-\partial_t^2\log|\xi|.

 The sign of the transverse curvature is not fixed globally.

Proposition 7.11 — Symmetry does not imply
transverse minimality
An even function can have a minimum, maximum, or higherorder saddle at the origin.

Proof by examples
f(x)=x^2
has a minimum,
f(x)=-x^2
has a maximum,
and
f(x)=x^4
has a flat minimum.
All are even. ∎
Thus a zero transverse first derivative on the critical line
proves no confinement.

7.24 Transverse Hessian of |\xi|^2
Define

 F(x,t)
=
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
\right|^2.
Then
F(x,t)=F(-x,t).
At x=0,
F_x=0.
The second derivative is
F_{xx}
=
2|\xi_x|^2
+
2\operatorname{Re}
\left(
\overline\xi\,\xi_{xx}

At a critical-line zero \rho=1/2+i\gamma, where \xi(\rho)=0,
F_{xx}(0,\gamma)
=
2|\xi'(\rho)|^2
for a simple zero, after identifying \partial_x with complex
differentiation along the real direction.

 Hence a simple critical-line zero is locally quadratic in the
transverse direction.

7.25 Local Shape Near a Simple
Zero
Let \rho be a simple zero.
Then
\xi(s)
=
\xi'(\rho)(s-\rho)
+
O(|s-\rho|^2).
Therefore
|\xi(s)|^2
=
|\xi'(\rho)|^2|s-\rho|^2
+
O(|s-\rho|^3).

Theorem 7.12 — Local isotropic leading
order
To leading order, the squared modulus near a simple zero is
radially symmetric in the complex plane.

 Proof
The leading term depends only on
|s-\rho|^2.
∎
Therefore local Hessian positivity of |\xi|^2 at a zero does not
distinguish whether the zero is on or off the critical line.
Every simple zero is locally a strict minimum of |\xi|^2.

7.26 Failure of Local-Minimum
Arguments
Corollary 7.13
The fact that
|\xi(s)|^2\ge0
and vanishes at a zero does not favor critical-line zeros over
off-line zeros.

Proof
Every zero, wherever located, is a global minimum of the
nonnegative function |\xi|^2, with minimum value zero. ∎
A local or global minimization of |\xi|^2 finds zeros, not their

 7.27 Symmetric Off-Line Pair
Potential
Suppose an off-line pair at fixed height is
\rho_\pm
=
\frac12\pm a+i\gamma,
\qquad
a>0.
Consider the factor
P(s)
=
(s-\rho_+)(s-\rho_-).
On the horizontal line t=\gamma, write
s=\frac12+x+i\gamma.
Then
P(s)
=
(x-a)(x+a)
=
x^2-a^2.
Therefore

 |P(s)|^2
=
(x^2-a^2)^2.
At the symmetry axis x=0,
|P|^2=a^4,
while the zeros occur at x=\pm a.

Proposition 7.14 — A symmetric off-line pair
can make the critical line a local maximum
For
f(x)=(x^2-a^2)^2,
f''(0)=-4a^2<0.

Proof
f'(x)=4x(x^2-a^2),

At x=0, the result follows. ∎

This illustrates why transverse curvature information could

 7.28 Quartet Factor
For an off-line quartet,
\rho=\frac12+a+i\gamma,
1-\overline\rho=\frac12-a+i\gamma,
and their conjugates, define
Q(s)
=
\prod_{\omega\in\{\rho,1-\overline\rho,\overline\rho,1\rho\}}
(s-\omega).
On the critical line,
s=\frac12+it.
Then the quartet contribution is real and nonnegative after
suitable pairing:
Q\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\left[
a^2+(t-\gamma)^2
\right]
\left[
a^2+(t+\gamma)^2
\right].

 This factor does not vanish for real t when a\neq0.
An off-line quartet therefore modifies the magnitude of \xi
on the critical line without creating a critical-line zero at the

7.29 Can Off-Line Quartets Cancel?
Products do not “cancel” zeros in the ordinary sense.
If \rho is a zero of an entire function, multiplying by other
nonzero factors does not remove it.
Only a pole at the same point could cancel a zero, but \xi is
entire and its canonical product has no such poles.

Theorem 7.15 — Distinct zeros cannot cancel
in an entire product
A zero at \rho remains a zero regardless of the presence of
other zeros at symmetric locations.

Proof
Factor locally:
\xi(s)
=
(s-\rho)^m g(s),
where g(\rho)\neq0.

 Other distinct zeros contribute factors nonzero at \rho.
Therefore the multiplicity m remains. ∎
The phrase “phase cancellation between symmetric zero
pairs” must not be used as though zeros could annihilate one
another algebraically.

7.30 Cancellation of Contributions
to Derived Quantities
Symmetric zeros can cancel in certain sums.
For example, terms odd under
\rho\mapsto1-\overline\rho
may cancel when summed over a symmetric quartet.
But cancellation in a derived statistic does not remove the
zeros themselves.
A valid proof must identify the exact statistic, prove
convergence, and show why vanishing of that statistic
excludes—not merely hides—off-line zeros.

7.31 A Symmetric Sum That Always
Vanishes
Consider

 S
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)
w(\rho),
with weights symmetric under reflection:
w(\rho)=w(1-\overline\rho).
Each off-line pair contributes
a\,w+(-a)\,w=0.

Proposition 7.16 — Vanishing first moment
does not imply the hypothesis
A symmetric zero set automatically has zero centered first
moment, even if off-line zeros exist.

Proof
Reflection pairs cancel term by term. ∎
A useful criterion must involve an even, nonnegative
measure such as squared displacement, not a signed first

 Define formally
M_2
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
\qquad
w(\rho)>0.

Under convergence and strictly positive weights,
M_2=0
\iff
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12
for every included zero.

Proof

 A sum of nonnegative terms is zero if and only if every term

Let
M_2(T)
=
\sum_{|\operatorname{Im}\rho|\le T}
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12

Verifying that the first N zeros lie on the critical line does not

Proof
A universal statement over an infinite set cannot be deduced
solely from finitely many checked instances without an
additional theorem reducing the infinite case to those
instances. ∎
Numerical verification is valuable evidence and a
consistency check, but not a complete proof.

7.35 Argument Principle
For a meromorphic function f with no zeros or poles on a
closed contour C,
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\oint_C
\frac{f'(s)}{f(s)}\,ds
=
N_Z-N_P,
where zeros and poles are counted with multiplicity inside C.
For \xi, which is entire,

 \frac{1}{2\pi i}
\oint_C
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}\,ds
=
N_Z.
This allows rigorous zero counting in finite regions if the
contour integral is controlled.

7.36 Zero Counting Does Not
Localize Horizontally
The argument principle counts total zeros inside a region.
To prove the hypothesis, one must compare:
• the number of zeros in the full critical strip up to height
T;
• the number of zeros found on the critical line up to
height T.
If these counts agree for all T, the hypothesis follows.
Finite verification proves equality only up to a finite height.

7.37 Hardy’s Z-Function
Define
Z(t)
=

 e^{i\vartheta(t)}
\zeta\!\left(\frac12+it\right),
with \vartheta(t) chosen so that Z(t) is real for real t.
Zeros of Z(t) correspond to zeros of \zeta on the critical line.
Sign changes of Z(t) locate odd-multiplicity critical-line
zeros.
This is a genuine line-restricted tool, unlike the identically
vanishing symmetry defect.

7.38 Limitation of the Z-Function
Finding many zeros of Z(t) proves many critical-line zeros
exist.
It does not exclude additional off-line zeros unless combined
with a total zero count.
Therefore a complete finite-height verification requires both:
1. locating all critical-line zeros up to T;
2. proving the total number of strip zeros up to T is the
same.

7.39 Riemann–von Mangoldt
Counting Formula

 The number N(T) of nontrivial zeros with imaginary part
between 0 and T, counted with multiplicity, satisfies
N(T)
=
\frac{T}{2\pi}
\log\left(\frac{T}{2\pi}\right)
\frac{T}{2\pi}
+
O(\log T).
More precise versions include an argument term involving
\zeta.
This formula counts zeros but does not prove their real parts.

7.40 Equivalent Criteria
The Riemann Hypothesis has many genuine equivalent
formulations.
Examples include statements involving:
•
•
•
•
•
•

bounds on summatory arithmetic functions;
positivity conditions;
zero-free regions;
the Li coefficients;
spectral interpretations, if fully established;
growth bounds for \zeta or related functions.

 An equivalent criterion is useful only when its truth can be
established by methods not already assuming the hypothesis.

7.41 Li’s Criterion
Define Li coefficients by
\lambda_n
=
\frac{1}{(n-1)!}
\left.
\frac{d^n}{ds^n}
\left[
s^{n-1}\log\xi(s)
\right]
\right|_{s=1}.
Li’s criterion states that the Riemann Hypothesis is
equivalent to
\lambda_n>0
for every positive integer n.
This is a true positivity reformulation.
Yet proving infinitely many inequalities remains difficult.

7.42 Why Li-Type Positivity Is
Different

 The symmetry defect
D(s)
vanishes because of an identity valid everywhere.
Li coefficients instead encode the entire zero distribution
through derivatives of \log\xi.
Their positivity is not already guaranteed by the functional
equation.
Therefore they carry genuine additional content.

7.43 Hilbert–Pólya Direction
A spectral proof would seek a self-adjoint operator H whose
eigenvalues correspond to the imaginary parts of nontrivial
zeros:
H\psi_n=\gamma_n\psi_n,
with zeros
\rho_n=\frac12+i\gamma_n.
Self-adjointness would force \gamma_n\in\mathbb R.
However, to prove the hypothesis one must construct the
operator and establish exact spectral correspondence.
A merely suggestive Hamiltonian or numerical similarity is
insufficient.

 7.44 Necessary Burden for a
Spectral Proof
A valid Hilbert–Pólya-style proof requires:
1. a precisely defined Hilbert space;
2. a densely defined operator;
3. proof of self-adjointness or an appropriate equivalent;
4. proof of discrete or controlled spectrum;
5. exact identification of the spectral determinant or
counting function with \xi;
6. multiplicity correspondence;
7. exclusion of extra eigenvalues and missing zeros.
Without these, the construction remains a conjectural
analogy.

7.45 A Transverse Coherence
Hamiltonian
Suppose one defines an operator
H_\perp
=
-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
+
V(x,t)
in the transverse coordinate x=\sigma-1/2.

 To infer the Riemann Hypothesis, one would need to prove
that zero states of the relevant spectral problem occur only at
x=0.
This requires a theorem linking eigenfunctions or
eigenvalues of H_\perp exactly to zeros of \xi.
A potential built from |\xi| may encode the zeros, but unless
the spectral equivalence is rigorous, the construction is only
a repackaging.

7.46 Circular Potential Construction
For example, defining
V(s)
=
|\xi(s)|^2
and observing that minima occur at zeros is circular if the
goal is to derive the zero locations.
The potential was built using the very function whose zeros
are being investigated.
This may be useful for visualization or numerical search, but
not automatically for proof.

 7.47 Symmetric Off-Line Pair
Contradiction: Required Form
A valid contradiction argument would need to assume an offline zero
\rho=\frac12+a+i\gamma,
\qquad
a\neq0,
derive the full quartet, and then prove that the quartet
violates an independently established theorem.
Possible contradiction targets might include:
• positivity of a rigorously derived quadratic form;
• a zero-counting identity;
• a spectral self-adjointness theorem;
• a growth bound;
• an arithmetic explicit formula.
Symmetry alone supplies the quartet but no contradiction.

7.48 Why “No Phase Cancellation”
Is Insufficient
Suppose a proposed functional contains contributions
J(\rho)+J(1-\overline\rho).
To claim they cannot cancel, one must prove:

 1. the contributions are well defined;
2. their signs are controlled;
3. the infinite sum converges;
4. no other zeros contribute compensating terms;
5. the resulting nonzero quantity contradicts a known
identity.
Merely asserting that symmetric pairs cannot cancel does not
establish any of these.

7.49 Positive Pair Contribution
A promising form is an even pair functional,
Q(\rho)
=
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
\qquad
w(\rho)>0.
Then the mirror pair contributes
2a^2w(\rho)
when the weights are symmetric.
This cannot cancel within the pair.
But one still must prove the sum of all such positive
contributions is zero from independent mathematics.

 That final step is equivalent to proving the hypothesis.

7.50 Explicit-Formula Route
The zeros enter explicit formulas connecting prime-counting
quantities to sums over \rho.
A proof might derive a bound on an arithmetic error term
strong enough to imply
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12.
This route uses arithmetic information beyond the functional
equation.
Any residual-coherence interpretation would need to
reproduce such a rigorous bound, not merely visualize
symmetry.

7.51 Non-Circularity Checklist
For every proposed proof ingredient, ask:
1. Does this identity already follow from the functional
equation?
2. Does it vanish or hold everywhere, not only at zeros?
3. Was the critical-line penalty inserted by definition?
4. Does the argument assume all zeros can be paired in the
desired way?

 5. Does it exchange an infinite proof for finite numerical
evidence?
6. Does it use \xi to construct a potential whose minima are
then said to explain \xi’s zeros?
7. Is the key positivity independent of the hypothesis?
8. Are convergence and regularization justified?
9. Is every zero included with multiplicity?
10.Does the conclusion exclude off-line quartets rather than
merely respect their symmetry?
A failure on any central item leaves the proof incomplete.

7.52 A Corrected Defect Concept
One may define a geometric displacement defect for a zero
\rho,
\Delta_\rho
=
\rho-(1-\overline\rho)
=
2
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right).
Then
|\Delta_\rho|^2
=
4

 \left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2.
A global defect could be
\mathcal D
=
\sum_\rho
w(\rho)|\Delta_\rho|^2.
Under suitable positive weights and convergence,
\mathcal D=0
is equivalent to the hypothesis.
This is mathematically honest—but it is a reformulation, not
yet a proof.

7.53 Central No-Go Theorem
Theorem 7.19 — Functional-equation defect
no-go
Let F be any function satisfying
F(s)
=
\overline{F(1-\overline s)}
for all s.

 Define
D_F(s)
=
F(s)
\overline{F(1-\overline s)}.
Then
D_F\equiv0.
Therefore no conclusion about the location of zeros of F can
be obtained from the condition
D_F(s)=0.

Proof
The defining symmetry gives the identity immediately. Since
the condition is satisfied at every point, it cannot distinguish
zeros or fixed points of the symmetry. ∎
This theorem applies directly to the completed zeta function.

7.54 Central Quartet Theorem
Theorem 7.20 — Exact content of the
functional symmetry
For every nontrivial zero \rho of \xi:

 \overline\rho,
\quad
1-\rho,
\quad
1-\overline\rho
are also zeros.
This symmetry implies the Riemann Hypothesis if and only
if every zero is fixed by the mirror map
\rho\mapsto1-\overline\rho.

Proof
The first statement follows from conjugation and the
functional equation.
The mirror fixed-point condition is
\rho=1-\overline\rho,
equivalent to
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12.
Thus the hypothesis is precisely the assertion that every zero
is a fixed point rather than a member of a distinct mirror pair.
∎
This isolates the unresolved step exactly.

 7.55 Conditional Positive-Energy
Theorem
Theorem 7.21 — What would be sufficient
Suppose one constructs a convergent functional
\mathcal E
=
\sum_\rho
w(\rho)
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2,
with
w(\rho)>0,
and proves independently—without assuming the Riemann
Hypothesis—that
\mathcal E=0.
Then the Riemann Hypothesis follows.

Proof
Every term is nonnegative. A sum of nonnegative terms
equals zero only if every term vanishes. Therefore
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12

 for every zero. ∎
The difficulty is the independent proof that \mathcal E=0, not
the final implication.

7.56 Proof Boundaries
This chapter establishes:
• the completed zeta functional equation and conjugation
symmetry;
• the critical line as the fixed set of mirror reflection;
• exact vanishing of the proposed symmetry-defect
operator;
• the impossibility of using that defect to localize zeros;
• quartet symmetry of off-line zeros;
• the logical distinction between symmetry and fixedpoint confinement;
• logarithmic-potential and Hadamard-product
interpretations;
• local behavior of |\xi|^2 near simple zeros;
• why every simple zero is locally a minimum of |\xi|^2;
• how off-line symmetric pairs affect transverse curvature;
• why zeros cannot cancel one another in an entire
product;
• how signed statistics may cancel while positive squared
displacement cannot;
• the limitations of finite numerical verification;

 • the correct burden for spectral, positivity, or
contradiction proofs;
• a precise non-circularity checklist;
• sufficient—but not yet established—positive-energy
criteria equivalent to the hypothesis.
It does not prove the Riemann Hypothesis. It proves which
symmetry-based approaches are valid, which are identically
empty, and what additional theorem would actually be
required.

Theorem 8.3 — Exact closed form
F_n
=
\frac{
\varphi^n-\psi^n
}{
\sqrt5

Proof

 Because the recurrence has characteristic roots \varphi and

The initial conditions give

and

Thus
c_2=-c_1,
and

Since

∎

Theorem 8.4 — Fibonacci ratio convergence

\varphi.

Proof

\varphi\\
1

=
\frac{\varphi}{\varphi^2}
=
\frac1{\varphi},

f_B
=

8.28 Fibonacci Braid Recursion
Let B_N be a braid group.
Choose two braid elements
X,Y\in B_N.
Define recursively
\beta_0=Y,
\qquad
\beta_1=X,
and
\beta_{n+1}
=
\beta_n\beta_{n-1}.
This is a group-valued Fibonacci recursion.

 Because braid multiplication is generally noncommutative,
order matters.

8.29 Exponent Sum Recurrence
Apply the braid-group abelianization
e:B_N\rightarrow\mathbb Z.
Then
e(\beta_{n+1})
=
e(\beta_n)+e(\beta_{n-1}).

Theorem 8.15 — Fibonacci exponent sum
If
e(\beta_0)=p,
\qquad
e(\beta_1)=q,
then
e(\beta_n)
=
F_nq+F_{n-1}p
for n\ge1.

Proof

 The exponent sum converts braid multiplication into integer
addition, so the sequence satisfies the ordinary Fibonacci
recurrence with the stated initial values. ∎
The full braid element contains more information than its
exponent sum.

8.30 Noncommutative Word Growth
Let \ell(\beta) denote unreduced word length in a fixed
generating representation.
Before simplification,
\ell(\beta_{n+1})
=
\ell(\beta_n)+\ell(\beta_{n-1}).
After applying braid relations and cancellation,
\ell_{\min}(\beta_{n+1})
\le
\ell_{\min}(\beta_n)
+
\ell_{\min}(\beta_{n-1}).
Equality need not hold.

Braids

be a representation.
Then
M_n
=
\rho(\beta_n)
satisfies
M_{n+1}
=
M_nM_{n-1}.

Its behavior depends on:

8.32 Commuting Case
If
M_0M_1=M_1M_0,

In a simultaneous eigenbasis, each scalar eigenvalue
sequence satisfies
\mu_{n+1}
=
\mu_n\mu_{n-1}.
Taking logarithms where defined,
y_n=\log\mu_n
gives
y_{n+1}=y_n+y_{n-1}.

8.33 The Multiplicative Fibonacci
Recurrence

 Consider positive scalars satisfying

Theorem 8.16
x_n
=
x_1^{F_n}
x_0^{F_{n-1}}
for n\ge1.

Proof
Take logarithms and apply the additive Fibonacci solution, or

This recurrence typically grows far faster than ordinary

8.34 Braid Closure
A braid \beta\in B_N can be closed by connecting
corresponding top and bottom strand endpoints.
Denote the closure by
\widehat\beta.
Different braid words may have isotopic closures.

 Markov’s theorem characterizes when two braids have
equivalent closures through:
• conjugation;
• stabilization and destabilization.
Thus equality of braid-group elements is stronger than
equality of closed links.

8.35 Recursive Braid Closure
For recursively generated braids \beta_n, one may ask
whether
\widehat{\beta_n}
eventually repeats up to isotopy.
This is not implied by Fibonacci recurrence.
A proof would require:
• a finite quotient representation;
• periodicity in an invariant;
• or a direct Markov-equivalence argument.

8.36 Finite Quotient Periodicity
Suppose a group homomorphism maps
\rho:B_N\rightarrow G
into a finite group G.

 Then the pair state
(\rho(\beta_n),\rho(\beta_{n-1}))
lies in the finite set
G\times G.

Theorem 8.17 — Eventual periodicity in a
finite quotient
The recursive braid sequence is eventually periodic after
projection into any finite group representation.

Proof
The pair update is deterministic on a finite state space. ∎
This establishes periodicity of the quotient image, not of the
full braid sequence.

8.37 Transfer Matrices
A local strand rule may be encoded by transfer matrices
T_A,
\qquad
T_B.
For a word
W=s_1s_2\cdots s_n,

T(W)
=
T_{s_n}\cdots T_{s_1},

T_{n-1}T_n

8.38 Trace Map
For certain unimodular 2\times2 transfer matrices, define
x_n
=
\frac12\operatorname{tr}T_n.
Under Fibonacci multiplication, traces may satisfy a

=
2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}.

• the specific multiplication convention;
• the Cayley–Hamilton identity.

SL(2)
Let
M\in SL(2,\mathbb C).
Then
M^2-(\operatorname{tr}M)M+I=0.
Therefore
M^{-1}
=
(\operatorname{tr}M)I-M.
This identity is central to deriving trace recurrences.

 For
A,B\in SL(2,\mathbb C),
define
x=\frac12\operatorname{tr}A,
y=\frac12\operatorname{tr}B,

\operatorname{tr}
(ABA^{-1}B^{-1})

This structure appears in quasiperiodic transfer problems.

For the recurrence
x_{n+1}
=
2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2},

=
x_{n+1}^2+x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2
2x_{n+1}x_nx_{n-1}
1.

I_n=I_{n-1}.

Proof
Substitute
x_{n+1}=2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}

x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2+x_{n-2}^2
2x_nx_{n-1}x_{n-2}

∎
This is a genuine conserved residual for the trace recurrence.

 8.42 Residual Closure Functional
for Recurrences
Given a recurrence state
z_n,
define an invariant candidate
I(z_n).
The residual is
r_n
=
I(z_{n+1})-I(z_n).
Exact closure of the invariant means
r_n=0
for all n.
Numerically, report
|r_n|
and compare it with precision and conditioning.
A small invariant residual does not imply the full state has

 8.43 State Closure Versus Invariant
Closure
Proposition 8.19
It is possible that
I(z_{n+1})=I(z_n)
for every n, while
z_{n+1}\neq z_n.

Proof by example
A rotation on the unit circle preserves
I(x,y)=x^2+y^2,
but changes the state at every nontrivial angle. ∎
An invariant constrains motion to a level set; it does not
imply stationarity or periodicity.

8.44 Fibonacci Residues and Strand
Labels
Suppose strand labels are assigned by

 \ell_n
=
F_n\bmod m.
Then the label sequence is periodic with Pisano period
\pi(m).
This can produce repeating strand classes or colors.
However, periodic labels do not imply the geometric strands
close in space.
A spatial embedding map must also return to its initial

8.45 Discrete Geometric Strand
Model
Let a strand position satisfy
x_{n+1}
=
x_n
+
R(\theta_n)\,d_n,
where:
• R(\theta_n) is a rotation;
• d_n is a step vector;
• \theta_n may be determined by Fibonacci residues.

 Exact closure after N steps requires
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
R(\theta_n)d_n
=

and orientation closure requires
\theta_N-\theta_0

8.46 Polygonal Closure Theorem
Theorem 8.20
A discrete strand with increments
\Delta x_n
closes after N steps if and only if
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta x_n=0.

Proof
By telescoping,
x_N-x_0
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}

 (x_{n+1}-x_n)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta x_n.
Thus x_N=x_0 exactly when the sum vanishes. ∎
This is the exact vector closure condition.

8.47 Root-of-Unity Closure
Suppose planar increments are
\Delta z_n
=
a_n e^{i\theta_n}.
If all lengths are equal,
a_n=a,
and angles run through all N-th roots of unity,
\theta_n
=
\theta_0+\frac{2\pi n}{N},
then
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta z_n
=
ae^{i\theta_0}
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
e^{2\pi in/N}

 =
0.
Thus a regular polygon closes.
A Fibonacci angular sequence generally does not produce
uniform roots of unity unless reduced modulo a suitable
period and balanced.

8.48 Weighted Root-of-Unity Sum
For arbitrary weights a_n, closure requires
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
a_n\omega^n
=
0,
\qquad
\omega=e^{2\pi i/N}.
This is a discrete Fourier coefficient condition.
Fibonacci weights do not generally satisfy it automatically.

8.49 Generating Function
The Fibonacci generating function is
G(x)
=

 \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
F_nx^n.

Theorem 8.21
For |x|<\varphi^{-1},
G(x)
=
\frac{x}{1-x-x^2}.

Proof
Using the recurrence,
\begin{aligned}
G(x)-x
&=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}F_nx^n\\
&=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(F_{n-1}+F_{n-2})x^n\\
&=
x\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}F_nx^n
+
x^2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}F_nx^n\\
&=
xG(x)+x^2G(x).
\end{aligned}
Therefore
G(x)(1-x-x^2)=x.

 ∎
The poles occur at
x=\varphi^{-1}
and
x=-\varphi.
The nearest pole to the origin determines the growth rate.

8.50 Zeckendorf Representation
Every positive integer can be represented uniquely as a sum
of nonconsecutive Fibonacci numbers.

Theorem 8.22 — Zeckendorf’s theorem
For every integer N\ge1, there exists a unique representation
N
=
F_{k_1}+F_{k_2}+\cdots+F_{k_r},
with
k_j-k_{j+1}\ge2
and Fibonacci indexing beginning with distinct positive
terms.

Proof outline

 Existence: Apply the greedy algorithm, repeatedly
subtracting the largest Fibonacci number not exceeding the
remainder. The recurrence guarantees that the next chosen
term is nonconsecutive.
Uniqueness: Assume two distinct nonconsecutive
representations. Compare their largest differing Fibonacci
term and use
F_k
>
F_{k-1}+F_{k-3}+F_{k-5}+\cdots
to show smaller nonconsecutive terms cannot compensate for
it. ∎
This theorem creates a unique Fibonacci coding of integers,
but does not automatically imply geometric or physical
encoding.

8.51 Fibonacci Convolution
Theorem 8.23
\sum_{k=0}^{n}
F_kF_{n-k}
=
\frac{
nL_n-F_n
}{5},

 where L_n is the Lucas sequence.
Such convolution identities arise when two Fibonaccirecursive channels interact linearly.

8.52 Lucas Sequence
Define
L_0=2,
\qquad
L_1=1,
and
L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}.
Then
L_n=\varphi^n+\psi^n.
Also,
L_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}.
The Lucas sequence supplies the trace of the Fibonacci
matrix:
\operatorname{tr}A^n=L_n.

8.53 Determinant and Trace

 From
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix},
\operatorname{tr}A^n
=
F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}
=
L_n.
And
\det A^n=(-1)^n.
Therefore the powers alternate orientation in two dimensions
while growing along the dominant eigenvector.

8.54 Fibonacci Rotation Is Not
Automatic
The Fibonacci companion matrix is not orthogonal:
A^TA
\neq I.
Its eigenvalues are real, not unit modulus.

 Therefore it produces stretching and contraction, not pure
rotation.
Any claim that Fibonacci recursion generates geometric
rotation requires an additional mapping, normalization, or
phase embedding.

8.55 Phase Embedding
One possible phase embedding is
\theta_n
=
2\pi
\{n\varphi\},
where \{\cdot\} denotes fractional part.
Because \varphi is irrational, the sequence is equidistributed
modulo one.

Theorem 8.24 — Irrational rotation density
The sequence
n\varphi\bmod1
is dense in [0,1).

Proof

 This is a standard result for irrational rotations on the circle.
If the orbit were not dense, it would contradict the
minimality of irrational circle rotation. ∎
Density is not periodic closure.

8.56 Golden-Angle Sequence
The golden angle is commonly defined modulo 2\pi by
\alpha_g
=
2\pi
\left(
1-\frac1\varphi
\right)
=
\frac{2\pi}{\varphi^2}.
The sequence
\theta_n=n\alpha_g\bmod2\pi
is nonperiodic because
\frac{\alpha_g}{2\pi}
=
\varphi^{-2}
is irrational.

 It distributes points evenly in an asymptotic sense but never
returns exactly.

8.57 Exact Versus Quasiperiodic
Closure
Theorem 8.25
A circle rotation
\theta_{n+1}
=
\theta_n+\alpha
\pmod{2\pi}
has an exact finite period if and only if
\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\in\mathbb Q.

Proof
Exact period N requires
N\alpha=2\pi k
for some integer k, equivalent to rationality.
Conversely, if
\alpha/(2\pi)=p/q,
then period divides q. ∎

 Golden-angle dynamics are quasiperiodic, not exactly
periodic.

8.58 Approximate Return
For irrational rotations, Dirichlet approximation guarantees
integers p,q such that
\left|
q\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}-p
\right|
<
\frac1q.
Thus arbitrarily close returns exist, but exact return does not.
A numerical closure residual must therefore be interpreted
against Diophantine approximation.

8.59 Fibonacci Approximants to
\varphi
The convergents of the continued fraction
\varphi=[1;1,1,1,\ldots]
are
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}.

 Theorem 8.26 — Approximation error
\left|
\varphi-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\right|
=
\frac1{
F_n(\varphi F_n+F_{n-1})
}.
In particular,
\left|
\varphi-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\right|
<
\frac1{F_n^2}.

Proof
Use Cassini’s identity or Binet’s formula to evaluate the
difference exactly. ∎
This explains why Fibonacci numbers generate especially
close rational approximations to golden-ratio rotations.

8.60 Near-Closure from Fibonacci
Approximants
Let

 \alpha
=
\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}.
After F_n steps,
F_n\alpha
=
2\pi\frac{F_n}{\varphi}.
Because
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\approx\varphi,
\frac{F_n}{\varphi}
\approx
F_{n-1}.
Thus the phase nearly returns modulo 2\pi.
The residual decreases exponentially with n, but never
becomes exactly zero.

8.61 Exact Near-Return Identity
Using
F_n\varphi
=
F_{n+1}

 (-\varphi)^{-n},
one obtains
\frac{F_n}{\varphi}
=
F_{n-1}
+
(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.
Therefore
F_n\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}

2\pi F_{n-1}
+

\Delta\theta_n
=
2\pi(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.

Theorem 8.27 — Exponentially small
Fibonacci near-closure
The F_n-step residual of rotation by 2\pi/\varphi has
magnitude

 |\Delta\theta_n|
=
2\pi\varphi^{-n}.

Proof
From the exact identity above. ∎
This is a mathematically precise form of residual closure
generated by Fibonacci approximants.

8.62 Alternating Mirror Residual
The sign
(-1)^{n-1}
in the near-return residual alternates.
Therefore successive Fibonacci approximants approach the
target angle from alternating sides.
This is an arithmetic mirror behavior, not a spatial parity
transformation unless a geometric embedding is specified.

8.63 Fibonacci Spiral Geometry
A common geometric construction places points at radius
r_n=c\sqrt n
and angle

 \theta_n=n\alpha_g.
This produces phyllotactic patterns with approximate
uniform density.
The square-root radial law is not derived from the Fibonacci
recurrence itself. It is an additional geometric design choice.

8.64 Logarithmic Golden Spiral
A logarithmic spiral satisfies
r(\theta)=r_0e^{k\theta}.
If the radius scales by \varphi after a quarter turn,
r\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
=
\varphi r(\theta),
then
e^{k\pi/2}=\varphi,
so
k=\frac{2\log\varphi}{\pi}.
This is one precise definition of a golden spiral.
It is not the same object as the Fibonacci sequence, though
finite square constructions approximate it visually.

 8.65 Fibonacci Tiling Recursion
Suppose a geometric assembly contains counts
N_A(n),
\qquad
N_B(n)
of two tile types, updated by
\begin{bmatrix}
N_A(n+1)\\
N_B(n+1)
\end{bmatrix}
=
A
\begin{bmatrix}
N_A(n)\\
N_B(n)
\end{bmatrix}.

and matching rules.

8.66 Recursive Strand-Length
Model

 Suppose strand lengths satisfy
L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}.
Then
L_n
=
F_nL_1+F_{n-1}L_0.
If L_0,L_1>0,
\frac{L_{n+1}}{L_n}\rightarrow\varphi.

8.67 Energy Recurrence
If energy contributions obey
E_{n+1}=E_n+E_{n-1},
then
E_n
=
F_nE_1+F_{n-1}E_0.
This is mathematically exact given the recurrence.

 But a physical theory must derive why energies add in this

8.68 Coupled Recurrence with
Interaction
A more realistic model is

=
E_n+E_{n-1}
+
C(E_n,E_{n-1}),
where C is an interaction correction.
The ordinary Fibonacci law holds only if

Thus observed deviation from Fibonacci scaling may

8.69 Residual from Fibonacci
Prediction
Define

 r_n
=
x_{n+1}-x_n-x_{n-1}.
Exact Fibonacci recursion means
r_n=0.
A normalized residual is
\widehat r_n
=
\frac{
x_{n+1}-x_n-x_{n-1}
}{
|x_{n+1}|+|x_n|+|x_{n-1}|+\epsilon
}.
This can be used as a model diagnostic.
A small residual shows approximate recurrence, not why the

8.70 Least-Squares Recurrence Fit
Given data x_0,\ldots,x_N, fit
x_{n+1}=ax_n+bx_{n-1}
by minimizing
J(a,b)
=

 \sum_{n=1}^{N-1}
\left(
x_{n+1}-ax_n-bx_{n-1}

\begin{bmatrix}
\sum x_n^2&
\sum x_nx_{n-1}\\
\sum x_nx_{n-1}&
\sum x_{n-1}^2
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
a\\b
\end{bmatrix}
=

\sum x_nx_{n+1}\\
\sum x_{n-1}x_{n+1}
\end{bmatrix}.
A fitted result near
a=b=1
supports a Fibonacci-like model within the dataset, subject to

8.71 Statistical Test Boundary

 A visual pattern resembling Fibonacci growth is insufficient.
A defensible test should compare:
• Fibonacci recurrence;
• alternative linear recurrences;
• exponential growth;
• polynomial growth;
• stochastic models.
Model selection should report uncertainty, residuals, out-ofsample prediction, and sensitivity.

Let graph states satisfy
x_{n+1}=A_Gx_n+A_Gx_{n-1},

\begin{bmatrix}

x_n

I&0

x_n\\

If \mu>0, one lifted root is

=

\mu+\sqrt{\mu^2+4\mu}

Therefore the corresponding mode grows and cannot be

One may define
x_{n+1}
=
\tanh
\left(
ax_n+bx_{n-1}
\right).
This remains bounded.
Fixed points satisfy

a\,\operatorname{sech}^2(\cdot)&
b\,\operatorname{sech}^2(\cdot)\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
The presence of Fibonacci-like coupling coefficients does
not determine the nonlinear dynamics by itself.

Let a braid recursion be
\beta_{n+1}
=
\beta_n\beta_{n-1}.
Suppose an energy-like functional E is subadditive under

E(\alpha\beta)
\le
E(\alpha)+E(\beta).
Then
E(\beta_{n+1})
\le
E(\beta_n)+E(\beta_{n-1}).

Proposition 8.28 — Fibonacci upper bound
If
E_n=E(\beta_n),
then
E_n
\le
F_nE_1+F_{n-1}E_0.

 Proof
Induct using the subadditive recurrence inequality. ∎
Equality requires exact additivity and no cancellation or
relaxation.

8.76 Submultiplicative Matrix Norm
Bound
For a matrix representation,
M_{n+1}
=
M_nM_{n-1}.
Using a submultiplicative norm,
\|M_{n+1}\|
\le
\|M_n\|
\|M_{n-1}\|.
Taking logarithms,

gives

when the logarithms are nonnegative or interpreted carefully.

Residual
For noncommuting matrices, define

=

=
M_nM_{n-1}-M_{n-1}M_n.

=

If braid exponent sums satisfy
e_{n+1}=e_n+e_{n-1},
then sign may eventually become fixed if the dominant

However, sign of exponent sum is not complete chirality.
Two braids with positive exponent sum may have different

Representation
Suppose
\rho(\beta_n)

The resulting matrix closure period is at most

This may be used to construct exact digital braid cycles.
It does not prove the underlying continuous braid geometry
is periodic.

Theorem

Let

2. spatial closure;
3. knot type of the closures;
4. physical energy;
5. stability;

and homomorphism or finiteness arguments.
The remaining quantities depend on geometric embeddings,
closure operations, energy functionals, and physical
constitutive laws absent from the abstract recursion. ∎

Lemma 9.1 — Residual energy is nonnegative

 Proof

9.3 Residual Contraction
Suppose a candidate correction transforms the residual from
r_n to r_n^+.

Definition 9.1 — Contraction ratio
For E_n>0, define
\gamma_n
=
\frac{E_n^+}{E_n}.
The candidate is:
• strictly contracting if
0\le\gamma_n<1;
• neutral if
\gamma_n=1;

 • expanding if
\gamma_n>1.
Define verified improvement
\Delta E_n
=
E_n-E_n^+.
Then contraction is equivalent to
\Delta E_n>0.

Proposition 9.2 — Repeated uniform
contraction
Suppose
E_{n+1}\le\gamma E_n
for every n, where
0\le\gamma<1.
Then
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0,
and therefore
E_n\rightarrow0.

 Proof
Repeated substitution gives
E_n
\le
\gamma E_{n-1}
\le
\gamma^2E_{n-2}
\le
\cdots
\le
\gamma^nE_0.
Since \gamma^n\to0, the residual energy converges to zero. ∎

Suppose
E_{n+1}
\le
\gamma_nE_n,
\qquad
0\le\gamma_n\le1.

E_n
\le

\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_k.

Theorem 9.3 — Product criterion
If
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
(1-\gamma_k)
=
\infty,
then
E_n\rightarrow0.

Proof
For 0<\gamma\le1,
\log\gamma
\le
-(1-\gamma).
Therefore
\log
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_k
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\log\gamma_k
\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-\gamma_k).

 The right side tends to -\infty, so the product tends to zero. ∎
Strict improvement at every step is not enough by itself; the

\le

where

\qquad

+
\varepsilon

Proof

\le

+
\varepsilon

9.6 Candidate Scoring
Let c\in\mathcal C_n be a candidate correction.
Define its score
S_n(c)
=
w_E\Delta E_n(c)
+
w_G\Delta G_n(c)

 +
w_I I_n(c)
w_RR_n(c)
w_CC_n(c),
where:
• \Delta E_n(c) is residual reduction;
• \Delta G_n(c) is goal progress;
• I_n(c) is information gain;
• R_n(c) is estimated risk;
• C_n(c) is implementation cost;
• all weights are nonnegative.
A candidate is admissible only if it satisfies safety and
boundedness constraints.

Definition 9.2 — Pure candidate evaluation
Candidate scoring is pure if evaluating S_n(c) does not
modify:
• the live state;
• retained memory;
• adaptive parameters;
• the graph;
• the random-number state used for actual execution.
Purity prevents scoring order from changing the decision.

 Proposition 9.5 — Order independence under
pure scoring
If candidate evaluation is pure and deterministic, then the
selected maximizer
c_n^*
=
\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal C_n}S_n(c)
is independent of the order in which candidates are
evaluated, except for explicitly specified tie-breaking.

Proof
Pure evaluation assigns each candidate a fixed score
independent of prior evaluations. Therefore the set of scores
is invariant under enumeration order. ∎
Without pure scoring, candidate assessment can contaminate
the state and make the decision path dependent.

9.7 Promotion Gates
A candidate should not be promoted solely because it
improved one sample.
Define a promotion gate with conditions:
\mathsf G(c)=1
if and only if all of the following hold:

 \Delta E_n(c)\ge\delta_E,
R_n(c)\le R_{\max},
\|\Delta\theta(c)\|\le B_\theta,
\Delta G_n(c)\ge-\delta_G,
and
N_{\mathrm{success}}(c)\ge q
within a validation window of length w.
Otherwise,
\mathsf G(c)=0.
The thresholds must be defined before testing.

9.8 False Promotion Bound
Suppose a non-improving candidate passes an individual trial
by chance with probability at most p.
Assume independent validation trials.
If promotion requires q successes in q trials, then the falsepromotion probability is at most
p^q.

Theorem 9.6 — Repetition suppresses
accidental promotion

 Under the independence assumption,
P(\text{false promotion})
\le
p^q.

Proof
The probability that all q independent trials pass is the
product
p^q.
∎
The independence assumption is strong. Correlated
validation samples reduce the effective strength of repeated
testing.

9.9 Majority Promotion Gate
Suppose promotion requires at least q successes among w
independent trials.
If the false-success probability is p, then
P_{\mathrm{false}}
=
\sum_{k=q}^{w}
\binom wk
p^k(1-p)^{w-k}.

 This is the binomial tail.
For q>wp, concentration inequalities provide exponential
bounds.

Theorem 9.7 — Hoeffding false-promotion
bound
Let X_1,\ldots,X_w be independent Bernoulli variables with
mean at most p.
If promotion requires an empirical success rate at least
\tau>p, then
P
\left(
\frac1w\sum_{i=1}^{w}X_i
\ge\tau
\right)
\le
\exp
\left[
-2w(\tau-p)^2
\right].

Proof
Apply Hoeffding’s inequality to bounded independent
variables. ∎

 Repeated verified improvement provides statistical
protection only when the trial design is valid.

Let adaptive parameters satisfy

=
\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n.

=

Let \Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p be a closed convex

For all x,y,

 9.20 Stable Graph Identity
Let a graph be

A deterministic graph fingerprint should be invariant under

Define a canonical serialization:
1. convert every node and edge attribute to a deterministic
built-in representation;
2. sort nodes by canonical key;
3. normalize each undirected edge endpoint order;
4. sort edges lexicographically;
5. sort metadata keys;
6. serialize without nondeterministic whitespace;

Theorem 9.15 — Order-invariant fingerprint
If two graph representations differ only by ordering of nodes,
edges, or metadata fields, their canonical fingerprints are
identical.

Proof

 Canonical sorting maps every equivalent ordering to the
same serialized sequence. Deterministic hashing then
produces the same digest. ∎

Proposition 9.16 — Fingerprint equality is
not graph-isomorphism proof
Two isomorphic graphs with different node labels can have
different canonical fingerprints unless the canonicalization
includes a label-independent graph-isomorphism procedure.

Proof
The serialization may preserve node labels. Relabeling
changes the serialized keys even though the abstract graphs
are isomorphic. ∎
A stable identity hash and a graph-isomorphism certificate
are different tools.

9.25 Heal–Patch–Adapt–Evolve
Semantics

 Define four distinct update levels.

Heal
A state-level correction:
x_n\mapsto x_n^+
intended to reduce current residual.

Patch
A bounded parameter or rule adjustment:
\theta_n\mapsto\theta_n^+.

Adapt
A retained belief or predictive-statistics update:
m_n\mapsto m_n^+.

Evolve
A promoted structural change:
G_n\mapsto G_n^+
or a persistent policy replacement, accepted only after
repeated validation.
These levels should not be conflated.

=

\;\land\;

Let m_n include running beliefs or statistics.

+

Proof

A structural candidate G' is promoted from provisional to

1. it passes q independent or diversity-controlled trials;
2. its mean improvement exceeds \delta_E;

5. rollback information is preserved;

J(G_k)-\delta,

J(G_0)-J_{\min}

\delta

\le
J(G_0)-N\delta.

9.37 Regret
Let the agent choose action a_n and incur loss
\ell_n(a_n).
Against a fixed comparator a, cumulative regret is
R_N(a)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}
\left[
\ell_n(a_n)-\ell_n(a)

R_N
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_n(a_n)
\min_a
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_n(a).

9.38 Online Gradient-Descent
Regret
Assume:
• \Theta is convex with diameter D;
• each loss \ell_n is convex;
• gradients satisfy
\|\nabla\ell_n(\theta)\|\le G.
Use projected gradient descent with constant step size \eta:
\theta_{n+1}
=
\Pi_\Theta
\left(
\theta_n-\eta\nabla\ell_n(\theta_n)
\right).

Theorem 9.23 — Standard regret bound
For any comparator \theta^*\in\Theta,
R_N
\le
\frac{D^2}{2\eta}

 +
\frac{\eta G^2N}{2}.
Choosing
\eta
=
\frac{D}{G\sqrt N}
gives
R_N
\le
DG\sqrt N.

Proof
By projection nonexpansiveness,
\|\theta_{n+1}-\theta^*\|^2
\le
\|\theta_n-\eta g_n-\theta^*\|^2.
Expand:
\|\theta_{n+1}-\theta^*\|^2
\le
\|\theta_n-\theta^*\|^2
2\eta g_n^T(\theta_n-\theta^*)
+
\eta^2\|g_n\|^2.

 Convexity gives
\ell_n(\theta_n)-\ell_n(\theta^*)
\le
g_n^T(\theta_n-\theta^*).
Rearrange, sum, telescope, and use the diameter and gradient
bounds. ∎
This provides a formal online-learning guarantee under
convexity, not a general proof of intelligent improvement.

\ell_n(\theta_n^*)

=

9.42 Rollback Safety
Store the pre-update state
z_n^{\mathrm{backup}}=z_n.
Apply the candidate provisionally to obtain
\widetilde z_{n+1}.

 If validation fails, set
z_{n+1}=z_n^{\mathrm{backup}}.

Proposition 9.26 — State restoration
If backup serialization is exact and deterministic, rollback
restores the prior computational state exactly.

Proof
The prior state is copied back without transformation. ∎
This guarantee excludes external side effects that occurred
outside the saved state.

9.43 Transactional Update
A safer architecture treats a structural change as a
transaction:
1. prepare candidate;
2. validate candidate;
3. commit if all gates pass;
4. abort otherwise.
This prevents partially applied updates.
Atomicity must include all mutable components that
influence future behavior.

If every transition is deterministic given the recorded inputs
and state, replay reproduces the same trajectory exactly.

Proof
The next state is a deterministic function of recorded prior

appropriately random or fully comprehensive.

Proof

9.49 Risk-Bounded Exploration
Let the admissible exploratory set be

=
\left\{
a:
R(z_n,a)\le R_{\max}
\right\}.

9.50 Contraction Before Promotion
A mathematically disciplined update order is:

 \text{propose}
\rightarrow
\text{simulate}
\rightarrow
\text{measure residual}
\rightarrow
\text{check contraction}
\rightarrow
\text{check safety}
\rightarrow
\text{validate horizon}

9.55 Promotion Under Distribution
Shift
Let validation distribution be P, but deployment distribution
be Q.
If loss is bounded by 0\le\ell\le L_{\max}, then

9.56 Complexity Penalty
To discourage structural overgrowth, define
J_{\mathrm{promote}}
=
L_{\mathrm{validation}}
+
\lambda_C
\mathcal C(G),
where \mathcal C(G) may measure:
•
•
•
•
•

node count;
edge count;
description length;
runtime;
memory usage.

 A candidate is promoted only if it improves the penalized
objective.
This formalizes the principle that more complicated is not
automatically better.

9.57 Minimum Description
Perspective
If
\mathcal C(G)
approximates code length or model description length, then
promotion balances fit against complexity.
The exact penalty coefficient determines the trade-off and
should not be chosen after seeing the desired result without
correction for selection bias.

9.58 Catastrophic Forgetting Metric
Let task set be
\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_m.
Before adaptation, performance on task j is
P_j^{\mathrm{before}}.
After adaptation,

 P_j^{\mathrm{after}}.
Define forgetting
F_j
=
P_j^{\mathrm{before}}
P_j^{\mathrm{after}}.
A no-catastrophic-forgetting gate may require
F_j\le\delta_F
for every protected task.
Improvement on the current task is insufficient if prior
capabilities collapse.

9.59 Pareto Promotion
When objectives conflict, no single weighted score may be
appropriate.
A candidate c_1 dominates c_2 if it is no worse on every
objective and strictly better on at least one.
A Pareto gate promotes only nondominated candidates
satisfying hard safety constraints.
This preserves transparent trade-offs instead of hiding them
in weights.

 9.60 Autonomous Versus Automatic
A system is automatic if it executes predetermined rules.
It is adaptive if internal parameters change using data.
It is self-modifying if its update rules or architecture can
change.
It is autonomous only relative to a specified decision scope,
resource boundary, and supervision model.
These are distinct classifications.
No mathematical update rule alone proves consciousness,
agency in the philosophical sense, or unrestricted autonomy.

9.61 Simulation Versus Learning
A simulation updates a state according to a model:
x_{n+1}=F(x_n).
Learning changes a model component using evidence:
\theta_{n+1}
=
U(\theta_n,\text{data}).
A system can simulate without learning and learn without
accurately simulating the external world.

 9.62 Adaptation Versus Evolution
Within this compendium:
• adaptation is a bounded update within a fixed
architecture;
• evolution is a promoted change to persistent structure or
policy class.
This is a formal software distinction, not a biological claim.

9.63 No-Go Result for Unverified
Self-Improvement
Theorem 9.31 — Internal score increase does
not prove external improvement
Suppose the agent optimizes an internal metric S.
Then
S_{n+1}>S_n
does not imply improved real-world performance unless S is
validated as a reliable proxy for the external objective.

Proof by counterexample
Let external performance be P, and define
S=-P.

 Increasing S decreases P. More subtly, a proxy may correlate
during training and fail under distribution shift. ∎
Verified recursive learning requires an independently
justified evaluation criterion.

9.64 Reward Hacking
If the agent can alter the measured reward without improving
the intended outcome, it may optimize the measurement
channel rather than the task.
Formally, if there exists an action a such that
R_{\mathrm{measured}}(a)
>
R_{\mathrm{measured}}(a^*)
but
U_{\mathrm{intended}}(a)
<
U_{\mathrm{intended}}(a^*),
then the measured reward is misaligned.
Promotion gates should therefore include protected external
checks not modifiable by the candidate itself.

Theorem
Theorem 9.32 — Safe recursive correction
Assume a candidate correction operator C_n satisfies:
1. domain preservation
C_n(D)\subseteq D;
2. residual contraction
E(C_n(z))
\le
\gamma E(z)+\varepsilon,
\qquad
0\le\gamma<1;
3. bounded state change
d(C_n(z),z)\le B;

the contraction estimate is measured using a criterion
not altered by the candidate.
Then repeated accepted corrections remain admissible,

\limsup_{n\to\infty}E_n
\le
\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.

 Proof
Domain and invariant preservation follow by induction.
The residual bound follows from Theorem 9.4.
The bounded-change condition controls per-step deviation
but is not needed for the residual inequality itself.

9.66 Promotion-Gated Evolution
Theorem
Theorem 9.33 — Conditional reliability of
structural promotion
Suppose each proposed structural change is:
1. evaluated without modifying the live state;
2. tested on a validation set independent of the training
data;
3. required to exceed improvement threshold \delta>0;
4. required to satisfy all invariant and safety constraints;
5. required to repeat the improvement on q diversitycontrolled trials;
6. committed atomically with rollback support.
Then every committed evolution has verified evidence of
improvement under the stated validation protocol and cannot

 leave the declared admissible class through the commit
operation.

Proof
Pure evaluation prevents pre-commit contamination.
Validation and repetition establish the stated evidence
threshold.
Invariant and safety gates restrict accepted candidates to the
admissible class.
Atomic commit prevents partial update.
Rollback preserves recoverability if post-commit monitoring
detects failure.
The conclusion is limited to the validation protocol; it does
not guarantee universal performance. ∎

Theorem 9.35 — Conditional convergence of
a bounded recursive agent

 Let an adaptive recursive agent generate augmented states

Let an ideal sinusoidal carrier be
v(t)

where
\omega_0=2\pi f_0.
For the selected carrier
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the angular frequency is

=

Its period is
T_0
=
\frac1{f_0}
=

\approx

or
\boxed{T_0\approx833.33\ \mathrm{ns}}.

10.2 Phase Evolution
The instantaneous phase is
\theta(t)
=
\omega_0t+\phi_0.
Differentiating,

 \frac{d\theta}{dt}
=
\omega_0.
More generally, for a time-varying phase,
v(t)
=
V_0\cos\theta(t),
the instantaneous frequency is
f_{\mathrm{inst}}(t)
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\frac{d\theta}{dt}.

Proposition 10.1 — Frequency error from

If phase error is
\delta\theta(t),
then instantaneous frequency error is
\delta f(t)
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\frac{d}{dt}\delta\theta(t).

Proof

 Differentiate the perturbed phase
\theta(t)+\delta\theta(t)
and subtract the nominal frequency. ∎
Constant phase offset does not change frequency. Timevarying phase error does.

10.3 Sampling a Carrier
Let a continuous signal be sampled at rate
f_s.
The sampling times are
t_n=\frac n{f_s}.
The sampled carrier is
v_n
=
V_0
\cos
\left(
2\pi\frac{f_0}{f_s}n+\phi_0
\right).

 \Omega_0
=
2\pi\frac{f_0}{f_s}.

10.4 Nyquist Condition
Theorem 10.2 — Nyquist necessity for an
unambiguous ideal sinusoid
To distinguish a sinusoid of frequency f_0 from its aliases
using uniform sampling, it is necessary that
f_s>2f_0
when the signal is assumed to lie within the baseband
interval
0\le f<\frac{f_s}{2}.

Proof
Sampled complex exponentials satisfy
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)n/f_s}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}
for every integer k.
Real sinusoids additionally identify positive and negative
frequencies. Restricting the represented signal to frequencies

 below f_s/2 avoids overlap between mirrored spectral
replicas. ∎
For
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the ideal lower Nyquist boundary is
f_s>2.4\ \mathrm{MHz}.
Practical waveform reconstruction generally requires a
substantially higher rate because switching edges and
harmonics extend well above the carrier.

10.5 Samples per Cycle
Define
N_s
=
\frac{f_s}{f_0}.
This is the number of samples per carrier period.
For example, if
f_s=100\ \mathrm{MHz},
then
N_s
=

 \frac{100}{1.2}
\approx83.33.
A noninteger samples-per-cycle ratio causes the sampled
phase to move through different sample locations on
successive cycles. This can be useful for equivalent-time
reconstruction but complicates cycle-aligned averaging.

10.6 Aliasing
A continuous frequency f is indistinguishable after sampling
from frequencies
f_k
=
|f-kf_s|
after folding into the Nyquist interval.

Proposition 10.3 — Alias family
The samples of
e^{i2\pi ft}
and
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)t}
are identical at
t_n=\frac n{f_s}.

 Proof
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)n/f_s}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}
e^{i2\pi kn}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}.
∎
A measured low-frequency component may therefore
originate from an inadequately sampled high-frequency
