10.7 Harmonics of a Switching
Waveform
An ideal square wave with amplitude \pm V and 50% duty
cycle has Fourier series
v(t)
=
\frac{4V}{\pi}
\sum_{\substack{n=1\\n\ \mathrm{odd}}}^{\infty}
\frac1n
\sin(n\omega_0t).
Only odd harmonics appear:
f_0,\ 3f_0,\ 5f_0,\ldots

 For a 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} carrier:
3f_0=3.6\ \mathrm{MHz},
5f_0=6.0\ \mathrm{MHz},
7f_0=8.4\ \mathrm{MHz}.
Real finite-rise-time switching reduces high-order harmonic
amplitudes but does not eliminate them.

10.8 General Duty-Cycle Spectrum
For a unipolar pulse train of amplitude V and duty ratio
D\in[0,1], the magnitude of the n-th harmonic coefficient is
proportional to
\left|
\frac{
\sin(\pi nD)
}{
\pi n
}
\right|.

Proposition 10.4 — Harmonic zeros
The n-th harmonic vanishes when
nD\in\mathbb Z.

Proof

 The harmonic coefficient contains
\sin(\pi nD),
which vanishes at integer multiples of \pi. ∎
Duty-cycle selection can suppress selected harmonics, but
parasitic effects and switching asymmetry limit exact
cancellation.

10.9 Rise Time and Measurement
Bandwidth
A common engineering approximation connects oscilloscope
bandwidth B and measured 10–90% rise time t_r:
Bt_r\approx0.35
for a single-pole Gaussian-like response.
Thus a signal with rise time t_r requires bandwidth roughly
B\gtrsim\frac{0.35}{t_r}.
If a switching edge rises in
10\ \mathrm{ns},
then a minimum approximate bandwidth is
B\gtrsim35\ \mathrm{MHz}.

 Accurately measuring overshoot and ringing often requires
substantially more bandwidth.

10.10 Timing Jitter
Let the nominal sampling or switching event occur at time
t_n, but the actual event occurs at
t_n+\delta t_n.
The carrier phase error is approximately
\delta\theta_n
=
\omega_0\delta t_n.

Theorem 10.5 — RMS phase jitter
If timing jitter has RMS value
\sigma_t,
then the corresponding RMS carrier-phase jitter is
\sigma_\theta
=
2\pi f_0\sigma_t.

Proof
The phase perturbation is linear in time displacement:

 \delta\theta=\omega_0\delta t.
RMS scaling by a constant gives the result. ∎
At
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
a timing jitter of
1\ \mathrm{ns}
corresponds to
\sigma_\theta
=
2\pi(1.2\times10^6)(10^{-9})
\approx0.00754\ \mathrm{rad},
or approximately
0.432^\circ.

10.11 Jitter-Limited Signal-to-Noise
Ratio
For an ideal sampled sinusoid with RMS timing jitter
\sigma_t, a common small-jitter bound is
\operatorname{SNR}_{\mathrm{jitter}}
\approx
-20\log_{10}

 \left(
2\pi f_0\sigma_t
\right)
\ \mathrm{dB}.

Derivation
For small \delta t,
v(t+\delta t)
\approx
v(t)+\dot v(t)\delta t.
For
v(t)=A\sin\omega t,
the error is
e(t)\approx A\omega\cos\omega t\,\delta t.
The RMS signal is
A/\sqrt2,
and the RMS jitter error is approximately
A\omega\sigma_t/\sqrt2.
Their ratio is
\frac1{\omega\sigma_t}.
Converting to decibels gives the expression. ∎

 10.12 Phase Noise
An oscillator with phase noise is modeled as
v(t)
=
V_0
\cos
\left(
\omega_0t+\phi(t)
\right).
The random process \phi(t) broadens the ideal spectral line.
Single-sideband phase noise is commonly reported as
\mathcal L(f_m)
in \mathrm{dBc/Hz} at offset frequency f_m from the
carrier.
Phase noise, cycle-to-cycle jitter, period jitter, and long-term
frequency drift are related but not identical specifications.

10.13 Relative Frequency Stability
Define fractional frequency error
y(t)
=
\frac{

 f(t)-f_0
}{
f_0
}.
If the absolute tolerance is
\pm0.01\ \mathrm{MHz}
around
1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
then the relative tolerance is
\frac{0.01}{1.2}
\approx0.008333,
or
\boxed{\pm0.8333\%}.
For precision phase-locking, this may be a broad tolerance
unless active synchronization continuously corrects the
phase.

10.14 Phase Accumulation from
Frequency Offset
Suppose two oscillators differ by
\Delta f.

 Their relative phase evolves as
\Delta\theta(t)
=
2\pi\Delta f\,t+\Delta\theta(0).

Proposition 10.6 — Phase-slip time
The time required to accumulate one full cycle of relative
phase is
T_{\mathrm{slip}}
=
\frac1{|\Delta f|}.

Proof
Set
2\pi|\Delta f|T_{\mathrm{slip}}=2\pi.
∎
For
|\Delta f|=10\ \mathrm{kHz},
one full phase slip occurs every
100\ \mu\mathrm s.
Frequency proximity does not guarantee persistent phase
alignment.

 10.15 Ideal Series LC Resonance
For an inductor L and capacitor C, the ideal natural angular
frequency is
\omega_0
=
\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},
so
f_0
=
\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}.

Theorem 10.7 — Resonance relation
The unforced ideal series LC charge equation,
L\ddot q+\frac qC=0,
has harmonic solutions with
\omega_0^2=\frac1{LC}.

Proof
Assume
q(t)=q_0e^{i\omega t}.
Then

 -L\omega^2q+\frac qC=0.
For nonzero q,
\omega^2=\frac1{LC}.
∎

10.16 Component Constraint at 1.2\
\mathrm{MHz}
To resonate at
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the product must satisfy
LC
=
\frac1{(2\pi f_0)^2}.
Numerically,
LC
\approx
1.759\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s^2}.
Thus a chosen L determines C:
C
=
\frac1{(2\pi f_0)^2L}.

 This relation describes an ideal lumped resonator. At high
frequency, component parasitics may be comparable to the
intended values.

10.17 Resonance Sensitivity
Take logarithms:
\log f_0
=
-\log(2\pi)
-\frac12\log L
-\frac12\log C.
Differentiating,
\frac{df_0}{f_0}
=
-\frac12
\frac{dL}{L}
\frac12
\frac{dC}{C}.

Proposition 10.8 — Small-tolerance
resonance shift
For small component changes,

 \frac{\Delta f_0}{f_0}
\approx
-\frac12
\left(
\frac{\Delta L}{L}
+
\frac{\Delta C}{C}
\right).

Proof
First-order logarithmic differentiation. ∎
A 1\% increase in both L and C produces approximately a 1\
% decrease in resonant frequency.

10.18 Series RLC Dynamics
A driven series RLC circuit satisfies
L\ddot q
+
R\dot q
+
\frac qC
=
V_d\cos\omega t.
Define
\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},

 and damping coefficient
2\zeta\omega_0
=
\frac RL.
Thus
\zeta
=
\frac R2
\sqrt{\frac CL}.

10.19 Damped Natural Frequency
For the underdamped case
0<\zeta<1,
the free response oscillates at
\omega_d
=
\omega_0\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}.
The amplitude envelope decays as
e^{-\zeta\omega_0t}.

10.20 Quality Factor
For a lightly damped series resonator,

 Q
=
\frac{\omega_0L}{R}
=
\frac1{\omega_0CR}
=
\frac1{2\zeta}.
Quality factor may also be defined through stored and
dissipated energy:
Q
=
2\pi
\frac{
\text{maximum energy stored}
}{
\text{energy dissipated per cycle}
}.
The exact equivalence depends on the linear steady-state
regime and convention.

10.21 Resonator Bandwidth
For a lightly damped second-order resonator, the half-power
bandwidth is approximately

 \Delta f
=
\frac{f_0}{Q}.

Proposition 10.9 — Fractional bandwidth
\frac{\Delta f}{f_0}
\approx
\frac1Q.
A high-Q resonator is spectrally selective but responds more
slowly to transients and parameter changes.

10.22 Ring-Down Time
The energy of a lightly damped resonator decays
approximately as
E(t)
=
E_0e^{-\omega_0t/Q}.
Therefore the energy decay time constant is
\tau_E
=
\frac Q{\omega_0}.
Amplitude decays with time constant

 \tau_A
=
\frac{2Q}{\omega_0}.
Conventions sometimes report one or the other, so the
measured quantity must be stated.

10.23 Driven Oscillator Amplitude
For
\ddot x
+
2\zeta\omega_0\dot x
+
\omega_0^2x
=
\frac{F_0}{m}\cos\omega t,
the steady-state amplitude is
A(\omega)
=
\frac{F_0/m}{
\sqrt{
(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2
+
(2\zeta\omega_0\omega)^2
}
}.

 The phase lag satisfies
\tan\phi
=
\frac{
2\zeta\omega_0\omega
}{
\omega_0^2-\omega^2
}.

10.24 Resonance Frequency with
Damping
The displacement-amplitude maximum occurs at
\omega_r
=
\omega_0\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}
when
\zeta<\frac1{\sqrt2}.
Thus the maximum-response frequency is slightly below the
undamped natural frequency.
The difference becomes negligible for high Q.

 10.25 Stored Energy in an Ideal
Resonator
Capacitor energy is
E_C
=
\frac12CV^2.
Inductor energy is
E_L
=
\frac12LI^2.
In an ideal resonator, energy alternates between electric and
magnetic storage while total energy remains constant.
At resonance,
\frac12CV_{\max}^2
=
\frac12LI_{\max}^2.
Therefore
I_{\max}
=
V_{\max}\sqrt{\frac CL}.

10.26 Average Sinusoidal Power

 For
v(t)
=
V_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos\omega t
and
i(t)
=
I_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos(\omega t-\phi),
average power is
P
=
V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos\phi.
Since
V_{\mathrm{rms}}
=
\frac{V_{\mathrm{pk}}}{\sqrt2},
and similarly for current,
P
=
\frac12
V_{\mathrm{pk}}I_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos\phi.
The factor
\cos\phi

 is the displacement power factor for a sinusoidal system.

10.27 Complex Power
Using RMS phasors,
S
=
VI^*
=
P+iQ_r,
where:
• P is real power;
• Q_r is reactive power;
• |S| is apparent power.
Reactive circulation can produce large voltage and current
even when net real power is comparatively small.
This does not create energy. It increases component stress
and stored-energy exchange.

10.28 Energy Conservation
For any driven electrical system over interval [0,T],
E_{\mathrm{in}}
=
E_{\mathrm{stored}}(T)

 E_{\mathrm{stored}}(0)
+
E_{\mathrm{dissipated}}
+
E_{\mathrm{exported}}.
In periodic steady state,
E_{\mathrm{stored}}(T)
=
E_{\mathrm{stored}}(0)
over an integer number of cycles, so
E_{\mathrm{in}}
=
E_{\mathrm{dissipated}}
+
E_{\mathrm{exported}}.
Resonance can redistribute energy and reduce required
reactive drive, but cannot produce net energy without an
external source.

10.29 Efficiency
Define efficiency
\eta
=

 \frac{
P_{\mathrm{useful,out}}
}{
P_{\mathrm{in}}
}.
For a passive system in steady operation,
0\le\eta\le1.
An apparent value above one indicates at least one of:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

stored energy being released;
measurement timing mismatch;
omitted input channel;
sensor calibration error;
sign convention error;
non-steady operation;
data-processing error.

10.30 Switching Loss
A simplified switching-loss estimate is
P_{\mathrm{sw}}
\approx
\frac12
V_{\mathrm{DS}}
I_{\mathrm D}
(t_r+t_f)
f_s.

 This assumes approximately linear voltage and current
overlap during turn-on and turn-off.
Additional losses include:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

gate-charge loss;
output-capacitance loss;
reverse-conduction loss;
dead-time loss;
conduction loss;
magnetic loss;
interconnect loss.

10.31 Conduction Loss
For a switch with effective on-resistance
R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}},
P_{\mathrm{cond}}
=
I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}}.
The resistance generally depends on junction temperature.
A thermal calculation must therefore be coupled to the
electrical loss calculation.

10.32 Gate-Drive Loss
A common first-order estimate is

 P_g
=
Q_gV_gf_s,
where:
• Q_g is total gate charge;
• V_g is gate-drive swing;
• f_s is switching frequency.
Because this loss scales linearly with frequency, it becomes
increasingly important at megahertz operation.

10.33 Output-Capacitance Loss
A simplified hard-switching estimate is
P_{\mathrm{oss}}
\approx
E_{\mathrm{oss}}(V)
f_s.
The energy E_{\mathrm{oss}} is generally nonlinear in
voltage and should be taken from measured or manufacturerprovided charge-energy curves rather than approximated
blindly by
\frac12CV^2.

10.34 Total Semiconductor Loss

 A first-order sum is
P_{\mathrm{device}}
=
P_{\mathrm{cond}}
+
P_{\mathrm{sw}}
+
P_g
+
P_{\mathrm{oss}}
+
P_{\mathrm{reverse}}
+
P_{\mathrm{dead}}.
This is an accounting framework. Individual terms may
overlap if inconsistent conventions are used.

10.35 Thermal Equilibrium
Let total dissipated power be
P_{\mathrm{loss}}.
With lumped thermal resistance
R_{\theta},
steady-state junction-temperature rise is approximately

 \Delta T
=
P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta}.
Thus
T_j
=
T_{\mathrm{ambient}}
+
P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta}.
Transient thermal impedance is required for pulsed
operation.

10.36 Electrothermal Fixed Point
Because switch resistance and loss depend on temperature,
thermal equilibrium satisfies
T_j
=
T_a
+
R_\theta P_{\mathrm{loss}}(T_j).

Theorem 10.10 — Local thermal stability
criterion
A fixed point T_j^* is locally stable under a first-order
thermal relaxation model if

 R_\theta
\left.
\frac{dP_{\mathrm{loss}}}{dT}
\right|_{T_j^*}
<1.

Proof
Write the fixed-point iteration map
F(T)
=
T_a+R_\theta P_{\mathrm{loss}}(T).
A scalar fixed point is locally attracting when
|F'(T^*)|<1.
For monotonically increasing loss, this reduces to the stated
inequality. ∎
If temperature-sensitive loss grows too rapidly, thermal
runaway may occur.

10.37 Dead Time
In a half bridge, dead time prevents simultaneous conduction
of both switches.
If dead time is too short, cross-conduction risk increases.

 If too long, reverse conduction and waveform distortion
increase.
The ideal value depends on:
• propagation delay;
• turn-off time;
• device variation;
• temperature;
• gate resistance;
• layout parasitics.
No universal dead-time value follows from carrier frequency
alone.

10.38 Parasitic Inductance
A current transition produces parasitic voltage
V_L
=
L_p\frac{di}{dt}.
For rapid switching, even small L_p can create significant
overshoot.
Similarly,
I_C
=
C_p\frac{dv}{dt}
describes displacement current through parasitic capacitance.

 These relations explain why high-frequency power-stage
behavior cannot be predicted from ideal LC values alone.

10.39 Ringing Frequency
A parasitic inductance L_p and capacitance C_p may ring at
f_r
=
\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{L_pC_p}}.
This ringing may be mistaken for a designed resonance.
Identification requires varying known circuit parameters and
checking whether the observed frequency follows the
predicted sensitivity.

10.40 Resonance Identification Test
Suppose an observed spectral peak is claimed to arise from L
and C.
Change the capacitance by a known factor:
C'\!=\alpha C.
The ideal prediction is
f_0'
=
\frac{f_0}{\sqrt\alpha}.

 Proposition 10.11 — Parameter-shift
falsification test
If the measured peak does not shift consistently with the
predicted relationship within uncertainty, the simple LC
model is incomplete or incorrect.

Proof
The frequency dependence follows directly from
f_0=(2\pi\sqrt{LC})^{-1}.
∎
This is stronger evidence than observing one unexplained
peak near a desired frequency.

10.41 Phase-Locked Loop Model
Let reference phase be
\theta_r(t)
and controlled-oscillator phase be
\theta_o(t).
Define phase error
\phi
=
\theta_r-\theta_o.

 A simple first-order sinusoidal phase model is
\dot\phi
=
\Delta\omega
K\sin\phi,
where
\Delta\omega
=
\omega_r-\omega_{\mathrm{free}}.
This is the Adler equation.

10.42 Locking Condition
Theorem 10.12 — Static phase lock
A stationary phase difference exists if and only if
|\Delta\omega|\le K.

Proof
At equilibrium,
0
=
\Delta\omega-K\sin\phi_*.

 Thus
\sin\phi_*
=
\frac{\Delta\omega}{K}.
A real solution exists exactly when the magnitude of the right
side does not exceed one. ∎
Inside the lock range,
\phi_*
=
\arcsin
\left(
\frac{\Delta\omega}{K}
\right)
for the stable branch.

10.43 Stability of the Locked Phase
Linearize around equilibrium:
\phi=\phi_*+\delta.
Then
\dot\delta
\approx
-K\cos\phi_*\,\delta.

 Theorem 10.13 — Stable branch condition
The equilibrium is locally stable when
K\cos\phi_*>0.
For K>0, this requires
|\phi_*|<\frac{\pi}{2}.

Proof
The scalar linearized system decays when its coefficient is
negative. ∎

10.44 Locking Time Constant
The small-signal phase-error decay rate is
\lambda_{\mathrm{lock}}
=
K\cos\phi_*.
Therefore
\tau_{\mathrm{lock}}
=
\frac1{
K\cos\phi_*
}.
Near the edge of lock,

 |\Delta\omega|\rightarrow K,
so
\cos\phi_*\rightarrow0
and lock recovery slows.

10.45 Injection Locking
An oscillator weakly driven near its natural frequency can
often be reduced to an Adler-type phase equation.
The lock range is proportional to coupling strength and
inversely related to effective resonator selectivity under
model-specific assumptions.
Exact lock-range formulas depend on oscillator topology and
amplitude dynamics.

10.46 Harmonic Locking
Two frequencies are harmonically related if
mf_1=nf_2
for positive integers m,n.
Equivalently,

 \frac{f_1}{f_2}
=
\frac nm.
Define generalized phase difference
\phi
=
m\theta_1-n\theta_2.
Harmonic synchronization means \phi remains bounded or
converges to a constant.

10.47 Subharmonic Lock
An oscillator may lock such that
f_o
=
\frac pq f_d,
where p,q are integers.
The relevant phase combination is
q\theta_o-p\theta_d.
Observing a rational frequency ratio is not enough; bounded
generalized phase must also be demonstrated.

 10.48 Rational Frequency Ratio
Versus Coherence
Proposition 10.14
Two signals can satisfy an exact rational frequency ratio
while having drifting or random relative phase if their timing
is not coupled.

Proof
Let
\theta_1(t)=\omega_1t+\phi_1(t),
\theta_2(t)=\omega_2t+\phi_2(t),
with
m\omega_1=n\omega_2
but random phase processes \phi_1,\phi_2.
Then the generalized phase is
m\phi_1-n\phi_2,
which need not remain bounded. ∎
Frequency ratio and phase coherence are distinct
measurements.

 10.49 Beat Frequency
For two close sinusoids,
\cos(2\pi f_1t)+\cos(2\pi f_2t)
=
2
\cos
\left[
\pi(f_1-f_2)t
\right]
\cos
\left[
\pi(f_1+f_2)t
\right].
The envelope varies at beat frequency
f_b=|f_1-f_2|.
A slow amplitude envelope may therefore arise from
ordinary superposition rather than nonlinear energy transfer.

10.50 Intermodulation
A nonlinear system driven at f_1 and f_2 may generate
frequencies
mf_1\pm nf_2.
Second-order terms produce

 f_1+f_2,
\qquad
|f_1-f_2|,
\qquad
2f_1,
\qquad
2f_2.
Third-order terms produce components such as
2f_1-f_2.
A spectral line at a combination frequency is evidence of
nonlinearity, not automatically of a new fundamental
resonance.

10.51 Amplitude Modulation
For carrier f_c and modulation f_m,
v(t)
=
A
\left[
1+\mu\cos(2\pi f_mt)
\right]
\cos(2\pi f_ct).
Expanding,

 v(t)
=
A\cos(2\pi f_ct)
+
\frac{A\mu}{2}
\cos[2\pi(f_c+f_m)t]
+
\frac{A\mu}{2}
\cos[2\pi(f_c-f_m)t].
The spectrum contains the carrier and two sidebands.
Sidebands do not require multiple independent oscillators.

10.52 Frequency Modulation
For
v(t)
=
A
\cos
\left[
2\pi f_ct+\beta\sin(2\pi f_mt)
\right],
the spectrum contains infinitely many sidebands
f_c\pm nf_m
with amplitudes determined by Bessel functions J_n(\beta).

 Phase modulation can therefore produce a rich harmonic
pattern from one carrier.

10.53 Spectral Resolution
For a finite observation time T_{\mathrm{obs}}, Fourier-bin
spacing is approximately
\Delta f
=
\frac1{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}.
To resolve two tones separated by
\delta f,
one generally needs
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\gtrsim
\frac1{\delta f}.
Window choice affects leakage and effective resolution.

10.54 Windowing
A finite record multiplies the time signal by a window w(t).
In frequency space, this convolves the true spectrum with the
window spectrum.
Trade-offs include:

 • main-lobe width;
• side-lobe suppression;
• amplitude accuracy;
• noise bandwidth.
A narrow spectral peak can be an artifact of window
selection or insufficient record length.

10.55 Coherent Sampling
Coherent sampling occurs when the record contains an
integer number of cycles:
f_0T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\in\mathbb Z.
Then an ideal tone aligns with a discrete Fourier bin,
reducing spectral leakage.
For N samples,
\frac{f_0}{f_s}
=
\frac{k}{N}
for integer bin index k.

10.56 Spectral Leakage
If coherent sampling is not satisfied, the finite-record
transform spreads tone energy across neighboring bins.

 Leakage can resemble phase noise or sidebands.
A frequency claim should therefore state:
•
•
•
•
•
•

sample rate;
record length;
window;
bin spacing;
interpolation method;
clock reference.

10.57 Frequency Estimation
Uncertainty
Even with high sample rate, frequency uncertainty is limited
by:
• observation duration;
• signal-to-noise ratio;
• phase noise;
• clock stability;
• model assumptions.
Sample rate determines the representable bandwidth, not by
itself the ultimate frequency resolution.

10.58 Clock Reference Error
If the sampling clock has fractional error
\epsilon_c,

 then all measured frequencies inherit approximately the same
fractional scale error:
\frac{\Delta f_{\mathrm{meas}}}{f_{\mathrm{meas}}}
\approx
\epsilon_c.
A frequency reported to many digits is not meaningful unless
clock accuracy supports those digits.

10.59 Allan Variance
For fractional-frequency samples y_k averaged over time
\tau, Allan variance is
\sigma_y^2(\tau)
=
\frac12
\left\langle
(\overline y_{k+1}-\overline y_k)^2
\right\rangle.
It distinguishes types of oscillator instability across
averaging times.
Standard deviation of repeated frequency estimates is not
always an adequate stability measure because oscillator noise
may be time correlated.

 10.60 Harmonic Energy
Distribution
For a periodic voltage with Fourier coefficients V_n,
Parseval’s identity gives
V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2
=
\sum_n
|V_n|^2
under consistent coefficient normalization.
The total RMS energy cannot be inferred from the
fundamental amplitude alone when harmonics are
significant.

10.61 Total Harmonic Distortion
For voltage harmonics,
\operatorname{THD}
=
\frac{
\sqrt{
V_2^2+V_3^2+\cdots
}
}{

 V_1
}.
A phase-locked carrier may still have high distortion.
Coherence and waveform purity are independent metrics.

10.62 Resonant Voltage
Magnification
In a series resonator at resonance,
I_{\mathrm{rms}}
=
\frac{
V_{\mathrm{source,rms}}
}{R}.
The inductor voltage magnitude is
V_L
=
\omega_0LI
=
QV_{\mathrm{source}}.
Similarly,
V_C
=
QV_{\mathrm{source}}.

 The reactive voltages may greatly exceed source voltage,
while ideally canceling in the series sum.
This is voltage magnification, not energy creation.

10.63 Resonant Current
Magnification
In parallel resonance, branch currents may greatly exceed
source current while canceling at the input node.
Again, internal circulating reactive current does not imply
excess output power.

10.64 Coupled Resonators
For two coupled modes with uncoupled frequency \omega_0,
coupling can split the resonance into two normal-mode
frequencies.
A simple symmetric model is
\ddot x_1+\omega_0^2x_1+\kappa x_2=0,
\ddot x_2+\omega_0^2x_2+\kappa x_1=0.
Define normal coordinates
x_\pm=x_1\pm x_2.
Then

 \ddot x_\pm
+
(\omega_0^2\pm\kappa)x_\pm
=
0.
Thus
\omega_\pm
=
\sqrt{\omega_0^2\pm\kappa}.
A pair of nearby spectral peaks may therefore indicate mode
splitting rather than two independent source frequencies.

10.65 Stability of Coupled Modes
The symmetric coupled system is stable only if
\omega_0^2-|\kappa|>0.
If coupling magnitude exceeds the uncoupled stiffness, one
normal-mode squared frequency becomes negative and the
equilibrium is unstable.
Coupling does not always increase coherence or stability.

10.66 Parametric Resonance
A parametrically modulated oscillator may satisfy

 \ddot x
+
2\zeta\omega_0\dot x
+
\omega_0^2
\left[
1+h\cos(\Omega t)
\right]
x
=
0.
Instability regions occur near
\Omega\approx\frac{2\omega_0}{n},
especially the principal region
\Omega\approx2\omega_0.
This is fundamentally different from ordinary forced
resonance.

10.67 Parametric Threshold
Damping creates a nonzero modulation threshold for
parametric growth.
The exact threshold depends on detuning and model
normalization.

 Therefore observing growth at a rational frequency relation
does not prove lossless amplification; input energy is
supplied through the time-varying parameter.

10.68 Power-Balance Audit
A defensible experimental power audit should measure:
P_{\mathrm{DC,in}},
P_{\mathrm{gate}},
P_{\mathrm{aux}},
P_{\mathrm{load,out}},
P_{\mathrm{thermal}},
and stored-energy change
\frac{dE_{\mathrm{stored}}}{dt}.
The residual balance is
R_P
=
P_{\mathrm{in,total}}
P_{\mathrm{out,total}}
\frac{dE_{\mathrm{stored}}}{dt}.
A correct accounting should give

 R_P
consistent with measurement uncertainty.

10.69 Uncertainty Propagation for
Power
If
P=VI
and voltage and current uncertainties are independent,
\left(
\frac{\sigma_P}{P}
\right)^2
\approx
\left(
\frac{\sigma_V}{V}
\right)^2
+
\left(
\frac{\sigma_I}{I}
\right)^2.
For AC power with phase,
P=VI\cos\phi,
phase uncertainty contributes approximately

 \left(
\frac{\sigma_P}{P}
\right)^2
\approx
\left(
\frac{\sigma_V}{V}
\right)^2
+
\left(
\frac{\sigma_I}{I}
\right)^2
+
\tan^2\phi\,\sigma_\phi^2.
Near
\phi=\frac{\pi}{2},
real-power estimation becomes highly sensitive to phase
error.

10.70 Probe Delay Error
If voltage and current measurement channels have relative

phase error.

10.71 Energy per Switching Cycle
If average power is P at switching frequency f_s, then
average energy transferred or dissipated per cycle is

=
\frac P{f_s}.
At megahertz frequency, modest average power corresponds
to small energy per cycle but a very large number of repeated
events.

If per-transition energy is approximately constant,
E_{\mathrm{tr}},

E_{\mathrm{tr}}

10.73 Frequency Optimization
Let useful power scale as P_u(f) and loss as P_\ell(f).
Define net objective
J(f)
=
P_u(f)-\lambda P_\ell(f).
An optimal carrier satisfies
J'(f_*)=0,
with
J''(f_*)<0
for a local maximum.
A chosen frequency is justified when it optimizes a clearly
stated measured or modeled objective under constraints.

=

=

=

a-\lambda b
}{
2\lambda c
}
when the numerator is positive.

The coefficients must come from measurement or a validated

10.75 Dimensional Analysis
A frequency cannot be derived from dimensionless numbers
alone.
To produce units of inverse time, a model must contain at
least one dimensional scale, such as
\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},
\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},
\frac{v}{\ell},
or
\frac E{\hbar}.

Theorem 10.15 — Dimensional necessity
A formula constructed only from pure numbers cannot yield
an absolute frequency.

Proof

 Dimensionless inputs combined through algebraic operations
remain dimensionless. A dimensional output requires at least
one dimensional input or unit-defining constant. ∎
Therefore 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} cannot follow solely from
geometric ratios such as 48, \varphi, 4/3, or an angle.

10.76 Scaling Nonuniqueness
Suppose a frequency is derived as
f=\frac{v}{\ell}.
Scaling the length
\ell\mapsto a\ell
changes the frequency to
f\mapsto\frac fa.
Thus the same dimensionless geometry can support infinitely
many absolute frequencies at different physical scales.
A claim of a universal frequency requires a universal
dimensional constant or independently fixed scale.

10.77 Harmonic Coincidence
Given an observed frequency f_0, many reference
frequencies can be chosen such that

 f_0=nf_r,
or
f_0=\frac pq f_r.
Without a prior reason to select n,p,q, harmonic numerology
is underdetermined.

Proposition 10.16 — Rational-fit
nonuniqueness
For any positive frequencies f_0 and f_r, rational
approximations can make
f_0/f_r
arbitrarily close to p/q.

Proof
The rational numbers are dense in the real numbers. ∎
A near-rational ratio is not compelling evidence without
uncertainty bounds and a mechanism that predicts that
specific ratio in advance.

10.78 Model-Selection Criterion for
a Frequency

 A selected carrier is scientifically supported when competing
models are compared.
For models M_k predicting frequencies f_k(\theta_k),
evaluate:
• prediction error;
• parameter count;
• uncertainty;
• out-of-sample tests;
• sensitivity under controlled changes.
A model that predicts 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} only after fitting
the same observation has not independently predicted it.

10.79 Falsifiable Resonance Claim
A strong claim should take the form:
Given independently measured L,C,R, the system predicts a
resonance at f_*\pm\sigma_f. Altering C by a known amount
shifts the peak according to the stated derivative, while
control configurations lacking the resonant path do not show
the same response.
This is testable.
A statement that 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} is a “root frequency”
without a dimensional derivation is not yet testable enough.

10.83 Causal Locking Boundary
Correlation or phase coherence does not establish direction
of causality.
Possible explanations include:
• oscillator A drives B;
• B drives A;
• a third source drives both;
• measurement channels share a clock;
• analysis filtering induces apparent coherence.
Perturbation experiments are needed to distinguish these
cases.

10.84 Frequency-Pulling Test
If oscillator A causally influences oscillator B, changing A’s
free-running frequency may pull B within a locking range.

 The observed lock boundary can be compared with an Adlertype model.
A shared measurement artifact will not necessarily reproduce
the predicted detuning-dependent phase lag and unlocking
behavior.

Condition 6 excludes unsupported energy claims.

hardware constraints.

10.86 Fundamental-Frequency NoGo Theorem
Theorem 10.18 — No absolute frequency
from dimensionless architecture alone
Let a proposed derivation use only dimensionless integers,
ratios, angles, symmetry counts, and algebraic constants.
Then it cannot uniquely derive an absolute frequency in

• 53.13^\circ;
• Flower-of-Life angles;

internally
Adding the two equations cancels F_a:
m_s\ddot z_s+m_u\ddot z_u
=
-k_t(z_u-z_r).

Proof
The actuator acts with equal and opposite forces on the two
masses. ∎
An internal suspension actuator redistributes motion between
sprung and unsprung masses; it does not create net external
momentum.

 11.22 Quarter-Car Stored Energy
Define
E_q
=
\frac12m_s\dot z_s^2
+
\frac12m_u\dot z_u^2
+
\frac12k_s(z_s-z_u)^2
+
\frac12k_t(z_u-z_r)^2.
Because the road coordinate is time varying, differentiating
the tire energy introduces road-input power.
Let
v_r=\dot z_s-\dot z_u.
The passive damper power is
-c_sv_r^2.
The actuator power transferred into the mechanical
suspension is
P_a
=
F_av_r.

 Theorem 11.14 — Quarter-car energy
balance
\frac{dE_q}{dt}
=
-c_sv_r^2
+
F_av_r
k_t(z_u-z_r)\dot z_r.

Proof
Multiply each mass equation by its corresponding velocity,
add, and differentiate the spring energies. ∎
The road-input power is
P_{\mathrm{road}}
=
-k_t(z_u-z_r)\dot z_r.
The actuator is regenerative when
F_av_r<0.

11.23 Regenerative Force Sign
Definition 11.2 — Instantaneously
regenerative force

 A suspension force is instantaneously regenerative if
P_a=F_av_r<0.
The extracted mechanical power is
P_{\mathrm{ext}}=-F_av_r>0.
A force may improve ride while consuming energy when
F_av_r>0.
Thus active control and regeneration are not synonymous.

11.24 Semi-Active Damping
Constraint
A semi-active damper cannot supply net mechanical energy.
Its force must satisfy
F_{\mathrm{sa}}v_r\le0.
A variable-damping law has form
F_{\mathrm{sa}}
=
-c(t)v_r,
with

 c_{\min}\le c(t)\le c_{\max},
\qquad
c_{\min}\ge0.
Then
F_{\mathrm{sa}}v_r
=
-c(t)v_r^2
\le0.

Theorem 11.15 — Passivity of bounded
variable damping
Any damping law
F=-c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x
with
c(t,x,\dot x)\ge0
is instantaneously dissipative.

Proof
F\dot x
=
-c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x^2
\le0.
∎

 The coefficient may be nonlinear, state dependent, or time
varying without violating passivity, provided it remains
nonnegative.

11.25 Skyhook Damping
An ideal skyhook controller applies force approximately
proportional to sprung-mass absolute velocity:
F_{\mathrm{sky}}
=
-c_{\mathrm{sky}}\dot z_s.
A physical suspension actuator acts between the two masses,
so the desired force is implemented conditionally or
approximately.
A common semi-active logic selects high damping when the
available damper force opposes sprung-mass motion:
\dot z_s
(\dot z_s-\dot z_u)>0.
Otherwise, low damping is selected.

11.26 Passivity Projection
Suppose an active controller requests force
F_d.

 To enforce semi-active behavior, project it onto the
dissipative force set.
For relative velocity v_r\neq0, require
Fv_r\le0.
With force bound |F|\le F_{\max}, the admissible interval is:
F\in[-F_{\max},0]
when v_r>0, and
F\in[0,F_{\max}]
when v_r<0.

Proposition 11.16 — Closest passive force
The Euclidean projection of F_d onto the admissible interval
gives the minimum-change passive approximation.

Proof
Projection onto a closed convex interval uniquely minimizes
squared distance to F_d. ∎
This provides a rigorous safety layer around an
unconstrained controller.

11.27 Clipped-Optimal Regenerative
Control

 Suppose an unconstrained optimal-control law requests
F^*(t).
A regenerative implementation may use
F_{\mathrm{regen}}
=
\Pi_{\mathcal F(v_r)}
(F^*),
where
\mathcal F(v_r)
=
\{F:Fv_r\le0,\ |F|\le F_{\max}\}.
This preserves the requested force whenever it is already
regenerative and clips it otherwise.

11.28 Active Suspension Power
An active actuator may draw electrical power
P_{\mathrm{elec,in}}
while delivering mechanical power
P_{\mathrm{mech}}
=
F_av_r.
Under motoring operation,

 P_{\mathrm{mech}}>0.
Under regeneration,
P_{\mathrm{mech}}<0.
A bidirectional power converter can exchange energy with
storage in both directions.

11.29 Bidirectional Efficiency
Let \eta_m be motoring efficiency and \eta_g be generating
efficiency.
For motoring:
P_{\mathrm{elec,in}}
=
\frac{
P_{\mathrm{mech,out}}
}{
\eta_m
}.
For generation:
P_{\mathrm{elec,out}}
=
\eta_g
P_{\mathrm{mech,in}}.
Both satisfy

 0<\eta_m,\eta_g\le1.
Round-trip efficiency is
\eta_{\mathrm{rt}}
=
\eta_m\eta_g
before storage losses.

11.30 Net Energy Recovery
Over interval [0,T], define generated electrical energy
E_g
=
\int_0^T
\max(0,-F_av_r)\eta_g\,dt.
Define consumed actuator energy
E_c
=
\int_0^T
\frac{
\max(0,F_av_r)
}{
\eta_m
}
\,dt.
Auxiliary electronics consume energy E_{\mathrm{aux}}.

 Net recovery is
E_{\mathrm{net}}
=
E_g-E_c-E_{\mathrm{aux}}.
A regenerative suspension can have positive gross generation
but negative net energy after actuation and electronics.

11.31 Energy-Neutral Control
Definition 11.3 — Energy-neutral operating
horizon
The controller is energy neutral over [0,T] if
E_g
\ge
E_c+E_{\mathrm{aux}}.
This is a horizon-based statement, not an instantaneous one.
A controller may consume energy during one event and
recover it during another.

11.32 Storage Dynamics
Let storage energy be E_b.
A simplified model is

 \dot E_b
=
\eta_cP_{\mathrm{charge}}
\frac{
P_{\mathrm{discharge}}
}{
\eta_d
}
P_{\mathrm{self}},
with bounds
E_{\min}
\le
E_b
\le
E_{\max}.
A controller requesting regeneration when storage is full
must divert or dissipate the energy elsewhere.

11.33 State-of-Charge Constraint
Let normalized state of charge be
s=\frac{E_b-E_{\min}}{E_{\max}-E_{\min}}.
Then

 0\le s\le1.
A constrained controller must satisfy forward invariance of
this interval.
For example, at s=1,
\dot s\le0,
and at s=0,
\dot s\ge0.

Theorem 11.17 — Interval invariance
condition
For scalar storage state s\in[0,1], if
f(0,u)\ge0
and
f(1,u)\le0
for every admissible boundary control, then solutions cannot
leave the interval through either boundary under standard
uniqueness assumptions.

Proof
At the lower boundary, the vector field does not point
outward. At the upper boundary, it also does not point

 outward. This is the one-dimensional tangent-cone condition
for invariance. ∎

11.34 Heave Natural Frequency
For a single sprung mass with effective suspension stiffness
k_s,
\omega_h
=
\sqrt{\frac{k_s}{m_s}},
and
f_h
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\sqrt{\frac{k_s}{m_s}}.
This is the ideal undamped heave frequency.

11.35 Wheel-Hop Frequency
Ignoring coupling for a first approximation, unsprung wheelhop frequency is
\omega_w
\approx
\sqrt{

 \frac{k_t+k_s}{m_u}
}.
Because m_u\ll m_s and k_t is high, wheel-hop frequency is
typically higher than body heave frequency.
Exact normal frequencies follow from the coupled
eigenvalue problem.

11.36 Quarter-Car Eigenvalue
Problem
For the undamped fixed-road system,
M\ddot q+Kq=0,
with
q
=
\begin{bmatrix}
z_s\\z_u
\end{bmatrix},
M
=
\begin{bmatrix}
m_s&0\\
0&m_u
\end{bmatrix},

 and
K
=
\begin{bmatrix}
k_s&-k_s\\
-k_s&k_s+k_t
\end{bmatrix}.
Normal frequencies satisfy
\det(K-\omega^2M)=0.

Theorem 11.18 — Quarter-car characteristic
equation
m_sm_u\omega^4
\left[
m_s(k_s+k_t)+m_uk_s
\right]\omega^2
+
k_sk_t
=
0.

Proof
Compute the determinant:

 \det
\begin{bmatrix}
k_s-m_s\omega^2&-k_s\\
-k_s&k_s+k_t-m_u\omega^2
\end{bmatrix}
=0.
Expanding and simplifying gives the polynomial. ∎
Its two positive roots correspond approximately to body
heave and wheel hop.

11.37 Positivity of Quarter-Car
Frequencies
Assume
m_s,m_u,k_s,k_t>0.
The quadratic in \lambda=\omega^2 has:
• positive sum of roots;
• positive product of roots.
Its discriminant is nonnegative because the generalized
stiffness problem has real eigenvalues.
Therefore both squared frequencies are positive.

11.38 Damped State-Space Model

 Define state
x
=
\begin{bmatrix}
z_s-z_u\\
z_u-z_r\\
\dot z_s\\
\dot z_u
\end{bmatrix}.
Then
\dot x=Ax+B_uu+B_rw,
where:
• u=F_a;
• w represents road velocity or acceleration, depending on
state definition.
This form supports linear control, estimation, and
optimization.
The exact matrices must be derived consistently from the
chosen coordinates.

11.39 Controllability
For
\dot x=Ax+Bu,

 the controllability matrix is
\mathcal C
=
\begin{bmatrix}
B&AB&A^2B&\cdots&A^{n-1}B
\end{bmatrix}.
The system is controllable if
\operatorname{rank}\mathcal C=n.
A suspension actuator may fail to control a mode if its force
direction is orthogonal to that mode in generalized
coordinates.

11.40 Observability
With measurements
y=Cx,
the observability matrix is
\mathcal O
=
\begin{bmatrix}
C\\
CA\\
CA^2\\
\vdots\\

 CA^{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
The state is observable if
\operatorname{rank}\mathcal O=n.
A controller requiring unmeasured suspension velocity must
use sensing, differentiation, or an observer.

11.41 Linear Quadratic Control
For
\dot x=Ax+Bu,
define cost
J
=
\int_0^\infty
\left(
x^TQx+u^TRu
\right)dt,
with
Q\succeq0,
\qquad
R\succ0.
The optimal state feedback is

 u=-Kx,
where
K=R^{-1}B^TP
and P solves the algebraic Riccati equation
A^TP+PA-PBR^{-1}B^TP+Q=0.
This controller generally consumes energy and is not
automatically regenerative.

11.42 Regeneration-Aware Optimal
Control
Include electrical power or storage energy in the objective:
J
=
\int
\left[
x^TQx
+
u^TRu
\lambda P_{\mathrm{regen}}(x,u)
\right]dt.
Because

 P_{\mathrm{regen}}
=
-\min(0,uv_r)
is nonsmooth, practical formulations may introduce auxiliary
variables or piecewise models.
The resulting controller balances ride and energy recovery
explicitly.

11.43 Passivity-Based Control
Let a mechanical system have storage function H(x)
satisfying
\dot H
=
y^Tu
D(x),
\qquad
D(x)\ge0.
If feedback is
u=-Ky,
\qquad
K\succeq0,
then

 \dot H
=
-y^TKy-D(x)
\le0.

Theorem 11.19 — Passive output feedback
stability
If H is positive definite and radially unbounded, and the
largest invariant set in
\{\dot H=0\}
is the equilibrium, then the equilibrium is asymptotically
stable.

Proof
The storage function is a Lyapunov function. Apply
LaSalle’s invariance principle. ∎
This provides a strong route to safe damping control.

11.44 Port-Hamiltonian Form
An electromechanical suspension may be written
\dot z
=
[J(z)-R(z)]
\nabla H(z)

 +
G(z)u,
where:
• J^T=-J represents energy-conserving interconnection;
• R\succeq0 represents dissipation;
• H is stored energy;
• u is external input.
Then
\dot H
=
-\nabla H^TR\nabla H
+
y^Tu,
with
y=G^T\nabla H.
This structure exposes conservation and dissipation directly.

11.45 Skew-Symmetric
Interconnection
Lemma 11.20
For any vector g and skew-symmetric matrix J,
g^TJg=0.

 Proof
g^TJg
=
(g^TJg)^T
=
g^TJ^Tg
=
-g^TJg.
Therefore the scalar equals its negative and must be zero. ∎
The J-term redistributes energy but does not create or destroy
it.

11.46 Mechanical Impedance
For harmonic motion with phasor velocity V, mechanical
impedance is
Z_m(\omega)
=
\frac F V.
For a mass–spring–damper,
Z_m(\omega)
=
c
+
i

 \left(
\omega m-\frac{k}{\omega}
\right).
At resonance,
\omega m-\frac{k}{\omega}=0,
so the impedance is purely resistive:
Z_m=c.

11.47 Electrical Reflection into
Mechanical Impedance
The transducer with electrical impedance
Z_e(\omega)
reflects a mechanical impedance
Z_{\mathrm{em}}(\omega)
=
\frac{k_t^2}{Z_e(\omega)}
under the chosen sign convention.
If
Z_e=R+iX,
then

 Z_{\mathrm{em}}
=
k_t^2
\frac{R-iX}{R^2+X^2}.
Its real part gives damping:
c_e(\omega)
=
k_t^2
\frac{R}{R^2+X^2}.
Its imaginary part modifies apparent stiffness or inertia.

11.48 Inductive Roll-Off
For
Z_e=R+i\omega L,
the reflected damping is
c_e(\omega)
=
\frac{k_t^2R}
{R^2+\omega^2L^2}.
At low frequency,
c_e\approx\frac{k_t^2}{R}.
At high frequency,

 c_e\sim
\frac{k_t^2R}{\omega^2L^2}.
Thus coil inductance reduces high-frequency damping and
harvesting.

11.49 Reactive Compensation
A capacitor can compensate coil inductance near a target
frequency.
For series electrical impedance,
Z_e
=
R+i
\left(
\omega L-\frac1{\omega C}
\right).
At electrical resonance,
\omega L=\frac1{\omega C},
so
Z_e=R
and reflected damping is maximized for that resistance.
Reactive compensation changes bandwidth and voltage stress
and must be analyzed with parasitics.

 11.50 Adjustable Damping Through
Power Electronics
A controlled converter can emulate an effective resistance
R_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)
at the generator terminals.
Then
c_e(t)
\approx
\frac{k_t^2}{R_c+R_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)}
in the quasi-static regime.
This enables semi-active damping without physically
changing the transducer.
The converter still has switching and conduction losses.

11.51 Negative Resistance Boundary
If the converter emulates
R_{\mathrm{eff}}<-R_c,
the denominator becomes negative and
c_e<0.

 The transducer then injects mechanical energy rather than
harvesting it.
This is active behavior and can destabilize the suspension.

Theorem 11.21 — Negative damping
instability of a simple oscillator
For
m\ddot x+c_t +kx=0,
if
c_t<0,
the equilibrium is unstable.

Proof
The characteristic equation is
m\lambda^2+c_t\lambda+k=0.
The sum of roots is
-\frac{c_t}{m}>0.
Therefore at least one root has positive real part. ∎

ẋ

Active negative damping requires additional stabilizing
control.

 11.52 Saturation
Real regenerative force is bounded:
|F_a|
\le
F_{\max}.
Generator current is bounded:
|i|
\le
I_{\max}.
Since
F_a=k_ti,
the current limit gives
|F_a|
\le
k_tI_{\max}.
Voltage limits also constrain force at high speed because
e=k_tv.

11.53 Voltage-Limited Regeneration
For a DC bus with allowable converter voltage V_{\max},

 |k_tv-L\dot i-R_ci|
\le
V_{\max}.
At high velocity, back EMF may exceed converter voltage
capability, limiting current control.
Field weakening or alternative winding configurations may
be needed, each with trade-offs.

11.54 Force–Velocity Feasible
Region
A simple quasi-static electrical relation is
V
=
k_tv-R_ci.
With
F=k_ti,
V
=
k_tv-\frac{R_c}{k_t}F.
Voltage and current limits define a feasible region in the (v,F)
plane.
A requested damping law outside this region cannot be
realized.

 11.55 Harvested Power Bound
Under current limit,
|i|\le I_{\max},
the instantaneous electrical conversion power satisfies
|P_{\mathrm{conv}}|
=
|k_tvi|
\le
k_t|v|I_{\max}.
Under force limit,
|F|\le F_{\max},
mechanical extraction obeys
P_{\mathrm{ext}}
\le
F_{\max}|v|.
These are actuator-envelope bounds.

11.56 Cauchy–Schwarz Energy
Bound
Over a horizon [0,T],

 E_h
=
\int_0^T
c_e(t)v(t)^2dt.
If
0\le c_e(t)\le c_{\max},
then
E_h
\le
c_{\max}
\int_0^T v(t)^2dt.
Thus harvested mechanical energy is bounded by the
velocity-energy content of suspension motion.

11.57 Road-Input Upper Bound
From the energy balance,
E_{\mathrm{harvested}}
+
E_{\mathrm{other\,loss}}
=
E_{\mathrm{road\,input}}
\Delta E_{\mathrm{stored}}
over a horizon.

 Therefore
E_{\mathrm{harvested}}
\le
E_{\mathrm{road\,input}}
+
E_{\mathrm{initial\,stored}}
when final stored energy is nonnegative.
No passive suspension can harvest more energy than enters
from excitation plus released initial storage.

Theorem 11.22 — Passive harvesting upper
bound
For a passive system beginning with stored energy E(0)\ge0,
E_{\mathrm{useful,out}}(T)
\le
E_{\mathrm{external,in}}(T)+E(0).

Proof
Integrate the total energy balance. All dissipative losses and
final stored energy are nonnegative. ∎
This excludes sustained energy-positive operation without a
corresponding external energy source.

11.58 Terrain Energy Source

 A vehicle traversing rough terrain exchanges energy among:
• propulsion system;
• vehicle kinetic energy;
• gravitational potential;
• suspension storage;
• tire deformation;
• terrain deformation;
• thermal dissipation.
Harvesting suspension motion may slightly increase the
propulsion energy required to maintain speed because added
damping resists motion induced by the terrain.
The full vehicle-energy balance must include this effect.

11.59 Constant-Speed Propulsion
Penalty
If suspension harvesting adds mean resisting force projected
along vehicle travel,
\overline F_{\mathrm{res}},
then maintaining speed V_x requires additional propulsion
power approximately
P_{\mathrm{prop,extra}}
=
\overline F_{\mathrm{res}}V_x.

 This quantity may exceed, equal, or be less than recovered
electrical power depending on the mechanical pathways and
efficiency.
A suspension harvester can still be valuable for damping and
recovering energy that would otherwise become heat, but it
cannot be evaluated from generator output alone.

11.60 Regeneration Versus Added
Drag
Proposition 11.23
Positive electrical generation does not prove reduced total
vehicle-energy consumption.

Proof
The generator may increase mechanical resistance, causing
the traction system to supply additional energy. Net benefit
requires comparing recovered energy with added propulsion
and conversion losses. ∎
The correct metric is vehicle-level net energy, not isolated
generator output.

11.61 Random Road Input

 Road profiles are often modeled as stochastic processes with
power spectral density
S_r(\omega).
For a linear system with transfer function from road input to
relative velocity
H_v(\omega),
the relative-velocity spectrum is
S_v(\omega)
=
|H_v(\omega)|^2S_r(\omega).
Mean-square velocity is
\mathbb E[v^2]
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
S_v(\omega)\,d\omega.

11.62 Mean Harvested Power Under
Stationary Random Excitation
For constant effective damping c_e,
\overline P_e
=
c_e\mathbb E[v^2].

 Therefore
\overline P_e
=
\frac{c_e}{2\pi}
\int
|H_v(\omega;c_e)|^2
S_r(\omega)\,d\omega.
Because H_v depends on c_e, maximizing average power
requires optimizing the full integral.

11.63 Stochastic Optimization
Let road spectra vary with road class and speed.
Define expected objective
J(c_e)
=
\mathbb E_{\rho}
\left[
w_pP_h
w_aA_s
w_tT_d
\right],
where \rho indexes operating conditions.

 A robust damping law maximizes expected or worst-case
performance over a specified distribution or uncertainty set.
A controller optimized on one road profile may perform
poorly elsewhere.

11.64 Adaptive Damping
Let the damping coefficient be adjusted according to
estimated state:
c_e(t)
=
\pi(\hat x(t)).
To retain passivity, enforce
0\le c_e(t)\le c_{\max}.
Then instantaneous extracted mechanical power is
P_e=c_e(t)v_r^2\ge0.
The electrical useful output remains
P_L=\eta_e(t)P_e
after conversion loss.

11.65 Estimation Error
Suppose estimated relative velocity is

 \hat v=v+\varepsilon_v.
A requested force
F=-c\hat v
has true mechanical power
P
=
Fv
=
-cv^2-c\varepsilon_vv.
The second term may be positive enough to violate passivity.

Theorem 11.24 — Robust passivity condition
with bounded velocity error
Assume
|\varepsilon_v|\le\bar\varepsilon.
For force
F=-c\hat v,
a sufficient condition for
Fv\le0
is
|\hat v|\ge\bar\varepsilon

 and force sign chosen to oppose every true velocity
consistent with the estimate.

Explanation
When the uncertainty interval for v includes both signs, no
nonzero force based only on \hat v can guarantee opposition
to the true motion. A safe controller may set force to zero or
minimum damping in that region.

11.66 Passivity Observer
Define cumulative controller energy exchange
E_c(t)
=
\int_0^t
F_a(\tau)v_r(\tau)\,d\tau.
A passive controller should not allow cumulative supplied
energy to exceed an allowed energy tank.
A passivity observer tracks E_c, and a passivity controller
modifies commands when the energy budget would be
violated.

11.67 Energy Tank
Let E_T\ge0 be a virtual stored-energy state:

 \dot E_T
=
-P_a-P_{\mathrm{loss}},
under a selected convention.
Active action is permitted only when sufficient tank energy
exists.
Regenerative events refill the tank.

Theorem 11.25 — Passivity with a
nonnegative energy tank
If:
1. total storage is
H_{\mathrm{tot}}=H_{\mathrm{plant}}+E_T;
2. the tank is constrained by
E_T\ge0;
3. active power is drawn only from E_T;
then the combined plant–controller system remains passive
relative to external ports, assuming all internal accounting is
exact.

Proof
Active controller output decreases E_T by the same amount
it increases plant energy. Internal exchange cancels in the
total storage derivative. Nonnegative dissipation remains. ∎

 This is a formal method for mixing active ride control with
previously recovered energy.

11.68 Magnetic Spring Force
A nonlinear magnetic spring may have potential
U_m(x),
with force
F_m(x)
=
-\frac{dU_m}{dx}.
Its tangent stiffness is
k_m(x)
=
\frac{d^2U_m}{dx^2}.
Local stability at equilibrium x_* requires
U_m'(x_*)=0
and
U_m''(x_*)>0.

11.69 Negative Stiffness
A magnetic arrangement may exhibit a region where

 k_m(x)<0.
Negative stiffness can reduce effective suspension stiffness
when combined with a positive mechanical spring.
Total tangent stiffness is
k_{\mathrm{tot}}
=
k_s+k_m.
Local static stability requires
k_{\mathrm{tot}}>0.

Theorem 11.26 — Static instability under
negative total stiffness
For potential U near equilibrium,
U(x_*+\delta)
=
U(x_*)
+
\frac12k_{\mathrm{tot}}\delta^2
+
o(\delta^2).
If
k_{\mathrm{tot}}<0,
the equilibrium is not a local minimum.

 Proof
Small nonzero \delta lowers the potential. ∎
Negative stiffness must be bounded and stabilized by
positive stiffness or control.

11.70 Progressive Magnetic Spring
A progressive spring has increasing tangent stiffness:
\frac{dk_m}{dx}>0
over the operating range, or more generally stiffness
magnitude grows with displacement.
For a polynomial potential
U(x)
=
\frac12k_2x^2
+
\frac14k_4x^4,
\qquad
k_2,k_4>0,
force is
F=-k_2x-k_4x^3,
and tangent stiffness is

 k_{\mathrm{tan}}
=
k_2+3k_4x^2>0.
This yields soft central response and stronger end-stroke
resistance.

11.71 Nonlinear Damping
A nonlinear damper may satisfy
F_d
=
-c_1v-c_3v^3,
with
c_1,c_3\ge0.
Power is
P_d
=
F_dv
=
-c_1v^2-c_3v^4
\le0.

Proposition 11.27 — Passivity of odd
monotone damping
Any force law

 F_d=-g(v)
with
vg(v)\ge0
is dissipative.

Proof
F_dv=-vg(v)\le0.
∎

11.72 Hysteretic Damping
If force depends on internal hysteresis state h,
F=F(x,v,h),
instantaneous force–velocity sign may not always be
nonpositive because energy can be temporarily stored and
returned.
Passivity must then be tested with an augmented storage
function
H(x,h).
A loop area in the force–displacement plane represents net
energy dissipated per cycle:

 E_{\mathrm{cycle}}
=
\oint F\,dx.
The sign depends on the plotting convention.

11.73 Eddy-Current Damping
For a conductor moving through a magnetic field at
sufficiently low speed, induced current can produce
approximately viscous force:
F_e=-cv.
At higher speed or frequency, skin effect, inductance,
geometry, and field nonuniformity make the damping
frequency dependent.
The electrical energy is primarily dissipated as heat unless
the induced current is routed into a useful load.
Eddy-current damping alone is not necessarily regenerative.

11.74 Piezoelectric Harvester Model
A simplified piezoelectric transducer can be written
F=kx+\theta v_p,
q=\theta x+C_pv_p,
where:

 • v_p is electrical voltage;
• q is charge;
• \theta is coupling coefficient;
• C_p is capacitance.
The reciprocal coupling coefficient appears in both
mechanical and electrical equations under a consistent
energy formulation.

11.75 Piezoelectric Stored Energy
A quadratic electromechanical energy may be written
H
=
\frac12kx^2
\theta xv_p
+
\frac12C_pv_p^2
under one choice of independent variables.
Positive definiteness requires
k>0,
\qquad
C_p>0,
\qquad
kC_p-\theta^2>0.

 Theorem 11.28 — Coupling stability
condition
The quadratic form
\frac12
\begin{bmatrix}
x&v_p
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
k&-\theta\\
-\theta&C_p
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x\\v_p
\end{bmatrix}
is positive definite if and only if
k>0
and
kC_p-\theta^2>0.

Proof
Apply the positive-definite criterion for a symmetric
2\times2 matrix. ∎

 Too-strong coupling relative to the selected uncoupled
coefficients would make the assumed quadratic energy
unphysical.

11.76 Hydraulic Energy Recovery
For hydraulic pressure p and volumetric flow Q,
P_h=pQ.
An accumulator stores energy through fluid compression.
A hydraulic motor–generator may convert this flow into
electricity.
Losses include:
• pressure drop;
• leakage;
• throttling;
• pump/motor inefficiency;
• generator loss;
• accumulator hysteresis.
A throttling damper dissipates energy; a controlled hydraulic
circuit may recover part of it.

11.77 Rotary Conversion
A ball screw or rack mechanism may convert suspension
velocity v into generator speed

 \omega_g=Gv,
where G is a kinematic ratio with suitable units.
Generator torque \tau_g reflects mechanical force
F=G\tau_g
under ideal power preservation:
Fv=\tau_g\omega_g.
Friction, inertia, backlash, and screw efficiency modify these
relations.

11.78 Reflected Inertia
A rotary inertia J_g reflected through ratio G appears as
translational inertia
m_{\mathrm{ref}}
=
J_gG^2.

Proof
Rotary kinetic energy is
\frac12J_g\omega_g^2
=
\frac12J_gG^2v^2.
Equate to

 \frac12m_{\mathrm{ref}}v^2.
∎
High conversion ratios increase generator speed but also
increase reflected inertia quadratically.

11.79 Reflected Damping
A rotary damping torque
\tau=-b_g\omega_g
reflects as translational force
F=-G\tau
under sign convention, giving equivalent damping
c_{\mathrm{ref}}
=
b_gG^2.
Again, the ratio enters quadratically.

11.80 Mechanical Backlash
Boundary
Backlash creates a dead zone in which suspension motion
does not transmit continuously to the generator.
This introduces:

 • impact;
• hysteresis;
• noise;
• delayed damping;
• control nonlinearity.
A linear regenerative-damping model is invalid inside the
backlash transition unless augmented.

11.81 Fatigue and Harvesting
Energy recovery may increase force cycles or local stress.
For stress amplitude \sigma_a, fatigue life may be
approximated by an S-N relation
\sigma_a^mN=C
over a limited material regime.
A design maximizing recovered power but sharply reducing
fatigue life may be unacceptable.
Structural durability must be part of the objective or
constraints.

11.82 Thermal Limit of a Generator
Copper loss is
P_c=i_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R_c(T).

 Resistance varies approximately as
R_c(T)
=
R_0
\left[
1+\alpha(T-T_0)
\right].
Higher temperature increases loss, reducing allowable
continuous current.
A transient high-power event may be feasible even when
continuous operation is not.

11.83 Regenerative Damping
Coefficient Under Thermal Drift
Because
c_e
=
\frac{k_t^2}{R_c(T)+R_L},
increasing coil resistance reduces effective damping for a
fixed load.
Thus suspension behavior can drift with temperature unless
compensated.

 11.84 Fault Modes
A regenerative suspension should account for:
• open circuit;
• short circuit;
• converter failure;
• sensor failure;
• overtemperature;
• storage full;
• storage disconnected;
• communication loss;
• mechanical jam.
Open circuit gives approximately
i=0,
\qquad
c_e\approx0.
Short circuit gives high damping approximately
c_e\approx\frac{k_t^2}{R_c}
subject to inductance and current limits.
The safe mechanical behavior of both extremes must be
evaluated.

11.85 Fail-Safe Passive Mode

 A robust architecture may default to a passive damping path
upon loss of control.
If the fallback force satisfies
Fv_r\le0
and remains within structural limits, loss of computation
does not produce active instability.
This is an architectural safety property rather than a
performance guarantee.

11.86 Robust Stability with
Damping Uncertainty
Consider
m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=0,
where
c\in[c_{\min},c_{\max}].
If
m>0,
\qquad
k>0,
\qquad
c_{\min}>0,

 then every member of the uncertainty family is
asymptotically stable.

Proof
The characteristic polynomial
m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k
has positive coefficients for every admissible c. The Routh–
Hurwitz criterion for a second-order polynomial gives
negative-real-part roots. ∎
If c_{\min}=0, the system may be neutrally stable but not
asymptotically stable.

11.87 Time-Varying Damping
For
m\ddot x+c(t)\dot x+kx=0
with
c(t)\ge0,
energy satisfies
\dot E=-c(t)\dot x^2\le0.

Proposition 11.29 — Lyapunov stability
under nonnegative time-varying damping

 The origin is Lyapunov stable.

Proof
The total mechanical energy is positive definite and
nonincreasing. ∎
Asymptotic convergence requires sufficient persistent
damping; c(t) could vanish too often to force decay.

11.88 Persistent Damping Condition
Suppose there exist T>0 and \alpha>0 such that
\int_t^{t+T}c(\tau)\,d\tau
\ge\alpha
for every t.
Under suitable oscillator observability conditions, this
persistent excitation of damping can imply asymptotic or
exponential decay.
The exact theorem depends on the time-varying system and
cannot be inferred from c(t)\ge0 alone.

11.89 Adaptive Damping Stability
Let
c(t)=c_0+\Delta c(t),

 with
c_0>0
and
\Delta c(t)\ge-c_0.
Then total damping remains nonnegative.
If adaptation is additionally bounded,
|\Delta c(t)|\le B_c,
the force remains bounded by
|F_d|
\le
(c_0+B_c)|v|.
This gives a simple robust passivity envelope.

11.90 Energy-Harvesting Controller
Audit
A complete audit should report:
1. mechanical equations;
2. transducer equations;
3. force and EMF constants;
4. electrical impedance;
5. converter efficiency;

 6. storage dynamics;
7. road-input model;
8. power-flow sign conventions;
9. suspension comfort metrics;
10.tire-load metrics;
11. actuator force, current, voltage, travel, and temperature
limits;
12.net energy after auxiliary consumption;
13.sensitivity to speed and road class;
14.failure-mode behavior;
15.independent validation.

11.91 Gross Versus Net Harvested
Energy
Define:
E_{\mathrm{gross}}
=
\int P_{\mathrm{generator,out}}dt.
Define total auxiliary and conversion cost:
E_{\mathrm{cost}}
=
E_{\mathrm{converter\,loss}}
+
E_{\mathrm{control}}
+
E_{\mathrm{sensing}}

 +
E_{\mathrm{storage\,loss}}.
Then
E_{\mathrm{net}}
=
E_{\mathrm{gross}}-E_{\mathrm{cost}}.
If an active suspension also consumes mechanical actuation
energy, that must be included separately.

11.92 Comparison with
Conventional Damping
A regenerative damper should be compared with a baseline
damper that would otherwise dissipate
E_{\mathrm{baseline}}
=
\int c_bv_r^2dt.
Define recovery fraction
\eta_{\mathrm{rec}}
=
\frac{
E_{\mathrm{net}}
}{
E_{\mathrm{baseline}}
}.

 This metric can exceed one only if the regenerative design
also changes the motion so that more mechanical energy
enters the suspension than in the baseline. It would not mean
conversion efficiency above 100%.

11.93 Equivalent Damping Match
To preserve comparable ride behavior, compare systems at
equal effective damping or equal comfort metrics.
Otherwise a harvester may appear to recover more energy
merely because it allows larger suspension motion or
imposes harsher damping.
Fair benchmarking requires matched operating constraints.

11.94 Control-Barrier Constraint
for Suspension Travel
Let suspension travel satisfy
|r|\le r_{\max}.
Define barrier function
h(r)=r_{\max}^2-r^2.
The safe set is
\mathcal S=\{r:h(r)\ge0\}.

 A control-barrier condition may require
\dot h+\alpha h\ge0.
Since
\dot h=-2r\dot r,
the condition is
-2r\dot r
+
\alpha(r_{\max}^2-r^2)
\ge0.
Higher-order barrier methods are required when the control
enters acceleration rather than velocity directly.

11.95 Tire-Contact Constraint
A simplified tire normal force is
F_t
=
F_{t0}
+
k_t(z_r-z_u)
under an appropriate reference convention.
Loss of contact occurs when
F_t\le0.

 A controller optimizing harvested power must preserve
F_t>0
with an appropriate safety margin.
Maximum energy recovery is unacceptable if it causes wheel
lift or severe tire-force variation.

11.96 Peak Force Constraint
For damper force
F_d=-c_ev_r,
a force limit gives
c_e
\le
\frac{F_{\max}}{|v_r|}
when v_r\neq0.
Thus the maximum allowable damping coefficient decreases
at high relative velocity.
A constant high damping command may saturate during
impacts.

11.97 Model Predictive Control
At each time step, solve

 \min_{u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}}
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
\ell(x_k,u_k)
+
V_f(x_N)
subject to:
x_{k+1}=f(x_k,u_k,w_k),
u_kv_{r,k}\le0
for regenerative operation,
|u_k|\le F_{\max},
|r_k|\le r_{\max},
and storage constraints.
Only the first control input is applied, then the optimization
is repeated.

11.98 Recursive Feasibility
A model-predictive controller is recursively feasible if
feasibility at one step implies feasibility at the next under the
applied control and admissible disturbances.
This usually requires:
• a terminal invariant set;
• a backup control law;

 • disturbance margins.
Feasibility of one optimization instance alone does not
ensure future feasibility.

11.99 Stability of MPC
A common stability proof requires terminal cost V_f and
terminal controller \kappa_f satisfying
V_f(f(x,\kappa_f(x)))
V_f(x)
\le
-\ell(x,\kappa_f(x))
inside the terminal set.
Then the optimal finite-horizon value decreases along the
closed-loop trajectory and serves as a Lyapunov function.
Energy harvesting can be incorporated into \ell, but safety
and positive-definite regulation terms must remain sufficient
for stability.

11.100 Central Electromechanical
Conversion Theorem
Theorem 11.30 — Passive regenerative
transduction

 Consider a reciprocal linear transducer satisfying
F_{\mathrm{em}}=-k_ti,
e=k_tv,
and connected to a passive electrical network with stored
energy E_e and dissipation P_d\ge0.
Then the combined mechanical–electrical energy satisfies
\frac{d}{dt}
(E_m+E_e)
=
P_{\mathrm{external}}
P_d
P_{\mathrm{other\,mechanical\,loss}}.
Consequently, electrical energy delivered to a load cannot
exceed external mechanical input plus released initial stored
energy.

Proof
The electromechanical conversion terms are equal and
opposite in the mechanical and electrical energy balances
and therefore cancel internally. The remaining terms are
external power and nonnegative losses. Integrate over time. ∎

 11.101 Central Regenerative
Suspension Bound
Theorem 11.31 — Net recovery bound
Let a suspension system begin with stored energy E(0),
receive road and vehicle mechanical input
E_{\mathrm{in}},
deliver useful electrical output
E_{\mathrm{out}},
and incur total nonnegative losses E_{\mathrm{loss}}.
Then
E_{\mathrm{out}}
=
E_{\mathrm{in}}
+
E(0)
E(T)
E_{\mathrm{loss}},
and therefore
\boxed{
E_{\mathrm{out}}

 \le
E_{\mathrm{in}}+E(0)
}.

Proof
Integrate the total energy balance from 0 to T. Since
E(T)\ge0
and
E_{\mathrm{loss}}\ge0,
the inequality follows. ∎

11.102 Central Semi-Active Stability
Theorem
Theorem 11.32 — Stability under bounded
regenerative damping
Consider
m\ddot x+kx+c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x=0
with
m>0,
\qquad
k>0,

 \qquad
0<c_{\min}\le c(t,x,\dot x)\le c_{\max}.
Then the origin is globally asymptotically stable.

Proof
Use
V(x,\dot x)
=
\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2.
Then
\dot V
=
-c(t,x,\dot x)\dot x^2
\le
-c_{\min}\dot x^2.
The derivative is nonpositive.
The set where
\dot V=0
is
\dot x=0.
For a trajectory to remain there, the equation requires
kx=0,

 so
x=0.
By LaSalle’s invariance principle, the origin is globally
asymptotically stable. ∎
The theorem applies to the isolated scalar mode. Vehicle
safety requires the full coupled model.

11.103 Central Harvesting–Comfort
Trade-Off Theorem
Theorem 11.33 — Added passive harvesting
cannot increase mechanical energy
Let two systems have identical mass, stiffness, forcing, and
initial conditions, but total damping coefficients satisfy
c_2(t)\ge c_1(t)\ge0.
For each individual system,
\dot E_j
=
P_{\mathrm{in},j}
c_jv_j^2.
The larger damping coefficient guarantees greater
instantaneous dissipation only for equal velocity. It does not

 guarantee lower response energy, lower acceleration, or
greater harvested energy under coupled excitation because
v_1 and v_2 differ.

Proof
The first statement follows directly from damping power at a
common velocity.
The lack of a global ordering follows because damping
changes phase and amplitude of the response and therefore
changes input power and velocity. Counterexamples occur
near and away from resonance. ∎
This theorem explains why damping must be optimized
dynamically rather than maximized blindly.

• irreversible demagnetization threshold,

13.2 Static Magnetic Equilibrium
Definition 13.1 — Static equilibrium
A point
x=x_0
is a static equilibrium when
\dot x=0,
\qquad
\ddot x=0,
and
F_m(x_0,i_{u0},i_{\ell0})=mg.

 The phrase Zero Point Equilibrium may be used as an
engineering label for this balanced operating location, but
it should not be confused with quantum-field zero-point

Theorem 13.1 — Equilibrium existence
condition
A static supported state exists at x_0 if and only if the net
upward magnetic force equals the applied static load:
\boxed{
F_\ell(x_0,i_{\ell0})
F_u(x_0,i_{u0})
=
mg
}
under the selected sign convention.

Proof
At equilibrium,
\ddot x=0,
\qquad
\dot x=0,

of motion reduces to
0=F_m(x_0)-mg.
Therefore
F_m(x_0)=mg.
Conversely, if the force balance holds and the system is
stationary, the acceleration is zero. ∎
Force balance proves equilibrium, not stability.

Let

where \xi is a small perturbation.
Expand the net force:
F_m(x_0+\xi)

+
\left.

\right|_{x_0}\xi

\frac{\partial F_m}{\partial x}

\xi=0.

The equilibrium is locally restoring in the controlled

\left.
\frac{\partial F_m}{\partial x}
\right|_{x_0}<0.

Proof
If \xi>0, stability requires the incremental force to point in

\approx
\frac{\partial F_m}{\partial x}\xi

13.18 Noncontact Does Not Mean
Zero Wear
If the primary load path is magnetic and no sliding
surfaces contact during nominal travel, sliding wear in
that interface may approach zero.
However, the system can still experience:

• wire fatigue;
• insulation aging;
• eddy-current heating;
• magnet temperature cycling;
• adhesive fatigue;
• structural stress;
• fretting at mounts;
• converter degradation.
A defensible claim is:
The architecture may substantially reduce wear associated
with direct sliding or impact contact in the principal
suspension force path.
An absolute claim of zero wear requires all degradation
mechanisms to be excluded, which is rarely supportable.

13.52 Envelope Bandwidth
If the suspension control bandwidth is B_m, the envelope
must respond at least over that range.
The carrier satisfies
f_c\gg B_m.
The resonator bandwidth must also permit envelope
modulation.
For a resonator with bandwidth
\Delta f=\frac{f_c}{Q},
a very high Q can prevent rapid force-envelope changes.
Thus there is a trade-off:
• high Q: high circulating current and narrow
selectivity;
• lower Q: faster control response and broader
tolerance.

\tau_A
\approx
\frac{2Q}{\omega_c}.
At fixed carrier, increasing Q increases the response time.

\tau_A\ll\tau_{\mathrm{mechanical}}
so magnetic force can respond before the mechanical state
changes significantly.

When harvesting current flows, Lenz’s law produces force

+
(c_m+c_h)\dot x
+
k_{\mathrm{eff}}x
=
F_{\mathrm{ext}}.

13.55 Optimal Harvesting Boundary
Increasing c_h raises extraction coefficient but reduces
velocity.
The mean harvested mechanical power is
\overline P_h
=
c_h\left\langle\dot x^2\right\rangle.
Because
\left\langle\dot x^2\right\rangle
depends on c_h, the harvested power is generally
maximized at a finite damping value rather than by
maximizing damping without limit.

Theorem 13.17 — Resonant suspension
energy bound
For a periodic steady-state MAGPIE-type assembly with
high-frequency drive power P_d, mechanical disturbance
power P_m, useful electrical output P_o, and nonnegative
loss P_\ell,
\boxed{
\overline P_o
=
\overline P_d
+
\overline P_m
\overline P_\ell.

Consequently,
\boxed{
\overline P_o
\le
\overline P_d+\overline P_m.

Proof

 Integrate Poynting’s theorem and the mechanical energy
balance over the complete electromechanical system. In
periodic steady state, net stored-energy change over a full
number of cycles is zero. Internal electromechanical
conversion terms cancel, leaving external inputs, useful
output, and loss. ∎
This does not prevent useful net recovery of energy that
would otherwise be dissipated. It prevents unsupported
creation of net energy.

14.1 The Original Insight
The original Howard Comma intuition was that ordinary
geometry can omit something structurally important.
Two objects may appear:
• far apart in ordinary space but function as one tightly
coupled unit;
• close together in ordinary space but interact weakly;
• geometrically aligned but operationally disconnected;

 • geometrically separated but connected through a
strong intermediary or shared pathway.
The first insight was therefore:
\text{visible distance}
\neq
\text{functional distance}.
The “comma” was conceived as the missing correction
between those two descriptions.
That insight was useful, but it was not yet mathematically
complete because the following remained unspecified:
1. What exactly counts as interaction?
2. How is interaction converted into distance?
3. When is that distance mathematically valid?
4. How are different units normalized?
5. How is the residual tested across triples or networks?
6. How is the model prevented from fitting its desired
conclusion circularly?
The perfected version answers each question explicitly.

14.2 Perfection Step One: Replace
Metaphor with Measurable Inputs
Let the entities be
x_1,\ldots,x_n.

 For every pair (i,j), define measurable quantities:
C_{ij}
for contact or direct coupling,
A_{ij}
for accessibility, transmissibility, or pathway strength,
and
d_{ij}
for ordinary geometric separation.
The interaction kernel is defined as
\boxed{
K_{ij}
=
w_C C_{ij}
+
w_A A_{ij}
+
w_D\phi(d_{ij})
}
with
w_C,w_A,w_D\ge0,
and

 w_C+w_A+w_D=1.
A standard geometric decay term is
\boxed{
\phi(d)=e^{-d/L},
}
where L>0 is an interaction-length scale.
kingmaker_howard_comma_one_pager.pdf
This was the first major perfection: the Howard Comma
was no longer defined by an image or intuition alone. It
was grounded in declared pairwise measurements.

14.3 Why the Weight Constraints
Matter
The normalization
w_C+w_A+w_D=1
makes the kernel a convex combination of its
components.

Proposition 14.1 — Convex boundedness
Suppose
0\le C_{ij},A_{ij},\phi(d_{ij})\le1.

 Then
0\le K_{ij}\le1.

Proof
Because the weights are nonnegative and sum to one,
K_{ij} is a convex combination of three values in [0,1]. ∎
This provides a consistent numerical scale and prevents
arbitrary coefficient inflation from masquerading as
stronger interaction.

14.4 Perfection Step Two: Require
Symmetry
The kernel is required to satisfy
K_{ij}=K_{ji}.
This means the basic perfected formulation describes
reciprocal pairwise geometry.
If a system is direction dependent, one must either:
• symmetrize the directional measurements;
• construct separate forward and reverse kernels;
• or use a directed-geometry extension.

 The symmetric requirement was added because an
ordinary Euclidean kernel distance cannot generally be
derived from an arbitrary nonsymmetric matrix.

14.5 Perfection Step Three: Require
Positive Semidefiniteness
The decisive mathematical correction was the requirement
\boxed{
K\succeq0.
}
That means
a^TKa\ge0
for every vector a\in\mathbb R^n.
This is not merely a technical preference. It guarantees
that the interaction matrix can be interpreted as inner
products in a feature space.

Theorem 14.2 — Kernel embedding theorem
If K is symmetric and positive semidefinite, then there
exist feature vectors
\Psi(x_1),\ldots,\Psi(x_n)

 in a Euclidean or Hilbert space such that
\boxed{
K_{ij}
=
\left\langle
\Psi(x_i),\Psi(x_j)
\right\rangle.
}

Proof
Because K\succeq0, it has an eigendecomposition
K=Q\Lambda Q^T,
where
\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,
\lambda_n),
\qquad
\lambda_a\ge0.
Define
\Phi=\Lambda^{1/2}Q^T.
Let \Psi(x_i) be the i-th column of \Phi. Then
\Phi^T\Phi
=
Q\Lambda Q^T

 =
K,
so
K_{ij}
=
\langle\Psi(x_i),\Psi(x_j)\rangle.
∎
This turned “functional relationship” into a genuine
geometry.

14.6 Perfection Step Four: Derive
Functional Distance from the
Kernel
The kernel-induced squared distance is
\boxed{
D_K(i,j)^2
=
K_{ii}+K_{jj}-2K_{ij}.
}
Using the feature-space representation,
\begin{aligned}
D_K(i,j)^2

 &=
\langle\Psi_i,\Psi_i\rangle
+
\langle\Psi_j,\Psi_j\rangle
2\langle\Psi_i,\Psi_j\rangle\\
&=
\|\Psi_i-\Psi_j\|^2.
\end{aligned}
Therefore
\boxed{
D_K(i,j)
=
\|\Psi(x_i)-\Psi(x_j)\|.
}
The perfected formulation defines
d_{\mathrm{eff}}(i,j)
:=
D_K(i,j).
This is the interaction-defined or functional distance.

Theorem 14.3 — Metric properties

satisfies:
D_K(i,j)\ge0,
D_K(i,j)=D_K(j,i),
D_K(i,j)=0
\iff
\Psi(x_i)=\Psi(x_j),
and
D_K(i,k)
\le
D_K(i,j)+D_K(j,k).

Proof
